evidence.root_cause: the pass at position p writes ring slots for p, p+1, p+2; the slot for p+2 is the same slot as p-2 (p+2 = p-2 + conv_k), so the second draft evicted the row for p-2. With k=0 the next pass starts at p+1 and its row 0 convolves over {p-2, p-1, p, p+1}, reading the discarded draft in place of p-2
evidence.why_it_hid: both extra rows are real rows of the same sequence, so the corruption is a one-row-old convolution input - small enough to normally change nothing, which is why I twice mislabelled the resulting divergence as floating-point noise at a near-tie
evidence.fix: ring is (conv_k + TILE).next_power_of_two() = 8 slots, indexed with a mask so the kernel costs exactly what it did before
evidence.method: QW_NO_ACCEPT=1 (force k=0) made the rejection path the only path and turned a rare corruption into divergence at token 4; QW_TILE_CHECK proves the tiled arithmetic is bit-exact (max|dlogit|=0.0). Together they separate wrong arithmetic from wrong state

evidence.why_safe: Q4_GEMV_KS is bit-identical per row to the k=1 kernel - same g = lane; g < n_groups; g += 32 walk, same Q4_WORDS_PER_GROUP unpack order, same simd_sum(acc[t]) per row - so a tile launch performs exactly the operations in exactly the order three k=1 launches would
evidence.bug_i_wrote: the first version copied accepted rows into the ring at end-of-pass from spec_step. WRONG because qkv_cur is one scratch buffer shared by every layer: by then it holds the last layer's rows, so every other layer's ring got that layer's data. Diverged at token 4, the same signature as round 035's ring bug; the byte-identical gate caught it in one run. The copy now happens inside each layer's own block right after its convolution
evidence.why_not_acceptance_dependent: k is only known after the logits are read, i.e. after the whole forward is encoded, so the copy cannot be restricted to the k+1 surviving rows. Copying all TILE rows is what the old per-row projection did and the ring is wide enough to absorb it

evidence.latent_trap: scratch.k is shared by two branches whose rows differ in width: the GDN branch defines key_dim = hk*dk while the attention branch's k projection is nkv*hd. The attention dispatch used the local key_dim as the row offset while scratch.pv used nkv*hd, so any refactor that treats the two names as the same number reads the wrong row - and the symptom is a spec-vs-plain divergence at a drifting token index, not obvious corruption. This cost most of the round

evidence.why_slower: batching requires the row to be decoded from the flattened index - one integer division per thread - while gate_mul does one load, one exp and one store, and kv_append two loads and two stores. The division costs more than the launch it removes, the opposite of the convolution and norms in rounds 036-037 where each thread does enough work to hide the decode
evidence.implication: the cheap batching lever is exhausted; two rounds of batching bought ~2% each and dispatch time is only ~6.5 ms of a 61 ms pass, so the tiled GEMV's issue cost is the remaining lever, not dispatch count

evidence.the_trap: runner.rs:982 defines key_dim = hk*dk = 48*128 = 6144 while the attention k row is nkv*hd = 4*256 = 1024. The per-row k_norm/k_rope pass row*(key_dim*2) as a byte offset, but the kernel addresses row*in_stride from the given base with in_stride = hd, so two different row strides live in one call and no flattened index (r*nkv+h) can satisfy both: (r*nkv+h)*hd is right for x and wrong for y. The q path has no mismatch (nh*hd*2 bytes == in_stride*nh), which is why only half the batching landed on wrong addresses
evidence.gate_value: parity 6/6 passed with the bug present - six short greedy prompts never exercise a mis-strided row; only the 300-token spec==plain comparison caught it
evidence.gated_only: rmsnorm_gated has no mismatch (value_dim = hv*dv, kernel row stride D = dv, so (r*hv+h)*dv is exactly the per-row address). Alone it passed parity 6/6, accept.sh 12/12 ACCEPTED and cut dispatches 1634 -> 1538

history.title: Answering 'can it serve concurrent requests?' turned up the real agent-usability bottleneck. Measured: (1) the engine is strictly serial - 3 requests fired simultaneously end in a 2.73/5.38/7.96 s staircase, wall-clock ratio 1.03 against the same three sent sequentially, so concurrency changes nothing; (2) a second process does not help either - two requests on two processes take 4.18/4.60 s against 2.21/4.53 s for two requests on one process, a 0.99x speedup, because each request streams the same 14.4 GB of weights and the two simply split the same DRAM bandwidth (and cost another 15 GB of RAM); (3) the far bigger finding: prefill feeds the prompt ONE TOKEN AT A TIME, each a full 14.4 GB weight sweep, with no batched prefill and no prefix cache (run_job calls model.reset()). Measured cost per prompt token: 47.6 ms at 10 tokens, 51.1 at 409, 64.6 at 1209, 84.4 at 3009 - a 3009-token prompt costs 253.8 s (4.2 min) before the first output token, and because every request resets, each turn of a multi-turn agent re-prefills the whole history, making N turns O(N x history). Prefill is ~3.4x more expensive per token than decode, which amortises ~3.4 tokens per sweep through MTP speculation.

evidence.multiprocess: 2 procs = 4.18/4.60 s (wall 4.60) vs 1 proc serving 2 = 2.21/4.53 s (wall 4.53); 0.99x
evidence.prefill_3000: 253.83 s to first token for a 3009-token prompt
evidence.why_serial: one engine thread owns Qwen38 (Metal engine is not shareable across threads) and loops on an mpsc receiver; run_job calls model.reset() per request, so there is no KV/state reuse even across turns of one conversation
evidence.why_multiprocess_fails: memory-bandwidth bound: 14.4 GB streamed per forward, 554 GB/s DRAM peak, ~130 GB/s when throttled

history.next: batched prefill is the highest-value change available and it is nearly free to try: the verify kernels already compute 4 rows in one forward (q4_gemv_k4_u4hx), so feeding 4 prompt tokens per sweep should cut prefill ~4x, and a prefix cache across requests would take multi-turn agents from quadratic to linear. Both rest on 'batched rows equal single-row results', which is exactly the property open_issues/spec-plain-intermittent questions - so that flake should be settled first. Until then the practical guidance is: serialise agent calls, keep histories short, keep agent loops under ~6 turns, and set client timeouts above 600 s.

history.title: batch-16 round 1: the 16-row kernel is numerically correct but SLOWER than serial, so the naive design is refuted.  Started the parallel-serving objective.  Added Q4_GEMV_KS_U4HX(q4_gemv_k16_u4hx, 16) - each threadgroup still produces one output row but consumes 16 activation rows, so one weight read could serve 16 tokens.  Added two gates: `check --rows N`, which pushes N DISTINCT activations through one weight read and compares every row against its own CPU reference (distinct inputs turn any cross-row contamination into a gross error), and `bench --rows 18 --tokens 16`, a paired in-process full-model comparison of one 16-row sweep against 16 single-row sweeps.  Result: correctness passes on all 8 representative tensors (norm_err 0.27-1.39%, Metal JIT 159 ms), but performance is 0.78x - ONE k16 sweep costs 635.60 ms against 30.9 ms for one single-row sweep, i.e. 20.6x the time for 16x the tokens, so the whole batch is 22% SLOWER than serving the 16 tokens serially.  Effective bandwidth 22.7 GB/s against 466 GB/s for the single-row kernel, so the kernel is not bandwidth-bound at all.

gates.G3: REFUTED: bench --rows 18 --tokens 16 gives gain_raw 0.777, calibration 0.994, gain_calibrated 0.782
gates.G4: n/a - the feature is not shippable in this form

evidence.k16_slow: batch16 635.60 ms vs serial 494.13 ms for the same 16 tokens (14.4 GB of weights either way); duplicate k16 632.02 ms
evidence.root_cause: per weight chunk (8 weights = two uint4 loads) the k1 kernel issues ONE x load; the k16 kernel issues SIXTEEN.  Weight bytes dominate but x INSTRUCTIONS dominate the instruction stream, so the kernel degrades from bandwidth-bound to load-instruction-bound, on top of 16 live accumulators of register pressure
evidence.why_batching_is_still_right: process-level parallelism cannot share the weight read (measured 0.99x for two processes); only row-level batching inside one dispatch can, so the axis is right and only this kernel structure is wrong
evidence.instrument: bench --rows 18 alternates k16 / 16xk1 / k16dup inside one process; the dup calibrates the method at 0.994, so the 0.78x is real

history.next: next design: keep the k1 per-thread structure exactly (one accumulator, one x load per weight chunk) and get the weight reuse from L2 instead of from per-thread registers - make the threadgroup id carry both row and activation index (row = tg/16, xr = tg%16) so 16 consecutive threadgroups share one weight row and DRAM serves it once.  Expected: time close to ONE k1 sweep for 16 tokens.  Risk: if L2 does not hold the row, it degrades to exactly the serial case, so the downside is bounded.  Numbers to beat: >1.0x calibrated on bench --rows 18.

history.title: batch-16 round 2: the L2-sharing kernel WORKS - 1.666x over serial, 52.2 tok/s aggregate across 16 concurrent tokens.  Round 055 concluded the amortisation has to happen between threads rather than inside one, so `q4_gemv_b16` keeps the q4_gemv_hx body byte for byte (one accumulator, one 16-byte x load and two dots per weight chunk) and moves the parallelism into the grid: grid = 16*out_f threadgroups with row = tg/16 and xr = tg%16, so 16 consecutive threadgroup ids cover one weight row for 16 different activations.  DRAM fetches the row once and L2 serves the other 15.  Added encoder QLinear::encode_b (grid grows with the batch, unlike encode_k) and extended check --rows to verify BOTH batch-16 shapes, plus a four-arm paired bench.

evidence.jit: b16 compiles in 24 ms against 159 ms for k16, consistent with far lower register pressure
evidence.why_not_16x: one b16 sweep is 10.2x a single sweep rather than 16x, so the weight amortisation is real but partial; under a one-threadgroup-per-output-row decomposition every output element still reads the whole activation row, so the x traffic through L2 is sum(out_f*K*2) = ~57.6 GB for one k1 sweep and ~921 GB for b16.  At 306 ms that puts L2 at ~3.0 TB/s, near the limit of this decomposition
evidence.k16_confirmed_dead: the per-thread-row kernel measured 0.483x in the same paired run, reproducing round 055's 0.78x direction (the two runs differ in thermal state, so the ratios are not directly comparable, but both are below 1.0)

history.next: the next lever is x reuse by blocking output rows: one threadgroup computing R output rows reuses a single x load R times, cutting the L2 x traffic by 1/R (~921 GB -> ~230 GB at R=4).  This is the opposite direction from the refuted k16 (R activations needing R x loads); here R output rows share ONE x load.  Also still to do: per-sequence KV/GDN/conv state, per-row (seq,pos) descriptors, the continuous-batching scheduler, server integration, and the tutorial rewrite once the engine actually serves batches

history.title: batch-16 round 3: per-sequence state partitioning is DONE and locked by a gate.  The scheduler, the batched forward and concurrent serving all share one prerequisite - the model must be able to hold 16 sequences' state at once - so that layer went in first.  A row-by-row read of the single-row forward showed only EIGHT sites touch sequence state (kv append, attention scores, attention out, the qkv write into the conv ring, the conv read, and the GDN recurrence), so giving each sequence a byte offset is enough: allocate state/window/snap/k_cache/v_cache for `batch` slots and pass buf_offset(i, buf, seq*stride) at those eight sites.  From inside a kernel the cache simply begins at that sequence's slice, so NO MSL kernel changed and `seq` never enters a kernel.  Added Qwen38::load_batch(dir, max_t, batch); load() keeps its old signature and means batch 1, so no call site changed.  QW_BATCH=<n> opts in.

evidence.bug_the_gate_caught: the first run failed 12 of 16 slots, with slots 0-3 correct and 4-15 emitting token 0.  Cause: kernels.q4_gemv_tile is a COMPILE-TIME 4-row specialisation (K4_U4HX), so passing n=16 projected only the first four rows and left the rest of the tile stale.  Fixed by routing every projection through the new QLinear::encode_rows, which sends >TILE rows to the round-056 grid-mapped b16 kernel.  13 projection sites changed.
evidence.conv_is_per_row_now: the tile-wide convolution shares one window across the tile, which is right for a verify pass (4 consecutive positions of one sequence) and wrong for a batch pass (16 different sequences with their own rings), so each row's raw qkv is copied from the staging buffer into its own ring slot with the existing copy_off kernel and convolved there.  The tile-wide convolution kernel is now dead and was deleted.
evidence.reset_seq: zeroes only the GDN state and convolution ring of ONE slot.  The KV cache needs no reset because attention at position p reads entries 0..=p and p was just written by kv_append, so a stale entry is unreachable - that cuts the per-slot cleanup from ~700 MB to ~165 MB
evidence.order_matters: before starting this I worked out that shipping a round-robin scheduler FIRST would have been a severe regression: plain decode costs 30.9 ms/token, so 16 rotating sequences take 494 ms per round and a single request would have become 21x slower.  The batched forward is a hard prerequisite for concurrency being a win rather than a throughput split.

Rewrote crates/qw-server/src/engine.rs from a strictly serial recv-run_job loop into a 16-slot continuous-batching scheduler, added the tools/conc.sh gate, and rewrote the tutorial (the summary table, section 6.4, the batch-16 status note and the FAQ all said concurrency was 1).

Distinct prompts matter - a shared prompt would let every slot read the same state and still agree with itself.
gates.G4: measured 16 way: 22.02 s for 16 concurrent requests averaging 1.38 s each, against 4.59 s each serially.  The shortfall from 16x is inherent and documented: one 16-row pass costs ~306 ms, which is 10.2x a single-row pass rather than 16x, and requests of different lengths leave the tail of the batch underfilled.

evidence.architecture: the engine thread now holds 16 slots instead of one job at a time.  Each round it admits queued jobs into free slots (reset_seq first), has every slot that can take a step contribute one row (slot, pos) - prompt tokens during prefill, the previous round's argmax during decode - issues ONE forward_rows over those rows, then reads each row's logits back, takes the argmax as that slot's next token, and streams the newly decodable text.  Slots that hit EOS or their token budget are flushed and recycled.  Admission only blocks when the engine is completely idle; otherwise it takes what has already arrived, so a burst is batched rather than serialised one by one.
evidence.distinct_sequences_required: forward_rows with more than TILE rows requires the rows to be DISTINCT sequences, because the convolution ring holds conv_k rows plus whatever the pass writes - one position per sequence satisfies that, sixteen consecutive positions of one sequence does not.  The engine guards it with an ensure! rather than silently computing garbage.
evidence.harness_bug_not_engine_bug: the first conc.sh run appeared to hang for 20 minutes after the concurrent phase had already returned all 16 correct responses.  The cause was in the harness, not the engine: the server is a background job of the script and a bare `wait` waits for it too, so the script blocked forever.  The diagnosis signature is worth remembering - response files all written, process CPU at 0%, and a freshly issued request answered in 3.3 s all at once means the script is stuck, not the server.  Fixed by collecting the curl pids and using wait "${pids[@]}".

history.next: the objective is met: the engine serves up to 16 concurrent requests, verified correct and 3.33x faster than serial, with the code committed and the tutorial rewritten.  The one deliberate gap is that the MTP draft head is still single-sequence, so the batch path runs plain decode and a lone request forgoes the speculative speedup it used to get (~30% single-stream).  Batching per-slot speculation, or using the speculative path when exactly one slot is active, is the next improvement if single-stream latency matters again.

history.title: agent-framework support round 1: a real user bug (OpenCode hangs on 'hello') traced end to end with a transparent logging proxy.  Two causes found: (a) the engine never noticed a dead client, so an abandoned request - and OpenCode asks for max_tokens=32000 - kept generating for the better part of twenty minutes while sharing every round with real work, and sixteen of those occupy the engine completely; fixed by checking the piece channel each round and releasing the slot.  (b) The real cost is prefill: OpenCode sends a 6867-token agent prompt (10 tools, 49 KB of JSON) and prefill is one full weight sweep per prompt token, so the first byte took 66.9 s and OpenCode issues follow-up requests in its agent loop.

evidence.how_it_was_found: tools/logproxy.py is a transparent logging proxy: it sits on the port the framework already points at and forwards to the real server, so nothing on the client side changes, and it logs the request shape plus the time to the first streamed byte.  That produced the exact numbers rather than a guess: two requests per user turn (a 550-token title request and a 6867-token build request with 10 tools and max_tokens=32000), first byte after 66.9 s.
evidence.the_two_causes: (a) No client-liveness check: the only stop conditions were EOS and max_tokens, so an abandoned request held one of the sixteen slots until it generated all 32000 tokens.  (b) Prefill costs one full 14.4 GB weight sweep per prompt token, and a coding agent re-sends its whole conversation every step, so every agent step costs ~70 s of prefill.
evidence.clamping_seen_in_the_wild: with --max-ctx 32768 the log shows the agent's 32000-token budget cut to 25901 for the 6867-token prompt.  At the 8192 default the same request would be cut to about 1300 tokens, which truncates the agent mid-task; a slightly larger prompt at the default would be rejected outright and OpenCode retries, which looks like a hang.

history.next: chunked prefill is the highest-value next step and the arithmetic is already understood: the four-row tile kernel reads the weights once for four rows at roughly the cost of a one-row pass, so prefilling TILE positions per pass should cut the first byte from ~67 s to ~20 s, and the convolution ring is already sized conv_k + TILE = 8 to make that legal.  forward_rows already permits up to TILE rows per sequence; the engine only needs to feed a chunk instead of a single token.  Prefix caching is the bigger prize for agents, since a coding agent re-prefills its entire conversation on every step.

evidence.the_floor: 25B activated params x 2 = 5e10 FLOPs per token; the M5 Max GPU is about 20 TFLOPS fp16 dense, so ~2.5 ms per prompt token is the floor.  32K tokens therefore cannot prefill in under ~80 s, and 6867 tokens cannot in under ~17 s.  1 s would require ~1700 TFLOPS, about 85x this GPU.  Measured best so far is 9.7 ms/token (66.9 s for OpenCode's prompt), i.e. ~3.9x off the floor.
evidence.the_real_fix: prefix caching, not a faster single prefill.  An agent re-sends its whole conversation every step, so step N pays a full prefill of N steps of history; caching the prefix turns every step after the first into a prefill of only the new tokens, which is the only route to sub-second TTFT in practice.  The machinery is partly there: the speculative snap buffer already snapshots the GDN recurrence, and the KV cache is position-indexed.
evidence.instrument_discipline: the thermal proxy is the engine load time; it went from 4.2 s to 19.4 s between the round-6 and round-7 measurements, which is why no round-7 timing is trusted.

history.title: TTFT round 2: chunked prefill is VERIFIED and now the default - a paired same-thermal-state A/B on a 1314-token prompt gave a TTFT of 130.08 s at one token per pass and 36.10 s at four, a 3.60x speedup, with byte-identical output.  The mechanism is bandwidth: a one-row pass still streams all 14.4 GB of weights, so feeding it a single token pays that entire read for one token, while the projection kernel computes four rows from the same read.

evidence.why_prefill_was_slow: a one-row pass is bandwidth-bound and must stream all 14.4 GB of weights, roughly 29 ms at DRAM peak, and prefill was paying that once per prompt token.  Feeding four consecutive positions per pass reuses that single read, which is what the tile kernel was always built to do.
evidence.the_floor_still_stands: even at the improved rate, 32K tokens cannot reach a one-second TTFT.  25B activated parameters is 5e10 FLOPs per token and this GPU is about 20 TFLOPS, so ~2.5 ms per token is the compute floor - about 80 s for 32K.  The measured 27.5 ms per token after this change is about 11x off that floor, so the remaining headroom is real but bounded.
evidence.process_lesson: running a benchmark and the acceptance suite at the same time invalidates both.  The failing oracle parity looked like a regression and was not one; the direct re-run was clean.

history.title: TTFT round 3: found why clients look hung regardless of speed.  The engine's Prompt(n) event - which arrives at admission, before any prefill - was being DROPPED by the SSE adapter, so the server wrote NOTHING to the client until the first token, tens of seconds later.  An idle socket is indistinguishable from a dead one, so OpenCode and KiloCode both sat there.  The Prompt event now becomes the opening role chunk, so the client has bytes immediately, and both SSE streams carry a 3 s keep-alive comment.  Measured on a 1314-token prompt: first byte 0.05 s (was 101 s of silence), 8 keep-alives during the prefill, and first CONTENT at 25.24 s.

gates.G4: measured; the wire-level first byte is 0.05 s but that is a role chunk, NOT the first content token - the honest TTFT is 25.24 s for 1314 tokens

evidence.the_hang_was_not_only_speed: even a fast prefill would have looked hung, because nothing was written until it finished.  The metadata event that already carried the prompt length was discarded by text_only, which is why the fix is three lines rather than a kernel.
evidence.why_it_matters_for_agents: a coding agent's prompt is ~6867 tokens, so at the measured 19-27 ms per token the first content token is minutes away.  Keeping the socket alive is what stops the framework from timing out and retrying, which is what the user saw as a freeze.
evidence.the_target_remains_impossible: 25B activated parameters is 5e10 FLOPs per token and this GPU is about 20 TFLOPS, so the compute floor is ~2.5 ms per token: ~80 s for 32K.  One second would need ~1700 TFLOPS, about 85x this GPU.  Measured today: 19 ms per token after chunked prefill, still ~8x off the floor.

history.title: Prefix cache.  The engine needed no snapshot storage at all: the KV cache is never cleared and only the delta-net recurrence is rewound, so a slot whose consumed token sequence is a prefix of a new prompt is ALREADY in the right state and the prefix can simply not be recomputed.  Measured on the 6.9K prompt that OpenCode actually sends: cold 230.41 s, and the agent's next turn 1.38 s after skipping 6875 of 6890 tokens - 167x, against a target of 20 s.  Hit rate is logged per request and cumulatively, token-weighted rather than request-weighted, because a request-count rate hides that almost all the work was done twice.

gates.G2: accept.sh re-run with nothing else on the machine
gates.G3: verified end to end on a 6866-token prompt, three sequential requests through the real HTTP server: cold 230.41 s (miss), byte-identical retry 324.36 s (miss), agent next turn with the assistant reply folded back in 1.38 s (HIT, 6875 of 6890 tokens skipped).  The engine log shows the same: 'prefix cache HIT - skipped 6875 of 6890 prompt tokens (100%)'
gates.G4: measured; the accepted target of 20 s is met many times over on the cached path, and not met on a cold first request, which physics bounds

evidence.why_it_is_free: reset_seq rewinds only the state and the window, never the KV cache, and positions are written once and read only up to the current position.  So a full-prefix match needs no copy: the slot is already correct.
evidence.why_token_weighted: a request-count hit rate is misleading - one request reusing 90% of its prompt counts the same as one reusing 1%.
evidence.known_limitation: a byte-identical retry misses.  After decoding, the slot's state sits at prompt + generated, past the prompt boundary, and a recurrent state cannot be rewound to a middle position, so only a complete match of the slot's history is usable.  Covering the retry case needs a prefill-boundary snapshot of state + window (about 179 MB per slot: 151 MB delta-net plus 28 MB window), which is next round's work and does not affect the agent path.
evidence.cold_start_unchanged: the first request still pays the full prefill - 230.41 s for 6866 tokens here - because no cache exists yet.  Prefix caching removes repeat work, not the first pass.

history.title: Prefix cache round 2: implemented the end-of-prefill snapshot that would let a byte-identical retry hit, since after decoding the slot's state sits past the prompt boundary and a recurrence cannot be rewound.  save_prefix/load_prefix copy a slot's state and convolution window (165 MB in total, mirrored per slot) and restore them on a boundary match; the copy is not consumed, so one boundary serves several requests.  It builds clean but is NOT verified end to end - the cold prefill for the same 6866-token prompt has measured anywhere from 230 s to over 600 s on this machine, and the run meant to check it did not finish inside the round - so it is opt-in behind QW_PREFIX_SNAPSHOT=1 and the verified round-4 behaviour remains the default.

gates.G2: accept.sh re-run with nothing else on the machine

evidence.why_it_needs_a_copy: the delta-net state is a running quantity; the only way back to a position a slot has already passed is a copy taken while it was there.
evidence.why_the_copy_is_kept: a snapshot is not consumed by a hit, so one boundary can serve many requests, and a miss (which rewinds the live state) does not invalidate it.
evidence.why_it_is_not_the_default: an unverified optimisation that can silently corrupt state is worse than a known miss.  The engine was confirmed alive during the slow run - a fresh small request on another slot was answered promptly - so the slowness was the machine, not a wedge, but 'slow machine' is not evidence that the copy is correct.

history.title: The hang is not a hang.  Reproducing two concurrent agent-sized requests exactly as OpenCode and KiloCode send them, both COMPLETED with correct output - the 550-token title request at 118.4 s and the 6867-token main request at 718.9 s to first token.  So the engine is alive and computing; a cold agent prompt simply needs minutes of prefill, and the log said nothing between admission and the answer, so a working request was indistinguishable from a dead one.  Added prefill progress at each 25% milestone and a completion line, then drove the real OpenCode client end to end: 'opencode run hello' answered correctly in 248.0 s cold, with the progress visible in the console throughout.

history.title: Chased the position-dependent prefill cost.  It is real and reproducible: two independent runs of the same 6865-token prompt gave nearly identical segment rates, fitting ms/token ~= 9.2 + 5.5e-3 * position, so the position term is about 80% of a 7K cold prefill (215-248 s, against ~63 s if it were removed).  It should not be there: the inherent attention work for 6865 tokens is ~7 ms of FLOPs and ~1.5 s of KV traffic, nowhere near the ~132 ms per pass that is actually observed, so it is an implementation inefficiency - most likely the 6x query-head re-read of each KV head under GQA combined with a 4x per-row re-read of the history inside a chunk, 24x redundancy in total.  I did NOT change any kernel: my own traffic estimate contradicts the measured time by orders of magnitude, which means my model of what the kernels actually touch is wrong, and rewriting a kernel on a wrong model is how silent wrongness gets shipped.  The next step is instrumentation, not a rewrite.

evidence.arithmetic_contradiction: the measured per-pass overhead at 7K is ~132 ms, while the inherent attention for that prompt is ~7 ms of FLOPs and ~1.5 s of KV traffic in total.  The gap is ~2 orders of magnitude, which is why the fix cannot be guessed.
evidence.suspects: GQA makes 6 query heads read one KV head; a 4-row chunk makes each row read the same history again.  24x redundant reads, and sharing them is the standard fix.
evidence.why_no_fix: an estimate that contradicts measurement by 100x is not a basis for rewriting a kernel.  Instrument first: time the individual dispatches at T = 1k / 4k / 7k and find which one grows with T.

history.title: Built the instrumentation instead of guessing, and it refuted the optimisation I had proposed.  Added `qwen38 pos-bench`, which feeds synthetic tokens and times each pass, with --slots N letting N sequences each contribute a row so the marginal cost of rows 5..16 is measurable without touching the convolution ring.  Measured in one session over 6000 tokens: 1 row/pass costs 53.87 ms at pos 1000, 4 rows cost 98.07, 16 rows cost 413.42.  Scaling 4 -> 16 rows multiplies the pass cost by 4.96x for 4x the work - no amortisation at all, and at pos 6000 sixteen rows are outright worse (58.46 vs 47.15 ms per token).  The reason is that encode_rows sends n > 4 to q4_gemv_b16, which is no cheaper per row than the tile kernel (25.84 vs 27.47 ms/row at pos 1000), so the engine's existing chunk of 4 is already on the faster path.  Widening conv_ring to feed 16 rows would have been real correctness risk for zero gain, and the measurement stopped it.  Also corrected section 14: normalised per row, the position term is more consistent (3.9e-3 at 4 rows, 6.5e-3 at 16), so it is charged per ROW rather than per pass.

history.title: Found and fixed the position-dependent prefill cost.  Kernel-level timing (new `qwen38 attn-bench`, which dispatches attn_scores and attn_out in isolation with a position-independent projection as a control) showed attn_scores and the projection flat with T while attn_out grew: 0.231 / 0.396 / 1.236 ms at T = 1000 / 3000 / 6000.  That is 1.236 x 16 layers = 19.8 ms per row, against the 20.06 ms per row that pos-bench had measured independently, so attn_out accounted for about 80% of the growth.  The cause was one line: a single `acc` made the whole T sweep one dependent FMA chain, so only one V load was ever in flight per thread, and 72 MB in 1.236 ms is ~58 GB/s, far under L2 - latency-bound, not bandwidth-bound.  Splitting into eight accumulators gives 2.2x / 3.8x / 5.3x at those three lengths and almost removes the T dependence.  Gates: oracle parity 6/6, batch-check 16/16 with worst logit difference 0.0000, accept.sh 12/12 ACCEPTED. Paired alternating A/B (same state, old/new/old/new) has the new kernel faster in both pairs, 174.0 -> 114.5 s and 124.9 -> 111.8 s, a mean 1.32x.

history.title: Closed the loop on how much the attn_out fix is actually worth, and the honest answer is smaller than the kernel numbers suggest.  Paired alternating A/B with the two binaries already on disk: at 2500 tokens old 174.0 / 124.9 s against new 114.5 / 111.8 s, at 4000 tokens old 248.5 / 93.0 s against new 87.7 / 81.6 s.  The new kernel won all four pairs, but the margin ranged from 1.12x to 2.83x, and the pair where BOTH binaries ran in a good state is only 1.12-1.14x.  So the end-to-end gain is about 1.1-1.3x, which does not meet the objective's 'significantly faster'.  This does not contradict the kernel measurement (attn_out 5.3x faster at T = 6000, where it was ~44% of the per-token cost): it means a degraded machine state amplifies a latency-bound kernel disproportionately.  In a good state attn_out was never the bottleneck, so fixing it saves little; in a bad state it dominates and fixing it is worth 2.8x.  The blocking obstacle is now that the noise is larger than the effect: the same old binary drifted between 93.0 s and 248.5 s across adjacent runs, a factor of 2.7, against an effect of 1.1-1.3x.  Chasing further optimisation before the measurement environment is stable is chasing noise.

history.title: New objective: TTFT under 10 s for the first hello in OpenCode.  Did the arithmetic first, and it says 10 s is not reachable on this machine, but the user's hunch about a deeper bug is right.  The model is dense 27B with 14.41234944 GB of 4-bit weights that every pass must read in full.  The hello prompt is 6867 tokens, prefill runs 4 rows per pass, so 1717 passes move 24.7 TB of weights; bench measures this machine's achievable bandwidth at 438 GB/s (32.93 ms for one full sweep), giving a floor of about 56 s.  Ten seconds needs 2.47 TB/s, 5.6x the measured ceiling, and even perfect 16-row L2 sharing at full bandwidth would be 14 s.  The real bug is in the weight stream: bench prints effective bandwidth per path and k=1 achieves 438 GB/s while the k=16 q4_gemv_b16 path achieves 33 GB/s - 7.5% of it.  Sixteen tokens take 430 ms moving not 14.41 GB but 230 GB, i.e. 536 GB/s of actual DRAM traffic, so the weights are being re-read from DRAM sixteen times.  The kernel's own comment promises exactly the opposite - that B consecutive threadgroups covering the same output row fetch it from DRAM once and serve the other B-1 out of L2 - so that L2 sharing is not happening.  The chunk-of-4 tile path the prefill actually uses runs at 175 GB/s, 40% of achievable.  So there is 2.5x to 13x of real headroom in the weight sweep, and pushing the tile path to 438 GB/s would take the 6000-token prefill from 139 s to about 56 s.

history.title: Completed the quantitative picture, and it settles both questions.  bench --tokens k gives the effective bandwidth of each path: k=1 477.5 GB/s, k=2 281.2, k=4 172.4, k=8 86.2.  Prefill uses k=4, and 6867 tokens at its 20.89 ms/token is 143 s, against the 138.8 s measured for 6000 tokens - so prefill is essentially nothing but the GEMV weight sweep, and attention, GDN, convolution and sampling are rounding error.  Ten seconds needs 1.46 ms/token, which is 14x better than the k=4 rate and 20x better than even the k=1 rate, so it is not reachable on this machine.  The real bug is that the multi-row kernel is issue-bound rather than bandwidth-bound: at 172 GB/s it is running 2.8x below the 477 GB/s that k=1 proves the hardware can do, and the source's own note about round 055 records the same failure in extreme form.  Get k=4 back to bandwidth-bound at 7.5 ms/token and the 6867 token prefill is about 52 s, which is the real ceiling here.  Also corrected a methodology error from last round: attn-bench puts a barrier between every dispatch, which inflates the apparent fixed cost per dispatch, so the claim that attn_scores costs 0.381 ms fixed was not trustworthy and I did not change any kernel on the strength of it.

history.title: Tried the most promising one-line fix and it was a regression; reverted.  bench --tokens 4 showed --rows 0 at 20.93 ms/token against --rows 1 at 10.87, so I concluded the engine had picked the wrong tile kernel (K_Q4_GEMV_K4_U4HX) and switched it to the plain K_Q4_GEMV_K4.  Both gates passed - oracle parity 6/6 and batch-check 16/16 with worst logit difference 0.0000 - so on gates and bench alone it looked like a win.  A paired alternating A/B on the real prefill path said otherwise: u4hx 51.9 s and 55.9 s against k4 60.0 s and 72.3 s, so the change was 1.16-1.29x SLOWER and I reverted it.  My error was reading bench's --rows as selecting the engine's kernel: rows=0 takes the else branch to QLinear::kernel_k, the default k-kernel, so neither of the two kernels I compared was the U4HX the engine actually uses.  Third time this session that a non-paired or wrong-subject comparison pointed the wrong way.  Conclusion: the engine's multi-row GEMV choice is not a bug - at 20.89 ms/token against k=1's 30.18 it is already capturing the 1.44x amortisation.  Going further means redesigning the kernel so x is reused across output rows, which is a much larger project whose best case is still ~52 s, far above the 10 s the objective asks for.

history.title: Found and fixed why the boundary snapshot never converged - the bug that made round 055's snapshot look disproved.  save_prefix and load_prefix only move the GDN recurrent state and the convolution window, and both are written correctly; the problem was WHEN the snapshot was taken.  The old code saved once a.pf >= a.ids.len(), that is after the whole prompt was fed, when the state has already consumed the last token and the logits for the first generated token exist only in a scratch buffer that save_prefix does not copy.  On a hit the engine set pf = pos = ids.len(), so the readiness test passed immediately, it sampled from a stale logits buffer unrelated to the restored position, and the first token was already wrong - which is exactly the observed 100% hit that never finished in ten minutes.  The fix is to snapshot before the LAST chunk instead of at the prompt end: the state is then at a clean chunk boundary, and on a hit an ordinary prefill re-walks at most `chunk` tokens, rebuilding state, KV and logits correctly with no need to persist logits.  Cost is at most about 80 ms.  A pf > 0 guard stops a short request clobbering a long prompt's snapshot with an empty one.  The edit is four lines added and eight removed in crates/qw-server/src/engine.rs; lookup, record_boundary and Reuse::Boundary were already right.  Verified with the same 1025-token prompt sent twice greedily: 15.5 s cold against 0.5 s on the boundary hit, outputs token-for-token identical, and the log shows skipped 1024 of 1025 tokens, 100%, a 30x gain.  Oracle parity 6/6, batch-check 16/16 at 0.0000, accept.sh 12 passed 0 failed ACCEPTED.  This mechanism being correct is the precondition for the disk cache, which did not hold before.

history.title: Implemented and verified cross-process prefix persistence.  Three small pieces: GpuBuffer::write_at/read_at, because copy_from can only write from offset 0 and a whole-buffer write is useless for one slot's slice of a batched buffer (the Metal backing is CPU-visible already, so these are plain memcpys); Qwen38::export_prefix and import_prefix, which serialise a slot's GDN state and convolution window plus the KV entries for positions 0..pos (the KV cache is head-major, so one head's live prefix is a contiguous run and both directions are a memcpy per head rather than a per-position gather); and a DiskPrefix in the engine keyed by the CONTENT of the token sequence rather than by slot, so it survives the process and is shared by all slots.  find reads only the header and pulls the blob in only once the ids match, since each file is a few hundred megabytes.  On a hit import_prefix writes this slot's slice and skip = n; only 0..n is touched and the prefill overwrites the rest, so the KV needs no clearing, the same argument as the in-memory path.  It only persists at pos >= 256 because a blob costs about 0.1 MB a token.  Verified cross-process: process 1 cold 15.5 s and then persisted 1024 tokens at 215 MB; a FRESH process 2 served the same prompt in 0.9 s with the log reading prefix cache HIT (disk prefix) - skipped 1024 of 1025 prompt tokens (100%), and the outputs are token-for-token identical.  215 MB per 1024 tokens is 0.21 MB per token, matching the 560 MB estimate for 6000 tokens.  Oracle parity 6/6, batch-check 16/16 at worst logit difference 0.0000, accept.sh 12 passed and 0 failed ACCEPTED.  Deliberately did NOT use a paired A/B here: a cache hit is not a comparison of two implementations but a semantic change from doing work to not doing it, and the right instruments are output identity and the skip ratio in the log.  Still open: no end-to-end run against real OpenCode at 6867 tokens, and both environment variables are still opt-in, so the user gets nothing until they set them.

history.title: Real OpenCode end-to-end, and it found the real problem.  Through tools/logproxy.py on 8080 forwarding to 8081, run 1 persisted and run 2 in a FRESH process hit the title request at 100% but MISSED the main 6891-token request.  The prompts are not byte-stable between sessions.  I did not need another run to find out where: the .pfx headers store the token ids, so diffing the two cache files gave the answer directly - first divergence at token 6566, so 6566 of 6888 tokens (95.3%) are shared and only the last ~322 vary.  So the problem was never that reuse was impossible; it was that I stored a single boundary at the very end, past the divergence, which therefore matched nothing.  The fix is a ladder of geometric offsets from the end, [0, 256, 384, 512, 768, 1024, 1536, 2048, 3072, 4096]: during prefill, whenever a chunk crosses one of those thresholds a boundary is persisted at that chunk boundary, each firing exactly once, spaced more finely near the end where the variation lives.  store() names files by content hash so re-persisting an existing prefix is free, and there is mtime-based eviction under QW_PREFIX_DISK_MB (8 GB default) because an agent's prompt grows every turn.  End to end with real OpenCode in a fresh process: the 550-token title request hit 100% and went 35.9 s to 11.6 s; the 6893-token main request skipped 6124 tokens, 89%, and went 195.8 s to 32.7 s; the whole opencode run went 197 s to 35 s.  Run 2 also persisted new boundaries at 6124, 6380 and 6508, so the cache is self-improving and TTFT should keep falling as sessions accumulate.  Oracle 6/6, batch-check 16/16, accept.sh 12 passed 0 failed ACCEPTED.  One measurement caveat worth recording: logproxy's 'first byte' is the first byte of the SSE stream, which arrives immediately and is NOT the TTFT of the first content token; the server log's prefill timing is the real one, about 13 s after the hit.  Still open: TTFT is about 13 s rather than single digits, and the post-convergence number has not been measured, and both env vars are still opt-in.

history.title: Converged, and it reaches the objective.  Added a time-to-first-token log line, because until now only the total was recorded and a warm hit was indistinguishable from a cold start in the log.  Then three consecutive FRESH-process runs of real OpenCode against the same cache directory: run 3 skipped 6124 of 6893 (89%) with a TTFT of 21.1 s; run 4 skipped 6636 of 6894 (96%) at 14.8 s; run 5 skipped 6892 of 6894 (100%) at 0.2 s.  The whole opencode run went from 197 s cold to 6 s.  The self-improvement is visible in the log: each run persists new boundaries closer to the divergence point, so the skip ratio climbs 89% then 96% then 100%.  Run 5's 100% means that session's prompt was identical to a stored boundary for 6892 of its 6894 tokens, so the new session's hello did no cold prefill at all.  The settled behaviour is 89-100% skipped, commonly about 96%, giving a TTFT of 0.2-15 s rather than a single fixed number, because the divergence point moves slightly from session to session.  Oracle 6/6, batch-check 16/16, accept.sh 12 passed and 0 failed ACCEPTED.  All three parts of the plan are done: the snapshot save/restore was proven numerically correct (round 17 found the snapshot was taken at the prompt end where the first token's logits are not copied, and moving it before the final chunk gave bit-identical output at 15.5 s cold against 0.5 s warm); the KV, GDN state and convolution window are persisted keyed by token content at 165 MB plus 0.0655 MB per token, matching the 560 MB estimate for 6000 tokens; and a fresh process imports on a hit and prefills only the remainder.  The one thing left for the user to decide is whether the two environment variables become the default, since the disk cache occupies several GB and writing that to someone's home directory unasked is not appropriate.

history.title: The user was right that the weights were already local, and I had been searching wrong: the full 18-shard bf16 checkpoint, 52 GB, is at /Users/waynewong/Claude/QWen3.8_27B/models/Qwen3.8-27B-BF16, and that project even has bench/endpoint_otps.py, so it was doing the same class of measurement.  My earlier search only looked for the *.gguf extension and so missed it entirely; this project's models/Qwen3.8-27B-bf16-mtp holds only shard 18, which made the local copy look incomplete.  No download was ever needed.  Built the GGUF locally using the converter in /Users/waynewong/dsh/Loop-Study/inference-engine/llama.cpp, a full recent checkout with the conversion package, gguf-py and a built llama-quantize, whose conversion/qwen.py carries MODEL_ARCH.QWEN35; the brew llama.cpp ships binaries only and has no Python converter, so borrowing that checkout was necessary.  HF bf16 52115 MiB at 16.00 BPW quantized to Q4_K_M 16021 MiB at 4.92 BPW, 16.81 GB, written to models/gguf/qwen38-27b-Q4_K_M.gguf.  Baseline from llama-bench with the Metal backend on the M5 Max: pp128 526.29, pp512 720.95, pp2048 561.08, tg128 24.10 tokens per second.  Head to head: decode is essentially a tie at 23.9 against 24.10, but prefill is 47.9 on the bench and 35.4 measured end to end against 526-721, so we are 11 to 15 times behind.  The reason is structural: llama.cpp's prefill is a simdgroup matrix multiply, a real GEMM, while our multi-row path is still a GEMV, and that is the same story the k=1-to-k=4 bandwidth table told from the other side - packing k rows into a GEMV that is partitioned by output row means each extra row costs another pass of arithmetic, sliding off the bandwidth bound.  No amount of tuning inside the GEMV framing recovers a 15x gap, which is also why the kernel swap in section 21 was rejected by the paired A/B: it was still a GEMV.  Winning prefill needs a real batched GEMM that dequantises weight tiles into threadgroup memory and uses simdgroup_multiply_accumulate, which the device reports as available.  Decode is a smaller, separate target: 23.9 real against 33.1 for the raw weight sweep leaves about 28% outside the weight stream.

history.title: Won otps.  The server was 40.2 ms per token against gen's 31.9, and QW_DISPATCH_HIST showed why: gen dispatched q4_gemv_hx 497 times while the server dispatched q4_gemv_k4_u4hx 497 times, at 1186 against 1234 dispatches and 31.9 against 38.4 ms per step.  linear.rs::encode_rows had only two branches, rows <= TILE going to encode_tile, so a single-token decode took the multi-token tile kernel - and K4_U4HX is a compile-time four-row specialisation, which the code's own comment says is exactly four rows, so feeding it one row still computes four.  gen reached the plain single-token kernel by another path.  The two are numerically identical: msl.rs line 122 states that q4_gemv_k4_u4hx is q4_gemv_hx's own body with K fixed at 4, one accumulator and one 16-byte x load.  Added a single_k parameter to encode_rows so rows == 1 takes self.encode, and inserted &kernels.q4_gemv at all 14 call sites; the server's step went 38.4 to 33.1 ms, 13.8 per cent.  Gates: oracle 6/6, batch-check 16/16 with greedy tokens identical across all 16 slots, and accept.sh 12 passed 0 failed ACCEPTED twice running.  One earlier accept.sh run reported 11 passed 1 failed, but it ran immediately after llama-bench with swap at 1030 MB, load 3.24 and the GPU not yet cool, and two clean runs followed, so it was environmental rather than caused by this change.  Head to head on decode with prefill excluded, which is the same basis as llama-bench tg: ours 33.9, 35.3 and 37.2 ms per token, median 35.3, so 26.9 to 29.5 tokens per second, median 28.4; llama.cpp tg256 24.58.  That is a 15.5 per cent win on otps; for reference llama.cpp's own tg128 is 24.10 and tg32 18.98, so it also sags on longer generations.  TTFT is still split: cold on a real 6900-token agent prompt we take about 195 s against llama.cpp's pp4096 of 353.57 tokens per second, about 19.5 s, so we lose by roughly 10x cold, while on a prefix-cache hit we take 0.2 s against their 19.5 s.  llama.cpp's pp falls off with length - 302 at 64, 526 at 128, 721 at 512, 561 at 2048, 354 at 4096 - which is the same small-batch weight-sweep problem: we read all the weights once per four tokens.  TTFT counts as a win only when the prefix cache hits.

history.title: Chased the remaining gap, cold prefill, and came back with two clean negatives.  Chunking was pinned at four by two separate locks.  In engine.rs the env var was clamped with .min(PREFILL_CHUNK), so QW_PREFILL_CHUNK could only ever lower the chunk and asking for 16 was silently reduced to 4 while the log still said four.  In forward_rows the per-sequence ceiling was derived, max_per_seq being the next power of two above conv_k plus TILE minus conv_k, which is four, so a sixteen-row single-sequence pass raised 'a pass may carry at most 4 rows of one sequence'.  TILE itself cannot move because it is the MTP speculative verify width, three drafts checked in one four-wide pass, so the right move was to size the convolution ring from BATCH_MAX and leave TILE at four; that is five sites, and all the scratch buffers were already allocated with tile = BATCH_MAX so only the ring needed enlarging.  Measurement one: a sixteen-row pass is CORRECT, since an interleaved paired 4/16/4/16 run over a 2016-token prompt produced identical output every time - but it is 1.67 times SLOWER, median 60.8 s against 36.4 s, because encode_b grows the grid to b times out_f times 32 and relies on L2 to reuse the weight row rather than reading it once and feeding many rows.  Measurement two: the other end was already closed, because msl.rs records that round 055 tried giving each thread one accumulator per activation, q4_gemv_k16_u4hx, and found the x loads going from one to sixteen per weight chunk, the kernel stopping being bandwidth-bound at 22.7 against 466 GB/s, and the whole batch coming out 22 per cent slower than serial.  The mechanism is that once K is large the bottleneck moves from reading weights to reading activations, and the only fix is to hold the activations in threadgroup memory, which is what llama.cpp's GEMM does.  Reverted the whole change: it bought 680 MB of resident memory for the larger window ring and a slower path, so there was nothing to deliver.  Oracle 6/6 and batch-check 16/16 after the revert.  The single remaining target is a real simdgroup GEMM for batched tokens, dequantising weight tiles into threadgroup memory and using simdgroup_multiply_accumulate - the device reports tensor support - which is the only way to win back cold TTFT.  Also corrected: chunk=4 cold prefill of 2016 tokens is 30-36 s, 56-67 tokens per second, when the machine is not heat-soaked; the 46.7 s in section 28 was measured immediately after llama-bench and was thermal throttling, not the steady state.

history.title: Pinned the prefill question down with the project's own calibrated instrument.  bench --rows 18 --tokens 16 runs four arms interleaved inside one process, of which b16-star is a duplicate of b16 and exists to calibrate the method itself, because this box's clock drifts by up to 4x within a single run and a cross-process A/B means nothing.  Results: b16 grid-shared 367.33 ms and 43.6 tokens per second; k16 per-thread 742.60 ms and 21.5; k1x16 serial 452.07 ms and 35.4; the b16 duplicate 431.22 ms.  So b16 over serial is 1.231x raw but only 1.048x calibrated, which means the advertised one-weight-read-feeds-sixteen-tokens does not actually happen, and k16 is twice as slow as serial.  That is the quantitative explanation for section 29's measured 1.67x slowdown at chunk 16, and it closes the direction.  The mechanism is in the macro's own comment: per group and word the inner loop issues NK x loads against ONE weight load, its own accounting being 28.8 G loads against 3.6 G, so once K is large the bottleneck moves from reading weights to reading activations.  Activations are shared across every output row of a layer and should be loaded once for many rows.  The fix is to store the activations transposed: today rows t sit K apart so one load serves one row, whereas with a feature-major layout a single 16-byte load carries eight rows' worth of one feature, taking NK=16 from sixteen x loads down to two, an eight-fold cut.  That needs a transpose of the residual stream once per layer rather than once per linear, a transposed branch in the tile macro, and the BATCH_MAX-sized ring that section 29 implemented and proved correct and then reverted for lack of benefit - it only becomes meaningful once the transposed x exists.  Status: otps won at 28.4 against 24.58, warm TTFT won at 0.2 s against 19.5 s, cold TTFT still lost by about 9x, and that gap needs a transposed-activation tile GEMM rather than tuning.  Asked the user to scope it, since in the actual agent workflow the prefix cache means the cold path never runs.

history.title: Built the full time model and it overturns the GEMM premise.  Before writing the transposed-activation GEMM the user asked for, I measured the kernel itself, and the kernel is not the bottleneck.  First I cleared a long-standing misreading: no --rows value could reach the kernel the engine's prefill actually uses, because encode_rows goes to encode_tile and then encode_k(K_Q4_GEMV_K4_U4HX, k), while --rows 0 takes K_Q4_GEMV_K, a different kernel entirely - so every sweep figure on record labelled the engine's kernel came from the wrong one.  Added --rows 5 to point at the real one.  Ranked in isolation at k=4 with per-linear x: K4_U4HX 35.68 ms and 404 GB/s, which is what the engine uses and is the FASTEST of the three, against K_Q4_GEMV_K4 at 39.68 and 363, and K_Q4_GEMV_K at 76.02 and 190.  That is 85 per cent of the 477 GB/s hardware limit, confirming section 21 and refuting the slow-kernel suspicion I had raised myself.  The rest of the sweep: k=1 477, k=2 482, k=3 with K3 437, k=4 404; row blocking is slower (385 at R=2 and 362 at R=4 for k=3), and large K collapses (K_Q4_GEMV_K at k=16 gives 35 GB/s).  The model that falls out: a real prefill pass of 2016 tokens at chunk=4 takes 59.5 ms per pass, of which 35.68 ms is the weight sweep and 23.8 ms is non-GEMV work, about 5.95 ms per token; and decode is 33 ms per token, of which 27.6 ms is the sweep and 5.4 ms is the same non-GEMV work.  So the non-GEMV work is about 5.4 to 6 ms per token and does NOT amortise across the chunk - it grows linearly with tokens - which makes it 40 per cent of prefill at chunk 4 and 16 per cent of decode.  The dispatch histogram says where it comes from: 689 non-GEMV dispatches per single-token pass, dominated by rmsnorm 129, rmsnorm_s 128 and ewise_add 128, then silu_mul 64, gdn_step 48, rmsnorm_gated 48 and rope_partial 32.  At roughly 6 microseconds each that is about 4.1 ms, so most of the 5.4 ms is dispatch overhead rather than arithmetic.  This changes the plan: the GEMM is not the current bottleneck, since the kernel already runs at 404 GB/s while the real engine reaches only 240, and the missing 1.7x sits outside the weight sweep.  A GEMM would still pay, but its value is enabling chunk 16 to amortise properly, which would take the weight part from 8.9 to 2.2 ms per token while the 5.4 ms of non-GEMV work remains, giving 7.6 ms per token and 131 tok/s against 67 today - so the ceiling is set by the non-GEMV work either way.  The right first step is therefore to cut those 689 dispatches, which helps decode and prefill together: fusing the residual add into the following rmsnorm removes 128 dispatches, about 0.8 ms per token, and folding silu_mul and rope_partial into their neighbours would take another 1.35 ms, for decode 33 to 31.7 ms and prefill 70 to 76 tok/s.

history.title: Found that a prefix-cache hit changes the output, and reverted the default-on.  The user asked for the memory-only prefix cache to be on by default, and the implementation is nearly free - Scratch's snap buffer is allocated whether or not the flag is set and PrefixCache holds nothing but token ids - so turning it on costs no extra memory.  With it on the function worked: a 613-token request took 8.2 s cold and 0.3 s on the repeat, logging 'prefix cache HIT (saved boundary) - skipped 612 of 613 (100%)'.  But the determinism check I ran before making it the default showed it is wrong.  One request at temperature 0, sent three times: with the cache on, run 1 cold gives a particular string while runs 2 and 3, both hits, give a DIFFERENT string and agree with each other; with QW_PREFIX_SNAPSHOT=0 all three runs give the cold string and are identical.  So the restored state is not equivalent to a real prefill, the cold path is self-consistent, and the hit path is the one that is wrong.  Why this was not caught before: the section 22 verification used a 1025-token prompt and found cold 15.5 s against a 0.5 s hit with token-for-token identical output, whereas this one is 613 tokens where the hit skips 612 and recomputes one.  The difference is the boundary position, because PREFIX_LADDER keys off the distance from the end of the prompt and 613 and 1025 land on different ladder values, at least one of which is a wrong case.  It is the same family as the bug section 22 fixed, where a snapshot at the prompt end leaves the first generated token's logits uncopied, and that fix was incomplete.  Reverted engine.rs to opt-in and confirmed oracle 6/6, batch-check 16/16 and three identical cold runs.  An optimisation that changes the output cannot be the default even when the user asked for it, since correctness outranks delivery, and this qualifies section 25's claim that the objective was met: 0.2 s is real, but on lengths like 613 tokens that path answers differently from a cold start.  Next, in priority order: find and fix the boundary bug with the determinism check - the same request sent N times must give identical output and must match QW_PREFIX_SNAPSHOT=0 - folded into accept.sh; then make the memory cache the default as the user approved; then cut the 689 dispatches from section 31.

history.title: Nailed down the prefix-cache bug: a boundary hit returns a prompt-independent answer.  A length sweep at about 63, 113, 213, 313 and 413 tokens shows every length failing, so this is not a length-specific edge case as section 32 supposed, and the most informative detail is that the second run's output is IDENTICAL across four different prompts - '<think>\nThe user wants me to reply' every time at reps 10, 20, 30 and 40.  So the hit path's answer does not depend on the prompt at all: it passes the cache check, it is fast (8.2 s down to 0.3 s) and its state is wrong.  I then ruled out the bookkeeping line by line.  is_prefix is correct, since h.len() <= ids.len() && ids[..h.len()] == h[..] cannot return more than the prompt length.  The lookup priority is correct: Live is tried first, and because hist holds the previous request's generated tokens its length exceeds ids, so is_prefix returns None and it falls through to Boundary.  The skip, pf and pos accounting is correct, the log showing each length starting with a miss and then a saved-boundary hit skipping len-1.  The boundary position is correct, because at chunk 4 a 63-token prompt has passes 0,4,...,60,63 and the k=0 condition rem>0 && rem_after<=0 fires at pf=60.  And copy_seq's src and dst selection and byte offsets are correct.  What remains is scope: copy_seq restores only the GDN recurrent state and the convolution window, and copies no KV at all, justified by a comment saying the KV is deliberately left alone since it is keyed by position and written once.  That argument assumes the KV's contents at 0..n still equal the current prompt's first n tokens; on repeated IDENTICAL prompts on one slot that assumption holds, which is exactly the case that fails here, so either the argument misses a quantity that must be saved explicitly or the state and window snapshot is itself incomplete, for instance a stride that does not cover all the rows a layer actually uses.  The memory-only boundary cache is therefore unusable until the root cause is found - its speed is bought with wrong answers - so the default-on the user approved cannot land and QW_PREFIX_SNAPSHOT stays opt-in.  The gate this needs is cheap and decisive and belongs in accept.sh: send the same request N times on one slot at temperature 0 and require identical output, matching QW_PREFIX_SNAPSHOT=0.  That is the test gap this round exposed - the section 22 verification checked one length and compared two runs, whereas the cross-length check that would have caught this takes thirty seconds.

gates.G4: boundary hit is prompt-independent; cache unusable until fixed

evidence.verdict: memory boundary cache unusable until root-caused; QW_PREFIX_SNAPSHOT stays opt-in.
evidence.gate_to_add: same request N times on one slot at temperature 0 must give identical output and match QW_PREFIX_SNAPSHOT=0.

history.title: Root-caused the boundary bug to snapshot scope and fixed the real half of it.  Section 33 had narrowed the suspects to copy_seq restoring only the GDN state and window and no KV, so first I killed the last non-scope hypothesis, async ordering: forward_rows ends with b.finish(true) which calls cb.wait_until_completed, so the state the save point sees is fully synced and it is not a race.  The fix then reuses the already-verified export_prefix and import_prefix pair from the disk path, which serialise the recurrent state, the window AND the KV for positions 0..pos, minus the disk write; a hit now goes through import_prefix, and a blob above four gigabytes is dropped with a fallback to the old load_prefix so memory cannot grow without bound.  The result changed the shape of the bug.  Before, runs 2 and 3 were IDENTICAL across different prompts, always the same string, so the hit answer did not depend on the prompt at all.  After, the hit answer does depend on the prompt - reps 10 gives a pangram-related continuation, reps 5 gives a different one - and runs 2 and 3 agree with each other, so the restored state is now deterministic.  That root cause, a hit returning a prompt-independent answer, is fixed.  What remains is narrower: the restored-and-recomputed tail is still not equivalent to a from-scratch prefill, with all three lengths showing runs 2 and 3 differing from run 1 while run 1 still matches the cache-off cold path.  The difference is deterministic and reproducible, so it is a state-fidelity problem rather than state corruption.  Suspects in order: layers skipped by the if stride == 0 continue in export_prefix if some row a layer actually uses is covered by no stride; whether win_stride covers the whole convolution window a layer uses, since a few missing rows would give the recomputed leading rows a wrong window; and whether import_prefix must first clear KV left past pos by the previous request's generated tokens.  Kept the fix, since it repairs a real defect, but the gate is still red so QW_PREFIX_SNAPSHOT stays opt-in - the accept.sh check requiring N identical responses on one slot to match the cold path does not pass yet.  Oracle 6/6 and batch-check 16/16 unaffected, as this path is not on it.

gates.G4: cache remains opt-in; determinism gate still red

history.title: Corrected an invalid experiment of my own and established that a full blob restore is still not equivalent to a cold prefill.  Having fixed the prompt-independence bug last round, I reasoned that the disk path uses import_prefix, that it had been verified token-for-token, and therefore that the blob approach must be sound; a cross-process test then appeared to confirm it with DISK HIT == COLD: True.  That conclusion was wrong.  Persisting to disk is gated on a.pf >= 128 and the prompt was 113 tokens, so neither process could ever store anything and both were cold misses - the log line 'prefix cache: miss - skipped 0 of 113 prompt tokens (0%), 0 reused' is the proof, and comparing two cold runs proves nothing.  I then ruled out save_prefix: the disk path uses only export_prefix and import_prefix with no save_prefix, so I deleted that redundant GPU copy from the memory path to make the two mechanisms identical, rebuilt, and the residual difference was unchanged - all three lengths still have runs 2 and 3 agreeing with each other and differing from run 1, while run 1 matches QW_PREFIX_SNAPSHOT=0.  So save_prefix is not the cause, and restoring the complete blob including the KV is by itself not enough to reproduce a cold prefill.  That changes the character of the problem.  export_prefix already carries everything a forward pass needs explicitly - the GDN recurrent state at state_stride bytes per GDN layer, the convolution window at win_stride bytes, and the KV for 0..pos at pos*hd*2 per head - yet the restore still is not equivalent.  So either the offsets or lengths in export and import systematically under-cover somewhere, with state_stride and win_stride being a single stride shared by every GDN layer so layers that actually use different row counts would be misplaced, or a forward pass depends on something the blob does not hold.  Both suspects are silent, because export and import use the same strides and offsets, so the blob round-trips itself perfectly without being equal to the real state - which is precisely why it slipped past the equivalence check.  The decisive next experiment needs instrumentation but no second process: at one position L inside one process, compare tensor by tensor the cold-prefilled state, window and KV against the same quantities exported at L and immediately imported back, and against those produced by importing at p < L and recomputing p..L; a mismatch in the first pair means the offsets or lengths are wrong, one in the second means the recomputation introduces the difference.  Kept the fix, since it repairs a real defect, and left QW_PREFIX_SNAPSHOT opt-in because the accept.sh gate requiring N identical responses on one slot to match the cold path still fails.  Oracle 6/6 and batch-check 16/16 pass.

gates.G3: residual cold-vs-hit difference is deterministic; still fails the determinism gate
gates.G4: cache remains opt-in; my own disk-path test this round was invalid and is retracted

history.title: Exonerated the snapshot mechanism and localised the fault to recomputing one step after a restore.  Built the instrument the previous round called for: QW_PREFIX_DUMP plus QW_PREFIX_DUMP_POS write a slot's state, window and KV at position L, the restore path immediately reads its own state back to L.roundtrip.bin, and the save point writes L.saved.bin.  With a 213-token prompt and L=213, two requests in one process give a decisive pair of results.  212.saved.bin and 212.roundtrip.bin are IDENTICAL, all 172,752,912 bytes of them, so export_prefix and import_prefix round-trip perfectly and the snapshot loses nothing - both are exonerated.  But 213.cold.bin and 213.resumed.bin DIFFER, 146,664,767 of 172,818,448 bytes, 85 per cent.  The shape of that difference carries information too: the first differing byte is at offset 16, immediately after the 16-byte header and so inside the first GDN layer's state, the last is the final byte, and the gaps between differing runs are 1,1,2,1,1,2, so the divergence spans the whole blob and every layer in it.  A defect in one place would leave localised differences; a global divergence across all 48 GDN and 16 full layers means the quantity fed into the first layer, or the position semantics after a restore, must be wrong.  That rules out the KV not being restored, since it is and round-trips exactly; it rules out misaligned snapshot offsets or lengths, because a stride error would not round-trip byte-for-byte; it rules out save_prefix, already deleted with no effect; it rules out an async race, since forward_rows ends in finish(true); and it rules out is_prefix, the accounting and the boundary position, all checked line by line.  What remains, in order of likelihood: the write pointer of the GDN convolution ring, because if the window is addressed as pos modulo conv_k then writing win_stride bytes back does not reset the pointer to where the cold path had it at 212 and the next token reads a misplaced window, which is exactly the kind of fault that starts at the first layer and propagates globally; the position or seq_len the attention uses after a restore, if the KV for 0..n comes back but attention still scopes itself by the previous request's pos; and import_prefix not clearing KV left past pos, which the invalid disk test of the previous round means has still never actually been verified.  Next: use the same instrument to export after exactly one step post-restore and compare with the cold path at n+1, which tells us whether the difference begins in the first layer or in a later one; if it is the first, check the ring pointer and the attention position.  Kept the instrument, which costs nothing when QW_PREFIX_DUMP is unset, and left QW_PREFIX_SNAPSHOT opt-in.  Oracle 6/6 and batch-check 16/16 pass.

gates.G3: export/import round-trip proven byte-identical; recompute path diverges globally
gates.G4: cache remains opt-in; fault now localised to the first step after a restore

evidence.ruled_out: KV restore, snapshot strides/offsets, save_prefix, async race, is_prefix, accounting, boundary position.

evidence.next: export after exactly one step post-restore and compare with cold at n+1 to see which layer diverges first.

history.title: The live hit is unsound too, which exonerates the snapshot machinery and moves the question to how the model is positioned.  I reasoned that the Live path needs no copy at all - the slot's state already covers the new prompt's prefix - so it should be sound by construction, and that in an agent framework the model's own reply is echoed back so hist becomes a prefix of the next prompt, which is exactly when Live fires.  I built a proper test for that with /v1/completions on raw text: send A, let the model generate g, then send A + g + more.  It produced 'prefix cache HIT (live state) - skipped 213 of 220 prompt tokens (97%)' and an answer different from the same prompt run cold.  Since Live copies nothing at all, the fault cannot be in the snapshot or the restore - export_prefix and import_prefix are now completely exonerated.  Both runs reach the same token position, but by different routes: the cold run prefills all 220 tokens in 4-token chunks, while the live run prefills 207 in chunks and then advances 6 tokens through single-token generation passes.  Batch-check already proves pass width itself is equivalent, one 16-row pass matching 16 independent passes with worst logit difference 0.0234 to 0.0332, so the contradiction lies elsewhere.  While tracing the position bookkeeping I found an unresolved anomaly worth recording: a.pos is assigned in exactly two places, pos: skip at construction and a.pos += 1 in the generation branch taken when the row is queued, while the prefill branch only ever does a.pf += take and never sets a.pos.  Yet forward_rows really does use pos - let slot = pos % conv_ring addresses the convolution ring by position, and pos is passed as the RoPE scalar.  So on a cold start with skip zero, a.pos would begin at zero rather than at the prompt length, and generation is nevertheless correct, matching llama.cpp in quality and passing the oracle 6 of 6.  I could not resolve that this round, so it is recorded as an open lead and not as a finding.  It is the most promising next target because it would explain both hit paths at once: if the position that indexes the KV cache and the convolution ring comes from a cursor inside the model rather than from the pos the engine passes, then changing skip moves the engine's bookkeeping without moving the model's cursor, which accounts for both the live and the boundary divergence.  I had briefly made Live the default on the grounds that it was sound by construction; the measurement refuted that and I reverted it, so QW_PREFIX_SNAPSHOT and QW_PREFIX_BOUNDARY are both opt-in and both off. The memory cache that was approved for default-on cannot land on this evidence.  Oracle 6/6 and batch-check 16/16 pass.

gates.G3: live hit verified unsound with a proper prefix-extension test; default-on reverted
gates.G4: both cache flags opt-in and off; snapshot machinery exonerated

evidence.action: reverted the default-on; QW_PREFIX_SNAPSHOT and QW_PREFIX_BOUNDARY are both opt-in and off.

history.title: Found the root cause: generation positions begin at skip, not at the prompt length.  The contradiction left open last round was that a.pos is never set to the prompt length while forward_rows really does feed pos to the kernels, indexing the GDN convolution ring as pos % conv_ring.  I settled it with instrumentation rather than more reading, adding QW_POS_DEBUG=1, and it confirmed the anomaly: a 213-token prompt with no reuse reaches generation with pf=213 but pos=0, so the positions handed to the model are 0,1,2.  That is the root cause of both hit paths failing, because setting skip is the whole job of a hit and skip is exactly where that sequence starts.  A cold run drives positions 0,1,2 while a hit that skipped n drives n,n+1,n+2 - the same prompt reaching the same position, shifted by n purely because one of them reused a prefix.  That fits perfectly with the snapshot machinery already being exonerated: no copy needs to go wrong, a different position sequence is enough.  I tried the obvious fix, setting a.pos to the prompt length when prefill completes, and reverted it.  It made pos absolute, the oracle still passed 6/6, but the output CHANGED for some prompts, from one string to another.  So pos does affect the result and the oracle cannot tell the two conventions apart.  I meant to use llama.cpp's greedy output as the arbiter by running the same raw prompt through llama-cli, my absolute-position build and my relative-position build, but the llama-cli invocation timed out after 600 seconds - it had dropped into interactive mode - so no evidence was obtained.  Under the standing rule that a behaviour-changing optimisation may not be kept unverified, I reverted it; all that remains is the QW_POS_DEBUG print, which costs nothing when the variable is unset.  A second, incidental finding is that the oracle has a blind spot: a change that turns relative generation positions into absolute ones alters the output of some prompts and still passes 6/6, so its cases do not constrain position semantics at all.  Until the semantics are pinned down the prefix cache cannot be made reliable, and knowing when it is fixed needs a discriminator that can separate the two conventions - most directly a token-by-token comparison against llama.cpp's greedy output, which ought to be part of this baseline anyway.  Next: obtain that llama.cpp greedy output with a correct non-interactive invocation, or via llama-bench or the server's completion endpoint; then pin the position semantics; then the two cache paths will feed identical position sequences and the hit defect should disappear; and add position-sensitive cases to the oracle, which is otherwise silent about this whole class of change.

gates.G3: unverified absolute-position change reverted; QW_POS_DEBUG instrumentation kept
gates.G4: root cause of both cache-path failures identified: generation positions start at skip

history.title:
Fixed the prefix cache: the generation position sequence no longer depends on skip.  Round 38 had localised the fault - positions handed to the model during generation begin at skip, and skip is the one thing a cache hit changes - so this round settled the convention question first and then realised it was the wrong question.  To settle it I ran llama-cli with -st and --simple-io, which exited 0, and compared greedy continuations: llama.cpp gives '[Start thinking]

We need answer user's prompt', my relative-position build gives '

Based on the text provided', and my absolute-position build gives '

fox.

fox.'.  Neither matches, but the prompt is twenty repetitions of one pangram, where greedy output is hypersensitive to tiny numerical differences, so it is a poor discriminator and the comparison yielded nothing usable.  The reasoning that did work: the cold path produces coherent text under the relative convention, so the engine works that way; the ONLY difference between a cold run and a hit is skip; therefore the fix is to make the position sequence independent of skip rather than to change the convention.  That is a one-line change, seeding pos with 0 instead of skip when Active is constructed.  Because a cold start has skip == 0, the cold path is bit-for-bit unchanged, and oracle 6/6 and batch-check 16/16 passed as they were.  The bug is gone: at 63, 113 and 213 tokens, on both the live-only and the boundary path, three repeats agree with each other and with QW_PREFIX_SNAPSHOT=0, where before a hit returned an answer with no relation to the prompt.  I folded the missing gate into accept.sh - three identical requests must agree, and a hit must equal a cold start - taking the suite from 12 to 14 passed and 0 failed, ACCEPTED.  That gate is exactly what this class of bug needed, since the six-case oracle is entirely silent about it, as round 38 recorded when an absolute-position change altered some outputs and still passed 6/6.  Both cache paths are now on by default, memory only and no disk, as the user asked: QW_PREFIX_SNAPSHOT and QW_PREFIX_BOUNDARY default on and can be disabled with 0, while QW_PREFIX_DISK stays off because it writes gigabytes into the home directory.  The boundary path has to be on because hist holds the prompt plus everything generated, so on a straight repeat hist is LONGER than the prompt, is_prefix declines on its h.len() <= ids.len() check, and no live hit is possible; measured, three identical 913-token requests were three misses with only the live path enabled.  Measured benefit out of the box with no environment variables: a 913-token prompt took 19.86 s cold and then 0.88 s and 1.03 s, all three outputs identical, 23 times faster, and hit 912 of 913 prompt tokens.  The objective still stands on otps won by 15.5 per cent, warm TTFT now won with a verified-correct path, and cold TTFT still about nine times behind.
