history.title: Fair warm-versus-warm TTFT against llama.cpp, which retired my 23x claim and then cut warm TTFT from 95 ms to 71 ms by deleting a redundant export.  I had flagged that our 0.88 s was being compared against llama.cpp's cold number, so I measured llama-server, which enables prompt caching by default: cold it processed 905 tokens in 2230 ms at 406 tokens a second, and warm it processed 4 tokens in 98 ms for a 0.19 s wall.  Two errors of mine came out of this.  The 0.88 s was the whole request rather than TTFT - 16 tokens of generation alone account for about 0.57 s - and the comparison was against a cold run.  Measuring TTFT properly over a stream needed care: counting the first data chunk gives a false 5 ms because the server emits a role or empty chunk first, so only chunks carrying actual content count, and our /v1/completions streams delta.content rather than text.  Done correctly, our warm TTFT was 0.095 s against llama.cpp's 0.068 s, a 40 per cent loss.  I instrumented the cache with QW_PREFIX_TIME and found the restore is not the problem at all: importing a 208 MB blob at position 904 costs 3.5 ms, while the export costs 17.8 ms and ran on EVERY request including warm hits, re-exporting precisely the state it had just imported, with record_boundary cloning another 208 MB on top.  The save point sits at a.pf, before the next chunk is computed, so the state is identical to the one just restored - pure duplicated work.  The fix tracks restored_at and skips the export when the save position equals it, which is safe because the boundary and its blob were recorded by the earlier request and are still cached, and this request's ids[..a.pf] is exactly the prefix it restored from, so the prefix bookkeeping is unchanged.  Warm TTFT went from 0.095 s to 0.071-0.077 s against llama.cpp's 0.066-0.068 s, turning a 40 per cent loss into a 5 to 15 per cent one - essentially parity - and the warm export disappeared entirely, with accept.sh at 14 passed and 0 failed ACCEPTED.  Two incidental findings: the blob is dominated by a length-independent part, 160 MB at 136 tokens against 208 MB at 904, which is the GDN recurrent state at a fixed size per layer while the KV is only about 62 KB a token; and a cold prefill performs five exports, one per ladder boundary, about 85 ms in total, which is under one per cent of cold prefill and not worth optimising.  Corrected objective status: otps won by 15.5 per cent, warm TTFT 6 per cent behind, cold TTFT 5.4 times behind at 11.9 s against 2.23 s.  The TTFT objective is not met; the warm path is close and the cold path is still the gap.

history.title: Found that QW_PREFILL_CHUNK was silently pinned to 4, re-confirmed rather than repeated the conv_ring refutation, and localised the cold-prefill gap to a missing amortising GEMM plus dispatch overhead.  I started on cold prefill, where we take 11.9 s against llama.cpp's 2.23 s for about 910 tokens, having worked out from the time model that llama.cpp processes roughly 12 tokens per weight sweep while we process 4.  The obvious experiment was simply to raise QW_PREFILL_CHUNK, and it turned out that could never have worked: the value was clamped with .min(PREFILL_CHUNK), so every setting was silently pressed back to 4 while the log still printed the usual line.  I wasted a measurement cycle on it, seeing three runs at 13 to 15.6 seconds for chunks 4, 8 and 16 and putting the spread down to thermal drift.  The clamp now caps at the structurally valid value and says so with a warning, naming the reason.  That limit is not arbitrary: max_per_seq is (conv_k + TILE).next_power_of_two() - conv_k, which is 4 with the ring at 8, and the kernels reject anything wider with an explicit message.  The ring is parameterised in the kernel and could technically be widened to 32 to admit 16 rows, but the notes already record that as zero benefit, measured: going from 4 rows to 16 costs 4.96 times as much for exactly 4 times the work, purely linear and worse at long positions, because encode_rows switches to q4_gemv_b16 above 4 rows and that kernel costs 25.84 ms a row against the tile kernel's 27.47 - no better.  So the engine's chunk of 4 is already the faster path, and I did not repeat the refuted experiment.  I then falsified my own hypothesis that position degradation was the main problem: measured marginal rates on a 3405-token prompt are 14.91 ms a token over positions 852 to 1704 and 16.55 over 1704 to 2556, only 11 per cent worse across 1700 tokens, far milder than the impression given by the recorded 44.58 ms a token at position 6000, which came from a different measurement context.  The whole run was 52.9 seconds, 15.5 ms a token.  So the deficit is a flat factor of about six, and the per-row figures pin it down precisely: the tile kernel does amortise, about 30 ms for 4 rows or 7.5 ms a token, while q4_gemv_b16 does not amortise at all at 25.84 ms a row because each row re-reads all 14.4 GB, and llama.cpp's 2.46 ms a token implies about 12 tokens per sweep with almost no non-GEMV overhead.  The gap is therefore a missing genuinely amortising GEMM plus the non-GEMV work, about 5.5 ms a token across 689 dispatches.  Both are multi-round kernel projects; the time model already warns that even the planned transposed-activation GEMM only reaches about 131 tokens a second against llama.cpp's 406, so dispatch reduction has to come with it.  accept.sh is 14 passed and 0 failed ACCEPTED after the clamp change.  Objective status is unchanged: otps won by 15.5 per cent, warm TTFT 6 per cent behind, cold TTFT 5.4 to 6 times behind.

gates.G3: QW_PREFILL_CHUNK clamp made explicit and logged; silent no-op trap removed
gates.G4: cold-prefill gap localised; position degradation falsified as the main cause

history.title: Won TTFT: the first token was waiting for a second weight sweep.  After round 41 localised the cold-prefill gap to a missing amortising GEMM plus dispatch overhead, I first closed off the GEMV routes so as not to repeat refuted work: q4_gemv_tile is weight-stationary and does amortise four ways, while q4_gemv_b16 uses grid mapping by its own comment and does not amortise at all at 25.84 ms a row, and the sixteen-accumulator variant is already measured 22 per cent slower, so both extensions are dead.  I then turned to warm TTFT, which was only six per cent behind, and measured the floor: a one-token prompt costs 0.066 to 0.068 s and a 913-token warm hit 0.074 to 0.075, so the cache adds only 7 ms and the floor itself is about 66 ms - two weight sweeps at 30 ms each, the same two llama.cpp pays.  The engine's own log reported 0.0 s for a one-token prompt, which put the time after the logits were ready, and the cause was in emit: the generation branch pushed a.feed into a.all BEFORE the pass, so the first token - which the pass that finishes the prompt has already produced - only reached a.all on the next iteration and could not be sent until a second sweep had gone by.  The fix moves the bookkeeping to just after the pass that produces the token, so emit can hand it over in the same iteration.  My first attempt at that was wrong and the comparison caught it: I put the recording inside the per-row loop, and a prefill chunk has take rows, so every row recorded a token.  Diffing the emitted text against the previous binary showed it immediately - the code prompt came out as the last row's argmax repeated.  Moving the bookkeeping after the row loop and recording once per slot, on its last occurrence, made all four prompts byte-identical to the old build.  Result: one-token TTFT 0.066 to 0.034 s, 913-token warm TTFT 0.075 to 0.038-0.040 s against llama.cpp's 0.066-0.067, so warm TTFT went from ten per cent behind to 1.7 times ahead.  accept.sh is 14 passed and 0 failed ACCEPTED.  Objective status: otps won by 15.5 per cent, warm TTFT now won by 1.7 times, cold TTFT still 5.2 times behind at 11.6 s against 2.23 s.  Measured on the deployment path, both TTFT and otps now beat llama.cpp; the cold prefill is the remaining gap.

history.title: Established the Ollama baseline, which the objective names but I had never measured, and it changes the picture in both directions.  Ollama 0.34.1 was installed with only llama3, so I imported the local GGUF through a Modelfile rather than downloading anything: ollama create with FROM pointing at qwen38-27b-Q4_K_M.gguf.  The first attempt used the :local tag and failed in a confusing way - /api/tags listed the model but /api/generate said it was not found and ollama run tried to pull it, even though the manifest on disk was valid with schemaVersion 2, the right media types and a model layer matching the GGUF size, and a second server instance on another port behaved the same way.  The :local tag was the problem; recreating with the default latest tag fixed it.  Measured on the same 913-token raw prompt at greedy: Ollama's cold prefill is 905 tokens in 1.728 s, 524 tokens a second, which is FASTER than llama.cpp's 406, and its warm TTFT is 0.066 to 0.067 s, identical to llama.cpp's.  Our warm TTFT of 0.038 to 0.040 s beats both by 1.7 times.  For otps I hit a measurement trap worth recording: on the degenerate repeated prompt Ollama stops after 3 tokens because its default repeat penalty breaks the loop, and the 41 tokens a second it reports there is a short-burst figure that cannot be compared with anything.  Using a natural long-form prompt with 256 tokens requested gives Ollama 26.12 to 27.48 tokens a second against our 28.68 to 29.51, so we win otps by 7 to 13 per cent, and against llama.cpp's tg256 of 24.58 by 15.5 per cent.  Cold prefill remains a loss of 5.2 times to llama.cpp and 6.7 times to Ollama, at 11.6 s against 2.23 and 1.73.  So measured on the deployment path, both TTFT and otps now beat both llama.cpp and Ollama; the cold prefill is the only remaining gap and it is an order of magnitude.  I removed the broken :local tag; the working qwen38-27b:latest is left in place and costs 16 GB of disk, which the user may want to reclaim.

history.title: Profiled the cold prefill and refuted my own round-41 model: it is not CPU dispatch-encode overhead but pure GPU time, and the real structure is that we re-read all 14.4 GB of weights 226 times.  The user chose to keep attacking cold prefill, so I took the dispatch distribution with QW_DISPATCH_HIST=1 and QW_ENCODE_TIME=1.  The headline number killed my previous explanation: CPU encode is 1.43 ms while commit+wait is 538.97 ms across 2194 dispatches in 1186 encoders, so the dispatch count and its encoding cost are not the problem at all - the time is entirely on the GPU.  Round 41's estimate of 689 dispatches times about 8 microseconds of encoding per token, giving 5.5 ms a token, was simply wrong.  The histogram per batch is q4_gemv_hx 497 at 40 per cent, rmsnorm 129, ewise_add 128, rmsnorm_nw_tile 96, silu_mul 64, then copy_off, conv1d_silu_ring, gdn_step and rmsnorm_gated at 48 each, rmsnorm_s and rope_partial at 32, and the rest at 16.  The real structure is a 226-fold difference in weight traffic: with chunk 4 we sweep the whole 14.4 GB every four tokens, so a 905-token prefill reads about 3.25 TB, while llama.cpp fits the prompt in one n_batch of 2048 and reads the weights once, 14.4 GB.  Checking the compute side explains why that is enough for it: 27 billion parameters times 905 tokens is about 4.9e13 FLOPs, and at roughly 30 TFLOPS on the M5 Max GPU that is about 1.6 s, which matches its measured 2.23 s - so llama.cpp is genuinely compute-bound while we are bandwidth-bound.  Of our 13 s, about 6.8 s is the 3.25 TB of weight traffic and about 6 s is other GPU work.  This also finally explains the round-20 measurement that going from 4 rows to 16 costs 4.96 times as much for four times the work: q4_gemv_b16 uses grid mapping, so each row still re-reads the weights.  Genuine reuse needs a row-amortising GEMM using simdgroup matrix multiply, and that gives a concrete target: even 64 rows a pass would cut weight traffic from 3.25 TB to about 202 GB, fourteen sweeps or roughly 0.42 s, which should bring the total into the 2 to 3 second range and the same order as the competition.  That is the only path that closes the cold-prefill gap, and it costs a real 4-bit affine simdgroup GEMM.

history.title: Nearly mistook a measurement artefact for a 2x speedup, caught it by reading the macro, and then proved with a purpose-built kernel that k=8 is genuinely slower - closing the cheap path to cold prefill.  I swept k with the existing bench and saw k=4 8.677, k=6 5.759, k=8 4.319 ms a token, which looks like a doubling.  The numbers were suspiciously exact - 8.677 times 4/6 is 5.785 against 5.759 measured, and 8.677 over 2 is 4.339 against 4.319 - so I read the macro: the accumulator loop is unrolled over a compile-time NK, not over the runtime k scalar.  K_Q4_GEMV_K4_U4HX has NK=4, so it processes exactly four tokens whatever --tokens says, while the bench divides by the number asked for.  That is a trap in the tool rather than a property of the kernel, so I closed it: --rows 5 now requires --tokens 4 and otherwise fails with a message naming the reason and pointing at --rows 6.  Because the macro does take NK as a parameter, the real question was answerable, so I instantiated Q4_GEMV_KS_U4HX(q4_gemv_k8_u4hx, 8) and wired --rows 6 to it.  Interleaved A/B on the same thermal state gives k=4 8.649 and 10.045 ms a token against k=8 11.000 and 11.766, so k=8 is 17 to 27 per cent slower, and the effective bandwidth collapses from about 417 GB/s to about 154-164, the signature of register spilling.  Round 20's refutation therefore stands, and now for the right reason: it is not only that q4_gemv_b16 uses grid mapping, the weight-stationary family itself fails beyond k=4 under register pressure, which is also why the k=16 variant was 22 per cent slower.  So four tokens per weight sweep is the ceiling in this GEMV formulation, and the row-amortising simdgroup GEMM of round 44 is not an optional optimisation but the only remaining path - 4-bit affine weights have to be dequantised into shared memory before the tensor cores can use them, and only then does one copy of the weights serve dozens of rows.  No speedup this round, but a cheap possibility is closed off for good and a tool trap that would have misled later experiments is sealed.

history.title: Refuted k=6 as well, which closes the GEMV route for good, and measured the bandwidth headroom that remains.  Last round's k=6 figure was an artefact of the same bench trap, so this time I used the real K_Q4_GEMV_K6_U4H kernel - which the macro already instantiates with NK=6 - wired to a new --rows 7 with the same guard requiring --tokens 6, and ran an interleaved A/B.  k=4 gives 8.636 and 8.992 ms a token at 417.2 and 400.7 GB/s, while k=6 gives 9.027 and 11.041 at 266.1 and 217.6, so k=6 is 4 to 23 per cent slower with the same bandwidth collapse seen at k=8 (17 to 27 per cent slower) and k=16 (22 per cent slower).  Every k above four loses to register pressure, so four tokens per weight sweep is the sweet spot and the GEMV route is closed.  Sweeping also turned up a real if modest headroom: the round-3 k=1 kernel reaches 440 to 536 GB/s while the k=4 tile kernel reaches only 352 to 418, a 20 to 25 per cent bandwidth deficit that matches the kernel comment about re-reads of x from L2 growing with k.  k=4 is still three times better per token, so the amortisation is real, but closing that deficit would need several output rows to share a threadgroup so x could live in shared memory, and round 20 already measured that breaking weight-load coalescing costs more than it saves.  That leaves the simdgroup GEMM as the only path, and I wrote the design down for the next round.  The reason it is not optional is register economy: a simdgroup_matrix<half,8,8> fragment is 64 halfs spread over 32 lanes, one register each, whereas the GEMV accumulator costs one register per output element per thread, which is exactly why k=8 spills.  The design is a 64 by 32 output tile per threadgroup with K chunked by 32, weights dequantised into shared memory once per tile so one copy serves 32 tokens, activations staged in shared, and simdgroup_multiply_accumulate for the MACs.  K=5120 divides by 32 cleanly, but out_f takes several values including 248320 so tail blocks need handling.  Correctness first: a single-layer, single-tile version compared element by element against the existing GEMV before anything is wired into the runner.  Expected payoff is weight traffic dropping from 226 sweeps to between 1 and 14, which should bring cold prefill from 11.6 s into the 2 to 3 second range.

history.title: Measured the cold-prefill split directly and refuted an encoder-overhead hypothesis: GEMV is 73 per cent, not the 60 I estimated, and the non-GEMV 27 per cent is a fixed per-chunk cost whose amortisation I could not confirm.  I used QW_SKIP_KERNEL=q4_gemv to attribute the time: the full prefill is 12.57 s and with every q4_gemv dispatch dropped it is 3.36 s, so GEMV is 9.21 s, 73 per cent - higher than round 44's estimate and a stronger argument that the simdgroup GEMM is the main lever.  The histogram's 2194 dispatches in 1186 encoders, with barrier() ending an encoder and the next dispatch starting a new one, made me suspect commit-and-wait overhead as the source of the 12 microseconds per dispatch.  The code already carries a diagnostic for exactly this, QW_NO_ENC_SPLIT, which puts every dispatch in one encoder - unsafe, since Metal gives no inter-dispatch visibility inside an encoder, but it bounds the cost: 3.31 s against 3.39 s for the non-GEMV prefill, a saving of 0.08 s or 2 per cent, and on the full prefill it is slower, 14.10 s against 12.69.  So the hypothesis is refuted and the 12 microseconds is genuine serialised GPU latency.  Interleaving three prompt lengths with GEMV skipped shows the non-GEMV cost is a fixed 13 to 16 ms per four-row chunk whether there are 57 chunks or 227, so it does not scale with the data - the activation traffic is only a few GB, which at 500 GB/s would be milliseconds, not 3.36 s.  The obvious follow-up is whether that fixed cost is per pass or per row, because if it is per pass then raising the chunk from 4 to 16 would amortise it four ways and take the non-GEMV time from 3.36 s to about 0.84 s.  Four concurrent requests with distinct prompts, which should put 16 rows in a pass, came out only about 10 per cent better at 4.2 to 4.7 ms a token against 4.75, not four times better - but the server log only records the chunk size and gives no per-pass row count, so I cannot tell whether those requests actually shared passes.  The test therefore neither confirms nor refutes the hypothesis, and I am deliberately not changing the conv ring on the strength of it.  What is established: GEMV is 73 per cent of cold prefill, encoder splitting is not the problem, and the non-GEMV quarter is a fixed per-chunk cost.  The GEMM remains the lever with quantified payoff.

history.title: Showed that concurrent prefills are not batched at all, which invalidates round 47's ambiguous concurrency test, and worked out the realistic ceiling of the GEMM: about 4.2 s cold prefill against llama.cpp's 2.23 s, because the non-GEMV quarter does not change.  Round 47 tested whether the non-GEMV fixed cost amortises over rows by sending four concurrent requests, saw about 10 per cent, and could not confirm from the log whether they shared a pass.  This round I used a judgement that does not depend on the log: if batching happened, four concurrent requests would need proportionally fewer dispatches.  Four serial 455-token requests took 27.13 s and the same four concurrent took 27.65 s, identical, so the engine does not batch concurrent prefills at all.  Round 47's 10 per cent was noise, and the question of whether a larger chunk amortises the non-GEMV cost cannot be answered through the concurrency path - it needs the structure changed.  I then tried to break the 3.36 s down by kernel family with QW_SKIP_KERNEL and the data was unusable: base 14.44 s against 12.06 for rmsnorm, 11.70 for gdn, 12.82 for attn, and then 18.34 for silu and 21.79 for conv, slower than the baseline, with every best-of-three being a 0.08 s prefix-cache hit.  Single cold runs scatter over 11.7 to 21.8 s, far wider than the effects being measured, so cold-prefill family attribution needs interleaved repeats and this attempt is void.  The valuable part is the ceiling calculation.  Weight traffic is the number of token tiles times 14.4 GB: at the current k=4 that is 226 sweeps, 3.25 TB, 9.21 s; a GEMM with 32 tokens a tile needs 29 sweeps, 418 GB, 0.84 s; with 64 tokens a tile, 15 sweeps, 216 GB, 0.43 s.  Adding the unchanged 3.36 s of non-GEMV work gives about 4.2 and 3.8 s against llama.cpp's 2.23 and Ollama's 1.73.  So even a completely successful GEMM leaves cold prefill around 1.9 times slower than llama.cpp, because the non-GEMV quarter is a serial chain of about 1216 dependent dispatches per chunk, roughly 304 per token, where llama.cpp uses a few large fused kernels.  Closing the cold-prefill gap therefore needs both a GEMM and kernel fusion - two large pieces of work, not one optimisation.

history.title: Wrote the row-amortising simdgroup GEMM and verified it correct against the CPU reference on real weights, including the awkward shapes - but it is currently slower than the GEMV it is meant to replace, so it is not wired in.  The user chose the full rework, GEMM plus kernel fusion, so this round delivered the first milestone.  The kernel q4_gemm_tile uses BM=32 output rows by BN=32 tokens by BK=64 K values a step, 128 threads in four simdgroups, each owning a 16x16 quarter as four 8x8 fragments, and dequantises the 4-bit affine weights into threadgroup memory once per tile so all 32 tokens reuse them.  A new qwen38 gemm-check compares it element by element against cpu_reference, deliberately covering shapes that hit the tile tails: out_f values that are not a multiple of 32, including the 48-row GDN a and b projections, and a token count of 40 that is not a multiple of the 32-token tile.  All four cases pass with a worst relative error of 3.347e-4, which is what half-precision dequantisation should cost.  The first run produced all zeros, and the cause is worth recording: dispatch_threads takes its grid in THREADS rather than threadgroups, so passing the tile count launched two threadgroups and left almost the whole output untouched; the existing encode_k multiplies out_f by 32 for exactly this reason.  The problem is performance.  At k=32 the GEMM costs 13.0 ms a token and at k=64 between 10.8 and 14.9, against the GEMV's 8.7 to 9.1 at k=4, and its effective bandwidth is only 15 to 35 GB/s against the GEMV's 396 to 414 - it reads 14.4 GB in about 416 ms, twelve times slower than memory.  So it is compute or synchronisation bound rather than bandwidth bound, which is the opposite of the point.  I tested the obvious lever and it went the wrong way: BK=128 is worse at 19.6 ms a token, so barrier count is not the cause, and BK=256 exceeds the 32 KB threadgroup memory limit at 36864 bytes, which is a hard constraint.  The kernel is therefore left out of the runner - encode_rows still sends rows above four to the GEMV b16 path - because shipping an unverified or slower kernel as the default is exactly what must not happen.  Next: occupancy is the likely culprit given the shared-memory footprint at this tile size, and raising BN to reuse each dequantised weight across more tokens, or double-buffering to hide the dequantisation, are the candidates.

history.title: Attributed the GEMM properly and found the time is in neither the dequantisation nor the MACs but in the loads, then tried double buffering, which broke correctness and was slower, and reverted it.  Instead of guessing further I added a diagnostic scalar to the kernel: mode 0 is the full kernel, mode 1 replaces the dequantised value with a constant, mode 2 skips the MAC loop.  At k=32 the full kernel is 14.124 ms a token, skipping the dequantisation is 14.168 - identical, so the dequantisation ALU cost is nothing - and skipping the MACs is 12.589, only 11 per cent faster.  So 89 per cent of the time is the staging: the weight loads and the barriers, reading 14.4 GB at 33.6 GB/s against the 477 GB/s the hardware reaches on a plain sweep.  I also closed off two cheaper explanations.  Bank conflicts looked promising because the weight tile's unpadded stride of 64 halfs is exactly 128 bytes, the 32-bank period, so eight rows of a simdgroup_load would land on the same bank; padding to 72 halfs, which is 36 words and 36 mod 32 is 4, made no difference at 13.4 against 13.0, so it is not the cause.  BK tuning went the wrong way too: 128 is worse at 19.6 ms a token and 256 exceeds the 32 KB threadgroup memory limit.  The textbook fix for a load-bound GEMM is double buffering, so I implemented it - staging the next K-step before consuming the current one so the device-memory latency overlaps the MACs.  It failed on both counts.  Correctness broke, relative error 1.27e-1, because a single barrier per step cannot protect the buffer being read from being overwritten by the next staging; protecting it needs a second barrier, which puts the barrier count back where it started.  And it was slower, 17.7 against 14.1 ms a token, because doubling the shared footprint halves occupancy, which more than cancels the prefetch benefit.  I reverted to the single-buffered kernel and re-ran gemm-check, which passes again with a worst relative error of 3.347e-4.  The conclusion is that the bottleneck is memory-level parallelism at this tile size - each thread issues only two loads per K-step and the barriers serialise them - and not ALU work, bank conflicts, or the barrier count itself.  The direction is therefore higher occupancy through a smaller tile and smaller shared footprint, not more buffering.  The mode scalar stays in the bench as QW_GEMM_MODE for future attribution.

history.title: Refuted the activation-traffic hypothesis and showed BM=64 is both wrong and slower, but sharpened the case for the GEMM: it is doing one weight sweep where the GEMV needs eight, so fixing its bandwidth would be an eight-fold win on that portion.  I had calculated that because a tile covers only 32 output rows the activation tile is re-read once per row block, making activation traffic about 57 GB against the weights' 14.4 GB.  A new mode 3 that skips the activation staging saved only 15 per cent, and since mode 1 came out slower than mode 0 the noise is about 10 per cent, so that saving is not significant - the activation re-reads are hitting L2, which is plausible since one linear's activation tile is only 320 KB.  Not the bottleneck.  I then tried BM=64 with 256 threads, eight simdgroups covering 64 by 32.  It failed correctness with relative error 1.0 because my stride replacement missed the first staging loop, so half the weight rows were never staged, and even so it was much slower at 24.4 against 14.1 ms a token, so a larger tile at this shared budget only makes things worse.  Reverted, and gemm-check passes again at 3.347e-4 with 14.003 ms a token.  The useful part is the framing.  For 32 tokens the GEMV at k=4 needs eight sweeps at 34.5 ms each, 276 ms, while the GEMM needs one sweep taking 429 ms - the GEMM replaces eight sweeps with one but its single sweep is twelve times slower per byte.  If the GEMM's sweep ran at the 417 GB/s the GEMV reaches, those 32 tokens would take 34.5 ms, eight times faster than the GEMV.  The prize is real and large, and the obstacle is precisely located: each threadgroup has only about 1 KB of loads in flight per K-step, so 80 concurrent threadgroups give roughly 80 KB when saturating 477 GB/s needs about 238 KB.  Double buffering would fix the bytes in flight but the 32 KB shared-memory budget will not let it keep its occupancy.  The candidates are to have each thread dequantise only the elements its own fragment needs, which removes the weight staging and its barriers altogether at the cost of depending on the simdgroup_matrix fragment layout, or to trade a smaller BK for double buffering at unchanged occupancy.

history.title: Found and fixed the real bug behind the GEMM's terrible bandwidth - every uint was loaded once per nibble, eight times over - which bought a genuine 30 per cent, and rejected two further attempts with the measurements recorded.  Last round I blamed bytes in flight; recomputing showed that was wrong, since the sixteen staging iterations are independent loads the compiler can issue in parallel, giving about 8 KB in flight per threadgroup and 640 KB across eighty, far above the 238 KB needed.  Reading the loop instead of theorising about it found the actual defect: the loop is indexed per nibble but loads the whole uint that contains eight of them, so every uint was fetched eight times and the useful bandwidth was an eighth of what the memory system was asked for.  Restructuring so each thread loads one uint and expands all eight nibbles took k=32 from 13.3-14.1 ms a token at 33.6 GB/s to 8.7-10.6 at 42-52, a real 30 per cent rather than the theoretical eightfold, because eight lanes of a warp reading the same uint get merged by the coalescer.  Re-attributing after the fix changed the picture: skipping the activation staging now saves 52 per cent, skipping the MACs 37, skipping the dequantisation only 12 - so the activation staging is the largest single item.  I then made two attempts and both were rejected by measurement.  Coalescing the activation read looked obviously right, since consecutive threads were K*2 bytes apart and each two-byte load should have been its own transaction; swapping the indices made the kernel 40 per cent SLOWER at 12.3-13.5 against 8.7-10.6, because the activation tile is only a few KB and every row block re-reads it, so it is L2 resident and the uncoalesced pattern costs nearly nothing, while the coalesced form makes the shared writes conflict.  I reverted it and wrote the reasoning into the comment so it is not retried.  BM=64 halves the activation traffic, which is out_f times k times K over BM, but it grows shared memory to 22.5 KB and loses more to occupancy than it gains, 13.0-17.6 against 8.7-10.6.  The state now is that the GEMM is at parity with the GEMV per token - 9.1-10.6 at k=32 against 10.0-10.4 at k=4 - and its per-token cost barely improves with k, which means it is not bandwidth bound but has staging and MACs serialised by the barriers, with the activation shared-memory round trip as the largest term.  That round trip is inherent to simdgroup_matrix, which requires its operands in memory.  Parity is not enough to replace a working kernel, so it stays unshipped; the one remaining path is to have each thread construct its own fragment elements directly and bypass shared memory entirely.

history.title: Widened the prefill chunk from 4 to 32 by giving the row path a loop over the tile kernel and sizing the convolution ring from a new PASS_ROWS_MAX, which is verified correct and consistently faster but only by 3 to 14 per cent, refuting my amortisation theory - the per-pass overhead turns out to be per-row.  I started by recomputing what llama.cpp actually does, and found I had it wrong: at pp512 it takes 0.71 s for 512 tokens, which is ONE weight sweep at 20 GB/s, so its prefill is compute bound at roughly 41 TFLOPS, while our GEMM at BN=32 needs sixteen sweeps for the same 512 tokens.  The gap is therefore both that each of our sweeps is slow and that we need too many of them.  The row path was the part I could change cheaply: encode_rows sent anything above four rows to encode_b, the batch-b kernel that costs 25.84 ms a row, so I replaced it with a loop over the tile kernel, and decoupled the convolution ring from TILE by introducing PASS_ROWS_MAX of 32, which makes conv_ring 64, BATCH_MAX 32 and the prefill chunk 32.  The subtlety is that K4_U4HX is unrolled over four tokens and ignores the k scalar - the trap from round 15 - so a partial chunk still computes and writes four rows; sizing BATCH_MAX at least as large as PASS_ROWS_MAX keeps those three extra rows inside the allocation, where their outputs are simply never read.  My prediction was that this would amortise the fixed per-pass overhead of about 14.5 ms eight-fold, taking the non-GEMV part from 3.36 s to 0.42 s.  It did not: an interleaved A/B on one prompt with fresh servers gave 1.03x and 1.14x, 11.822 and 11.630 against 12.126 and 13.242 seconds.  That refutes the model - the non-GEMV cost is per row, not per pass, and the round-17 measurement that looked like a fixed per-chunk cost was taken with four rows in every chunk, so it could not tell the two apart.  I also feared the ring growth would cost eight times the convolution window buffer, but measurement says memory is neutral: RSS 41.82 GB at chunk 4 against 41.81 at chunk 32.  All three gates pass: verify at parity 6 of 6, the batch gate with a worst logit difference of 0.0000, and accept.sh at 14 passed and 0 failed.  So the change is kept - verified, consistently faster, and memory neutral - but it is a modest win, not the one I predicted.  Separately, an interleaved A/B of the GEMM against the GEMV over three rounds gives 1.09 to 1.15 times, 240 to 253 ms for one sweep against 275 to 276 for the eight sweeps the GEMV needs, which is the next step: wiring the GEMM into this wide row path.

history.title: Tried wiring the GEMM into the wide-row path and got apparently catastrophic numbers, then found the measurement environment was contaminated - this Web GUI is itself consuming 45-55 per cent of the GPU, leaving idle utilisation at 61-70 per cent and inflating every timing by roughly 25-35 per cent.  The conclusion is therefore void rather than negative, and I reverted to the committed chunk=32 version.  The structural finding that motivated the attempt stands: standard GEMM weight traffic is out_f times K times half a byte times k over BN, so at BN=32 a 512-token prompt costs 230 GB of weight traffic and sixteen sweeps, while BN=128 would cost 57.6 GB and four - llama.cpp's prefill is fast because its BN approaches the whole batch, and ours is pinned by the GDN recurrence step.  I wired the GEMM into encode_rows for rows above TILE, replacing the tile-kernel loop, and got 21.5 and 18.3 seconds against the loop's 11.6 and 11.8.  I guessed the cause was small out_f values, where the GEMM's 32-row tiling leaves out_f=48 with two threadgroups against the tile kernel's forty-eight, so I gated it on out_f at least 2048 - and it got worse, 22.7 and 25.9.  Reverting gave 23.8 and 26.3, which is when the real explanation appeared: the code was not the variable.  WindowServer and this GUI's renderer are together burning the GPU, idle utilisation reads 61 to 70 per cent, and the timing tracks it, 14.7 seconds at 61 per cent against 16.3 at 70.  Re-measuring the reverted build in that state gives 14.4 to 16.3 seconds, so the GEMM's 18.3 to 25.9 and the loop's 23.8 to 26.3 overlap and the apparent two-fold regression was a load artefact.  I reverted to the committed chunk=32 version, whose correctness is unaffected - all gates had passed with the GEMM wired, verify at parity 6 of 6 and accept.sh at 14 of 14, so it was correct, merely unmeasurable.  The lesson is that qwen38 bench weights linears by bytes, where the huge ones dominate, while in the engine every linear sits on the serial critical path, so the two cannot be inferred from each other; and that every A/B must record idle GPU utilisation first, or the GUI's load will be read as a code regression.

history.title: Produced a valid same-load head-to-head - Ollama 1.76-1.86 s against our 14.6 s on a 905-token cold prefill - and found a sharp diagnostic in the process: Ollama is barely affected by the GUI's GPU contention while we are badly affected, which says its prefill is throughput bound and ours is latency bound.  Getting there needed a methodology fix.  I first warmed Ollama with the same prompt I then measured, and it reported 0.102 s for 957 tokens, 9300 tokens a second, which is a prefix-cache hit and not a prefill; with genuinely fresh prompts sent once each, Ollama takes 1.763 and 1.858 s for 957 tokens, about 525 tokens a second, against our 14.575 and 14.697 s for 905 tokens, about 62 - so we are 8.1 times behind on cold time to first token.  Both were measured with idle GPU utilisation between 83 and 98 per cent, so the load is the same on both sides.  The diagnostic is in comparing that with the clean-state numbers: Ollama went from 1.73 to 1.76-1.86 s, essentially unmoved, while we went from 11.6 to 14.6, up 26 per cent.  A kernel that saturates the arithmetic units does not care that something else is using the GPU; one whose effective bandwidth is 33 to 60 GB/s against the 477 the hardware reaches is latency bound and collapses under contention.  That is direct evidence for what the attribution has been saying, and it sets the goal for the kernel work: make it throughput bound.  On environment, minimising the GUI window did not help - idle utilisation held at 63 to 71 per cent across three minutes, from WindowServer and this app's renderer - so every comparison has to be collected in pairs under the same load, and mixing numbers from different load states systematically understates us.  I also found Ollama's qwen38-27b:local manifest is invisible to the running server, the same stale-manifest problem as before, and created qwen38-27b:bench from the same GGUF rather than restarting the user's service.

history.title: Refuted the barrier cost outright - removing the per-K-step barrier changed the timing by nothing at all - and then turned the dispatch histogram on the non-GEMV half for the first time, which shows it is pure per-row dispatch latency: about 218k dependent dispatches for 905 tokens at roughly 12 to 15 microseconds each, matching the measured 3.4 seconds.  I added mode 4 to the GEMM, which skips the per-K-step barrier and gives wrong answers but valid timing, and interleaved it against the full kernel: 8.031 and 8.078 ms a token for mode 0 against 8.029 and 8.070 for mode 4, 257 and 258 ms a sweep either way.  Identical.  That closes the list of explanations for the GEMM's slowness - bank conflicts, barrier count, occupancy, bytes in flight, BM=64, double buffering, activation coalescing, the MACs at 17 per cent, the dequantisation at 12 per cent, and now the barriers at zero - leaving only the staging itself, about 212 ms a sweep, still unexplained.  The more productive half of the round was the histogram.  One prefill pass of sixteen rows issues 7525 dispatches: 1988 tile-kernel GEMVs, and then 768 each of copy_off, conv1d_silu_ring, gdn_step and rmsnorm_gated, 512 each of rmsnorm_s and rope_partial.  Those 768s are 48 GDN layers times 16 rows, so the non-GEMV work is dispatched per row; 905 tokens times 29 passes times 7525 over 16 rows is about 218k dependent dispatches, which at 12 to 15 microseconds each is 2.6 to 3.3 seconds and matches the measured 3.4.  That also explains why round 22's chunk 4 to 32 bought so little: the cost is per row, so carrying more rows per pass does not reduce it.  I also found a silently imposed cap: the pass row budget was computed as MAX_BATCH minus the decoders, and MAX_BATCH is the slot count at 16, so a single prefilling slot could only ever get 16 rows - visible in the histogram as four tile-kernel sub-chunks per linear instead of eight.  I decoupled the row budget to PASS_ROWS_MAX of 32, leaving the slot count and KV allocation untouched; the histogram then shows 3976 GEMV dispatches, exactly 497 times 8, while the dispatches per token are unchanged because twice the dispatches now cover twice the rows.  That change is performance neutral today, 13.339 s within the noise of the 13.6 to 14.7 s the previous build measured, but it is a prerequisite for the GEMM's BN of 32 to cover a whole pass.  Gates pass: verify at parity 6 of 6 and the batch gate with a worst logit difference of 0.0000.  The roadmap is now clear and it is the only remaining way to cut the non-GEMV: batch the row-parallel kernels.  copy_off, conv1d_silu_ring, rmsnorm_gated, rmsnorm_s and rope_partial are 44 per cent of the dispatches and are all parallel over rows, so they can collapse to one dispatch a pass; gdn_step is a recurrence and must stay per row at 10 per cent.  The target is 3.4 seconds down to about 0.8.

history.title: Found that the tile-wide convolution kernel was written, commented and never wired up, wired it for the prefill case, removed 87696 dispatches from a 905-token prefill, and then measured it 0.43 to 0.99 times - a serious regression - so reverted it.  The more important result is that this refutes the dispatch-latency model I built last round.  conv1d_silu_ring_tile was already defined and even folds the ring update in, with a comment saying it removes a copy launch per row; its semantics are exactly what a prefill chunk needs, since row r uses slot slot0+r, reading this pass's rows from the staging buffer and older ones from the ring.  I gated it on all rows being one sequence at consecutive positions, falling back to the per-row loop for a batch pass, and the dispatch histogram went from 14633 to 11609 a pass: conv1d_silu_ring from 1536 to zero and copy_off from 1536 to zero, 3024 fewer dispatches a pass and 87696 fewer across the prompt.  Both gates passed.  But the interleaved A/B, with md5 confirming the two binaries differ, gave 0.99 and 0.77 times on the first two rounds and then 0.43 and 0.65 on the next two, 39.5 and 26.9 seconds against 16.9 and 17.6.  The tile kernel is much slower per element: it has a data-dependent branch choosing between the staging buffer and the window, a variable base address, and an extra ring store, while the per-row kernel addresses the window with a constant slot and coalesces cleanly.  Per-element efficiency beats dispatch count.  Reverted, and the rebuilt binary's md5 matches the pre-change one exactly.  That kills last round's model: I had computed 218k dispatches times 15.6 microseconds as 3.4 seconds, matching the measured non-GEMV time, and set the roadmap from it.  Removing 87696 dispatches made things slower, so the match was a numerical coincidence and not causal evidence.  The non-GEMV 3.4 seconds is real per-element kernel work, not dispatch overhead, and the roadmap of batching the row-parallel kernels is void.  One more warning worth recording: after the revert, verify reported oracle parity failed once and then passed 6 of 6 on an immediate re-run of the byte-identical binary, and the batch gate's worst logit difference moved from 0.0000 to 0.0352.  Under this GPU contention a gate failure needs a re-run before it means anything.

history.title: Mapped the GEMM's cost structure and knocked out both remaining hypotheses.  Raising the shared footprint hurts (a 256-wide weight staging span, which gives each row 128 contiguous bytes, went from 256 to 298 ms; BM=16 went to 334) and lowering it hurts too (BM=16 at 9.5 KB, three threadgroups per SM, 334 ms), so the baseline BM=32 BK=64 is a local optimum and occupancy is not the limit.  Then I built a direct bandwidth probe: mode 5 reads the weights at the address a K-major layout would put them at, which is wrong on purpose but times the access pattern.  My first version of that probe was dishonest - it changed the address without changing the lane mapping, so consecutive lanes still strode across out_f and it came out worse at 269 ms - and I fixed it so consecutive lanes take consecutive output columns, which is what a K-major layout actually needs to read 128 contiguous bytes.  Corrected, it was 268 ms against the row-major 259, so the 32-byte-per-row granularity is not what costs the bandwidth.  That closes the access-pattern explanation as well.  What the mode diagnostics do give is the cost structure: weight staging about 120 ms for 14.4 GB, which is 120 GB/s against the GEMV's 400, the activation staging about 92 ms, and the MACs about 47 ms.  The activation staging is the one that is clearly wrong rather than merely slow: consecutive lanes take consecutive tokens, so neighbouring lanes are K*2 = 10240 bytes apart and every load is its own line, saved only by the tile being L2 resident.  The comment in the kernel records that swapping the indices to coalesce the read was tried and made the kernel 40 per cent slower, because the shared write then conflicts.  Getting both at once needs the shared tile stored as [token][k] - contiguous lanes read contiguous k, so the global read coalesces and the shared write stays contiguous - followed by a transposed load into the fragment.  I tried that twice, once straight from device memory and once from a transposed shared tile, and both gave a relative error of 1.7 with numerically identical errors, so the transpose semantics are still not pinned down and I am not adopting it.  The fallback for next round is to avoid the transposed load entirely: stage the weights as [k][row] and the activations as [token][k], load both without transpose, and let the accumulator come out as [token][out], storing it back with simdgroup_store's transpose flag.  gemm-check passed at 3.347e-4 after every experiment and after the revert.

history.title: Wired the simdgroup GEMM into encode_rows, where its kernel argument had been sitting unused behind a let underscore, and the batch gate caught it: 16 of 16 slots disagreed with their independent runs, worst logit difference 17.02.  Isolated cleanly by moving the threshold - 17, which sends the sixteen-row pass through the GEMV, passes at 0.0000, while 16, which sends it through the GEMM, fails at 17.0195.  So the GEMM is correct in isolation, where gemm-check puts it at 3.347e-4 on a single linear with forty tokens, and correct for the single-sequence passes that verify exercises at 6 of 6, but wrong on the engine's thirty-two-row batched pass.  The more useful discovery is why this stayed hidden: no gate covers the GEMM by default.  verify's prompts are sixteen to twenty-four tokens, so their single pass is below the threshold and takes the GEMV; and batch-check's independent runs use the single-row kernel, which the dispatch histogram confirms by showing 497 q4_gemv_hx even when the threshold is forced down.  Only forcing the threshold to 16 or below made the GEMM meet an end-to-end gate for the first time, and it failed immediately - which also means the earlier accept 14 of 14 with the GEMM wired was never evidence that the GEMM was correct.  Before that I corrected a measurement trap of my own making: the k=8 kernel is unrolled over a compile-time NK of 8 and processes eight tokens whatever --tokens says, so timing it at thirty-two tokens reported 98 ms and 146.8 GB/s, a fictitious 2.6 times better than the GEMM.  Measured at the token count it actually does, k=4 is 9.951 ms a token at 362 GB/s, k=6 is 10.811 and k=8 is 12.169, so the engine's choice of k=4 is right and the earlier refutation of the wider GEMV kernels stands.  The bench guards rows 5 and 7 with an ensure but not rows 6, which is the hole the bad number came through.  What the round does establish is the break-even: the GEMV sweeps the weights once per four rows at 39.6 ms and the GEMM once per thirty-two at 257 ms, so at thirty-two rows the GEMM is 257 against 317 and would be 19 per cent better, and below about 26 rows the GEMV wins.  Reverted, since shipping an unverified path is not an option; verify is back to 6 of 6 and the batch gate to 0.0000.

history.title: Proved the GEMM's end-to-end defect is real and found why gemm-check misses it.  gemm-check passes at 3.347e-4 with 32 tokens, the exact row count of the engine's batched pass, so the fault is not the token count.  The decisive test was a templated long chat prompt through the real endpoint, long enough to force a 32-row prefill pass, compared between the two paths: the GEMV answers correctly that the user is asking how a refrigerator works, while the GEMM misreads the question as being about the evaporator.  That is a wrong answer, not numerical noise.  The reason gemm-check cannot see it is its activations: it feeds uniform random values in minus one to one, which have no outliers, while real activations do, and MLX's four-bit format shares one scale across each group of sixty-four K values, so a single large channel raises the whole group's scale and costs the other channels precision.  Random uniform input systematically understates that error.  I added QW_GEMM_CHECK_ALL to sweep all 497 quantised linears, since the default four shapes all pass, but the CPU reference is too slow and it timed out at 600 seconds; the right next step is a GPU-against-GPU comparison of the GEMM against the GEMV kernel rather than against the CPU.  Reverted the wiring again - verify back to 6 of 6, batch gate to 0.0000, gemm-check to 3.347e-4, and the all-linears switch kept as a diagnostic.  The strategic picture after eleven rounds on cold prefill: otps is won against both rivals at 28.7 against 24.58 and 26.1 to 27.5, warm TTFT is won at 0.039 against 0.067, and cold TTFT is lost by 6.6 times at 11.6 seconds against 1.76.  Cold prefill is 232 weight sweeps, 3.34 TB at about 400 GB/s, which is 8.35 seconds, plus 3.4 seconds of non-GEMV work.  The GEMM's BN of 32 would cut the sweep count eightfold but runs at 56 GB/s, so the net gain is only 19 per cent, and even at an ideal 36 ms a sweep it would be 1.04 plus 3.4 seconds, still two and a half times behind Ollama.  Cold TTFT is structurally out of reach in this architecture, and the GEMM's bandwidth has resisted eleven rounds of hypotheses - bank conflicts, barriers, occupancy, bytes in flight, BM, double buffering, coalescing, the MACs, the dequantisation, access granularity and K-major layout.

history.title: Pinned down the GEMM defect exactly as the user asked and closed the gate blind spot that hid it.  The kernel is clean: I rewrote gemm-check's all-linears mode as a GPU-against-GPU comparison against the GEMV tile kernel the engine actually runs, and all 497 quantised linears pass at a worst relative error of 9.662e-4 on uniform random activations, 9.718e-4 with a ten-times outlier in one channel of every sixty-four, and 9.416e-4 at thirty times. That also refutes my own hypothesis from last round that outliers were the cause.  The real defect is not in the kernel but in the numerical path: the GEMM accumulates with simdgroup_matrix in a different order from the GEMV, so it agrees only to about 1e-3 per linear, whereas the GEMV path is bit-identical to the single-row kernel by construction.  That difference compounds through sixty-four layers and the GDN recurrence into roughly seventeen logits, which is enough to flip tokens, and on a long prompt the GEMM misread the question - answering about the evaporator where the GEMV correctly explained how a refrigerator works.  So the nineteen per cent cold-prefill gain is not worth breaking bit-identity and changing, and in the one case measured degrading, the answer.  I am not shipping it.  The oracle blind spot is now explained precisely: all six oracle prompts are five to twenty tokens, far below the twenty-six-row switch, so verify never reaches the GEMM, and batch-check's independent runs use the single-row kernel.  To close it I added a prefill-width determinism gate to accept.sh: the same long prompt under QW_PREFILL_CHUNK=4, which must take the GEMV, and =32, which takes the wide path, has to give the same answer. I proved the gate works rather than assuming it: with the GEMM wired in it fails with chunk 4 and chunk 32 disagreeing, 14 passed and 1 failed, NOT ACCEPTED, and after the revert it passes at 15 passed and 0 failed, ACCEPTED.  Two diagnostics are kept: QW_GEMM_CHECK_ALL for the all-linears GPU comparison, since the CPU reference is too slow to sweep them, and QW_GEMM_CHECK_OUTLIER for injecting channel outliers.

history.title: Re-verified the otps lead with a paired measurement and found the biggest remaining win: speculative decoding is worth 40.6 per cent but the server does not support it at all.  Paired against Ollama on the same prompt with 128 tokens and prefill excluded, we lead by 12.0 and 9.8 per cent, so the otps win is real at about ten to twelve per cent, and the three-metric picture is unchanged: otps won, warm TTFT won by 1.7 times, cold TTFT lost by 6.6.  Then I measured QW_SPEC in gen: 26.65 tokens a second without it and 37.46 with it, a 40.6 per cent gain, with the output byte-identical under the existing spec-versus-plain gate.  qw-server has no support for QW_SPEC whatsoever - the string does not appear in that crate - so the server leaves that forty per cent on the table, and wiring it in would turn a ten per cent lead over Ollama into roughly sixty-four.  I worked out what the integration needs.  spec_step is a complete single-sequence speculative step: it drafts three tokens through mtp_step, verifies with a four-row forward2, takes the longest agreeing prefix, and rolls the recurrent state back with commit_row.  Three things pin it to one sequence: forward2 hardcodes sequence zero in its row list, commit_row copies into the recurrent state at offset zero, and the MTP head's k and v caches are single-sequence.  For a single-request server that is exactly the case that matters, since the first request lands in slot zero, so spec_step can be reused as it stands.  The plan is a strictly guarded fast path: only when QW_SPEC is set - default off - and exactly one slot is active and that slot is zero and it is decoding, call spec_step and emit the accepted tokens; warm the MTP cache during that slot's prefill by calling mtp_step per row after the pass; and extend the byte-identity gate to the server endpoint.  The cost is that warming the MTP cache slows prefill by about 3.3 per cent, measured at 0.979 against 0.948 seconds in gen - a little cold TTFT for forty per cent more otps.

history.title: Found the biggest remaining win - speculative decoding is worth 40.6 per cent and the server has none of it - did the enabling refactor, then discovered the blocker before touching the engine, and closed the gate that blocker sits behind.  First I re-verified the otps lead by paired measurement against Ollama: plus 12.0 and plus 9.8 per cent, so otps is genuinely won at about ten to twelve.  Then QW_SPEC in gen: 26.65 tokens a second without, 37.46 with, a 40.6 per cent gain, byte-identical under the existing gate.  qw-server never mentions QW_SPEC, so the server leaves all of that on the table.  I worked out that spec_step is a complete single-sequence step - draft three through mtp_step, verify with a four-row forward2, keep the longest agreeing prefix, roll the recurrent state back with commit_row - pinned to sequence zero by forward2, by commit_row writing the recurrent state at offset zero, and by the draft head holding one k and one v cache.  The first real piece of work is done and verified: mtp_step reads the decoder hidden at offset zero, so only a one-row-at-a-time prefill can keep the draft head in step, and a chunked prefill that computes up to thirty-two rows in one weight sweep needs to point it at whichever row produced each token.  I renamed the body to mtp_step_at(hrow, ...) and kept mtp_step as a thin wrapper at row zero, offsetting only the decoder-hidden read and leaving the head's three internal scratch accesses at zero; the spec-versus-plain gate still shows byte-identical output over three hundred tokens.  Then I stopped, because I found the blocker before writing any engine code.  Generation is driven with relative positions - QW_POS_DEBUG prints pos zero then pos one - while a prefill pass feeds absolute ones, and gen's spec_step starts at ids.len().  Those positions are load-bearing: the GDN convolution ring indexes by pos modulo conv_ring and the draft head keys its own cache by them.  Worse, that area was ungated: it was already known that turning the relative generation positions absolute altered some outputs and still passed the six-case oracle, because every oracle prompt is short enough to hide it.  So integrating spec now would mean building on an unverified convention.  Instead I closed the gate first.  accept.sh now pins the server's entire answer to a long prompt, 293 characters, against a stored expectation, and I proved the gate works rather than assuming it: advancing the decode position by two instead of one makes it fail with the answer drifting at character eight, from 'The user is asking' to 'You', and reverting makes it pass.  The engine itself is untouched, so no risk was taken. The suite is at 16 passed and 0 failed, ACCEPTED.

history.title: Found and fixed a real generation-quality defect in the server: it restarted the position sequence at zero.  prepare() initialised the decode position to zero so that a prefix-cache hit and a cold start would drive the same sequence, but a prefill pass feeds ABSOLUTE positions, so starting at zero restarts the sequence in the middle of the prompt: the first generated token is announced as position zero when it really sits at the prompt length, and both the rotary embedding and the GDN convolution ring are driven from it.  On the same twelve prompt tokens with greedy decoding the CLI, which feeds absolute positions and is what the mlx-lm oracle pins, answers with the founding of the city of Rome in 753 BC and the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 AD, while the server degenerated into 'The Roman Empire was a vast and powerful state' repeated.  A two-build A/B on three prompts confirms the direction: the refrigerator answer changed from 'a step-by-step visual guide' to 'a step-by-step explanation' with no images supplied, the chat answer for the water-tank question changed from 'the user is asking me to discuss a topic' to 'the user is asking me to describe the main design decisions', and the raw-completion answer changed from the meta-commentary 'The question is asking for a practical, real-world engineering answer' to the actual answer beginning '1. Capacity and geometry'.  The fix is one line - pos becomes prompt_len, captured before ids moves into the slot - and because that value depends only on the prompt, a cache hit and a cold start stay identical, which the existing cache gate confirms still passes.  No gate had caught it: the six oracle cases only exercise the CLI, the endpoint tests check response shape rather than content, and the cache test compares the server against itself so both sides were wrong the same way.  Server-side generation content had no coverage at all.  I added one: accept.sh now requires the server's raw-completion text for a long prompt to equal gen's greedy_text over 64 tokens, and I proved it catches the bug by running the old binary's server against the CLI, which diverges at character two.  The suite is at 17 passed and 0 failed, ACCEPTED.  This also removes the blocker on the speculative-decoding integration, because spec_step expects absolute positions and the server now drives the same convention.

history.title: Wired speculative decoding into the server (it had none, while gen measured +40.6%) and fixed the two real bugs that exposed.  (1) commit_row rewound the recurrent state with state.len_bytes()/2, which carries neither the slot count nor the row count: state holds `batch` sequences back to back, so on the sixteen-slot server that expression names EIGHT sequences' worth and the rewind copied eight sequences of snapshot into sequence 0.  At batch 1 - what gen loads - it is exactly right, which is why gen's spec==plain gate passed over 300 tokens at a 57.4% acceptance rate while the server diverged from the CLI at character 36 of a 64-token answer.  Localised by QW_SPEC=1 QW_NO_ACCEPT=1 matching the CLI exactly, which cleared the verify pass and left only the rewind.  Now len_bytes()/batch/2.  Two plausible-looking derivations (snap_stride/TILE as offset and length; snap_stride/TILE as offset with state/2 as length) both BROKE gen, which is the useful lesson: keeping the verified batch-1 path byte-identical mattered more than the formula that looked right.  (2) completion_tokens counted pieces, not tokens, so a four-token answer from a multi-token speculative step was billed as two; EngineEvent::Piece now carries its token count.  Also added draft-head warming during prefill, mirroring gen exactly (every row with a known successor, never the last), without which the drafts are junk and spec is slower than plain.  Gates 19 passed / 0 failed, ACCEPTED, with two new content-level gates on the server's speculative path (server spec: answered; spec==plain (server), 218 chars identical).

Localisation: QW_SPEC=1 diverged @char 36, QW_SPEC=1 QW_NO_ACCEPT=1 matched exactly.  Strides measured with QW_STRIDE_DEBUG=1: state_stride 3145728, snap_stride 12582912, snap/TILE 3145728 at both batch 1 and 16, old state/2 1572864 (batch 1) and 25165824 (batch 16).  Throughput NOT quotable: the machine's Metal throughput collapsed mid-round (gen 26.65 -> 0.90 tok/s, a 12-token prefill 0.615s -> 14.4s, GPU utilisation reporting 0%, no thermal warning, memory 93% free); the plain path is equally slow and is untouched by this change, so it is environmental.  Paired ratios before and during the collapse agree spec is faster on the server: 3.30 -> 2.87s at 64 tokens (1.15x), 296.65 -> 215.14s at 128 tokens (1.38x).  Re-measure on a quiet machine.

history.title: Re-measured last round's claims on a single server (two servers plus Ollama had left only 60 MB free, which is what broke the speculative number) and in doing so refuted three of my own measurements. (1) QW_PREFIX_DISK is a PATH, not a flag: QW_PREFIX_DISK=0 opened a disk prefix cache in ./0/ and every 'cold' number taken with it was a cache hit ('prefix cache HIT (disk prefix) - skipped 896 of 900'). Unset is off. The stray 0/ directory in the repo was this and is deleted. (2) Counting SSE chunks as tokens understated the speculative path 2.6x, because one multi-token step emits one chunk; reading usage.completion_tokens shows the round-32 spec win is real. (3) gen never uses the wide prefill path at all - 897 tokens ran as 899 single-row batches of 1186 dispatches, 38.3 s, against the server's 14.2 s. RESULT otps, interleaved paired single-server: plain 15.23 tok/s vs Ollama 11.06 = 1.377x; spec 24.52 vs 14.88 = 1.647x; spec accepts 2.64 tokens/step; plain and spec text byte-identical. TTFT, content-chunk timed: true cold (fresh server, fresh 900-token prompt, no disk cache) ours 14.225 s vs Ollama 1.984 s = 7.2x behind; warm ours 0.044 s vs Ollama 0.082 s, level. NEW DECOMPOSITION of the cold prefill, measured by dropping all GEMV dispatches with QW_SKIP_KERNEL=q4_gemv: full pass 14633 dispatches / 435-500 ms, non-GEMV-only 10657 / 65-103 ms, so GEMV 11.2 s (79%) and non-GEMV 2.99 s (21%). The non-GEMV cost is linear in DISPATCH COUNT, not rows - chunk=32 309k dispatches 2.99 s, chunk=1 663k dispatches 6.18 s, both 9.3-9.7 us per dispatch - so it is launch latency on tiny kernels, and the per-row ops (conv1d_silu_ring, gdn_step, rmsnorm_gated, copy_off at 48 layers x rows each) should collapse to one dispatch per layer. QW_NO_ENC_SPLIT=1 (one encoder per pass, unsafe) is SLOWER, 20.95 s vs 14.2 s, so the 600-3100 encoders per pass are not the cost and merging encoders is not a lever. This overturns the 4.4 s floor of sections 48/60, which assumed non-GEMV 3.4 s was irreducible: with it at ~0.15 s the floor is ~1.2 s, below Ollama's 1.98 s. Separately, section 51's refutation of the bytes-in-flight hypothesis used 16 staging iterations; the current BM=32/BK=64 geometry has exactly 2 (2 x 4 B per thread, 128 threads, 80 concurrent threadgroups = 80 KB in flight against the ~238 KB needed for 477 GB/s, a 3x shortfall that matches 120 vs 400 GB/s). No engine code changed this round; the gates stand at 19 passed / 0 failed, ACCEPTED.  LATER IN THE SAME ROUND: TTFT was then measured by prompt length and ours loses at every length - short ~12 token 0.394 vs 0.323 cold and 0.379 vs 0.143 warm, mid ~128 2.429 vs 0.510, long ~900 14.531 vs 2.388 - so TTFT is not won even warm, and the warm path's remaining cost is one last prefill pass past the last saved boundary plus ~0.35 s of fixed overhead.  A 10-token prompt costs 341 ms in a single 5108-dispatch prefill pass, of which the GEMV is only 3 sweeps (119 ms): the other 3617 non-GEMV dispatches cost ~61 us each, six times the 9.5 us measured when the GEMV is skipped, so the non-GEMV chain is much more expensive when it shares a pass with the GEMV.  Finally the GEMM's three costs were measured fresh with the bench mode probes: weight staging 100 ms (14.4 GB => 144 GB/s), x staging 112 ms, MAC 60 ms (36 TFLOPS, faster than Ollama's effective 24.5 TFLOPS) - the GEMM's problem is staging, never arithmetic, and the 3x weight-staging shortfall matches the 80 KB vs 238 KB bytes-in-flight gap.  Best case after fixing all four items is a TIE with Ollama's 1.98 s, because MAC alone at BN=128 is ~1.7 s.  The user is asked for a direction before more rounds go into the GEMM line.

history.title: Did the first of the two cheap items and refuted it. (1) A one-step REGISTER lookahead in the GEMM weight staging - issue the next K-step's two words before this step's shared stores and barrier, two register sets, no extra shared, arithmetic and shared layout untouched - is bit-identical (gemm-check worst rel unchanged at 3.347e-4) and faster in 4/4 interleaved pairs, but by only 1.5% (258.7 -> 255.0 ms). So the 80 KB vs 238 KB bytes-in-flight gap is NOT why weight staging runs at 144 GB/s; the compiler was already keeping the two independent loads in flight. Reverted - 1.5% does not justify 40 lines of macro in a kernel that is not on any shipped path. ALSO CORRECTED MY OWN ARITHMETIC: the 61 us/dispatch I reported for the non-GEMV chain was contaminated by a one-time first-pass cost. Separating it out, the first pass of a session carries ~170-180 ms of page-in/warm-up regardless of row count (full 10-token pass 341 ms first vs 171 ms after; non-GEMV-only 195 ms vs 17 ms; non-GEMV-only 32-row 239 ms vs 65-103 ms), and the steady-state non-GEMV cost is ~8 us per dispatch. A 900-token prefill is 225 weight sweeps, which is where the 14.2 s comes from. RULED OUT a tempting scalar fix: a threadgroup holding one output row's weights in shared memory (2.5 KB) and looping over the 32 tokens reads the weights once per pass, but 27e9 params x 32 rows = 864 GMAC at the measured 2.7 TMAC/s scalar rate is 320 ms/pass against 317 ms for the eight k=4 sweeps - no gain. Once the weights are read once, the scalar MAC rate (~5.4 TFLOPS) is the binding constraint, so only MMA can make prefill faster. SCOPED item (2): of the 10657 non-GEMV dispatches in a 32-row pass, 6144 (58%) are the per-row families copy_off / conv1d_silu_ring / rmsnorm_gated / gdn_step at 48 x rows each, and gdn_step CANNOT be batched because consecutive prefill rows are consecutive positions of one sequence with a serial recurrence. Batching the other three takes a pass from 85 ms to ~36 ms, i.e. 2.99 s to ~1.25 s over 29 passes - 12% of the cold prefill, ~5% of short-prompt TTFT - for three kernels plus the runner's row mapping. NEW HYPOTHESIS, not yet tested and the only one left standing for the 144 GB/s: warp count, not occupancy. At BN=32 the GEMM grid is out_f/32 threadgroups - 160 for a 5120-wide linear but TWO for the 48-row GDN projections - and 13.8 KB of shared admits only 2 threadgroups/SM, about 8 warps per SM against 40+ slots. This differs from the BM=16 / BK=128 occupancy tests of section 58 because both of those also changed the work per threadgroup. Testing it needs NT 128 -> 256, which means rewriting the four-simdgroup fragment mapping (sg>>1, sg&1), or BN 32 -> 128. No engine code changed (the experiment was reverted); gates unchanged at 19 passed / 0 failed.  Also probed the warp-count hypothesis cheaply by halving BK to 32 (shared 13.8 -> ~9 KB, 3 threadgroups/SM instead of 2, ~12 warps/SM instead of 8): it is 6% SLOWER (275.2 vs 260.0 ms over 3 interleaved pairs), but that is not a clean test because BK=32 also doubles the number of K-steps and therefore the number of exposed latencies. The hypothesis is neither confirmed nor refuted and is not worth a dedicated round unless NT=256 is rewritten. Change reverted; the binary md5 is identical to the baseline.

history.title: Warm TTFT pulled from 2.5x behind to a tie.  The only boundary a repeat request ever resumes from is the one before the LAST prefill chunk (ladder offset 0), so the size of that chunk is exactly the work a cache hit still has to redo: at the default 32 rows it is eight weight sweeps (317 ms), at four rows it is one sweep (~40 ms).  Added PREFILL_TAIL=4 so the final chunk is capped at four rows; the cold path pays almost nothing (28 rows + 4 rows is still eight sweeps, only the per-pass dispatch chain is paid twice, ~40 ms).  Log confirms the mechanism: 'prefix cache HIT (saved boundary) - skipped 106 of 110' where it used to skip 96, and 'skipped 784 of 788' where it used to skip 758.  GATES 19 passed / 0 failed ACCEPTED, including 'chunk 4 and chunk 32 give the same answer' and server==cli, so the changed chunking is still bit-identical.  PAIRED A/B with a fresh server and an unseen prompt each round, old/new alternating: warm TTFT 0.268/0.265/0.279 (mean 0.271) -> 0.133/0.147/0.136 (mean 0.139), 2.0x faster, with no cold regression (27.7 -> 27.2 s, inside noise).  PAIRED AGAINST OLLAMA at three lengths, warm measured three times alternately: ours 0.219/0.246/0.272 (first sample inflated, later ones 0.157-0.187) against Ollama 0.182/0.171/0.162 - a TIE, where the same method previously gave 0.379/0.377/0.873 against 0.143/0.130/0.114.  Note the machine degraded about 2x during this round (cold ~900 went from 8.2 s to 18.1 s and Ollama from 1.26 to 2.94 s), so only the paired numbers are quoted.  What is left: a hit still re-prefills four rows, and one sweep (40 ms) is the floor for ANY re-prefill, plus 36 ms for the first decode step, so our floor is ~0.10-0.12 s against 0.16-0.19 s measured.  Winning outright needs the hit to re-prefill NOTHING: record the boundary at the prompt end and include the first generated token's logits in the snapshot (export_prefix stores only state/window/KV, which is precisely why the snapshot stops one chunk early).  Estimated 0.17 -> 0.12 s, a 1.4x win.

history.title: No engine change: profiled the remaining warm-TTFT budget and wrote the exact construction plan for the one change that can still flip a verdict.  A 10-token prompt, instrumented: the warm request is one 2194-dispatch prefill batch at 50.2 ms plus three 1234-dispatch decode batches at 36-38 ms, and the server's own TTFT log says 0.1 s - so the 50 ms prefill is the four-row pass a hit still recomputes, half the warm TTFT, and removing it is the only remaining 1.4-2x win.  Boundary export measured at 28.6 ms for 204 MB and it is on the COLD critical path because it is called before the final pass; import is only 4.2 ms, so the warm path is not copy-bound.  Confirmed from the code that the pass cannot simply be dropped: export_prefix stops one chunk early precisely because the first generated token's logits live in a scratch buffer it does not copy.  Plan for next round is in docs section 69: export_prefix gains a row argument and appends scratch.logits row (496 KB, magic Q38PFX1 -> Q38PFX2 with import tolerating the old tail), the engine records an extra pf == len boundary after the final pass, and a hit at pf == len samples logits_row(0) and emits without any pass.  Deliberately not started: three files plus gates plus a paired measurement does not fit in what is left of this session, and an unfinished engine change is worse than none.

history.title: LANDED the change that stops a cache hit from recomputing anything.  export_prefix_with_logits appends the first generated token's logits to the blob (496 KB, magic Q38PFX2, import accepts v1 and v2 and installs the tail at logits row 0) and the engine records a pf == len boundary after the pass that consumes the last prompt row, keyed on the LAST row of that slot so the logits are the ones that decide the first token.  A request whose restore lands exactly on the prompt end now enters no pass at all: it samples logits_row(0), emits, and goes straight to decode.  Gates 19 passed / 0 failed ACCEPTED, including the two that matter most here, 'cache hit matches the cold start' and 'cache on: three identical requests agree'.  Added a dedicated equivalence test over 14 prompt lengths (7-145 tokens, covering every tail alignment): cold == warm == warm2 byte-identical, 14/14, with all 28 warm requests confirmed on the cached-end path.  WARM TTFT, paired against Ollama in one session: ours 0.007 / 0.013 / 0.104 s against 0.227 / 0.243 / 2.673 s, i.e. 19-32x; Ollama's own KV hit failed to fire this round (its ~900 warm was 2.67 s, near its cold time), so against its best earlier warm numbers (0.16-0.18 s) we are still 13-25x faster.  Cost on the COLD path is one extra snapshot export, measured at 28.6 ms for 204 MB, roughly 5% of a short cold TTFT; the paired A/B meant to confirm that was inconclusive because the machine was saturated this round (cold short prompt ranged 7.5-20.9 s on both sides against 0.5 s normally).  Net position: otps wins on both paths, warm TTFT now wins by 13-32x, and cold TTFT is the only metric still lost.  Recorded a follow-up that makes the cold path net-zero and upgrades the disk cache: drop k=0 from PREFIX_LADDER and move DiskPrefix::store into the prompt-end block, noting that 128-256 token prompts currently reach disk only through k=0.

history.title: (1) Made the cold path net-zero again: removed offset 0 from PREFIX_LADDER, because the prompt-end snapshot supersedes it, and moved DiskPrefix::store into the prompt-end block.  A cold prompt now exports once instead of twice (saving the 28.6 ms the previous round added) and the disk cache stores the v2 blob, so cross-process hits recompute nothing either.  Gates 19 passed / 0 failed ACCEPTED.  (2) REFUTED a conclusion that had closed the cold-prefill line for ~35 rounds: 'the GEMM is numerically unusable, 1e-3 per linear amplified to ~17 logits'.  A full 497-tensor accuracy sweep (QW_GEMM_CHECK_ALL=1 gemm-check) reports worst relative error 9.662e-4 with every tensor PASS, and the SHIPPED GEMV path, measured the same way against the same CPU reference, reports max_abs 5.0e-4 to 1.6e-3 on the eight tensors the gate checks.  Same order of magnitude, worst case 1.95e-3 against 1.6e-3 - so the GEMM is not less accurate than what we ship, and the shipped path passes oracle parity 6/6 while carrying that error.  A 1e-3 perturbation amplified over 64 layers giving ~17 logits of difference is what any two ~1e-3-accurate implementations do, not a GEMM-specific defect.  The correct acceptance test for the GEMM is oracle parity against mlx-lm, not byte-identity with the GEMV.  Caveat recorded in docs section 71: numerically usable is not yet fast - the GEMM is only 1.17x quicker than the GEMV (272 vs 317 ms per 32-token pass) because staging is 212 of the 272 ms - so this reopens the line but does not by itself win cold TTFT.  Also note: the first gate run this round reported 'spec==plain: 230 of 300 tokens differ' - investigated and it is the known flaky spec-plain issue under load, not a regression: the same binary gives MATCH 300/300 three times in a row and the re-run of the whole suite is 19/0 ACCEPTED.

history.title: Wired the GEMM into the wide prefill path and it is 2.2x faster end to end.  Linear::encode_rows now takes a GEMM branch when rows >= QW_GEMM_MIN_ROWS (read once through a OnceLock so the default path does not pay 497 env lookups a pass): one dispatch per linear instead of rows/4, grid (out_f/32*128, ceil(rows/32), 1), threadgroup (128,1,1), scalars 5=in_f, 6=rows, 7=out_f, 8=mode.  It is OFF by default (usize::MAX) because the two paths round differently and the acceptance test has to be the oracle, not byte-identity.  Paired cold-prefill timing on a 390-token prompt with a fresh prefix each round: scalar 21.32 / 28.81 s against GEMM 12.09 / 11.56 s - about 2.2x, far more stable, and better than the best scalar cold prefill ever recorded (14.2 s).  The gain is much larger than the 1.17x the isolated bench predicted because the dispatch count per linear drops from rows/4 to 1, so the whole per-pass encoder chain disappears.  On the one prompt tested the server's 64-token answer with the GEMM is BYTE-IDENTICAL to the scalar path.  Gates 19 passed / 0 failed ACCEPTED, though since the GEMM is off by default they still only exercise the scalar path.  Deliberately not made default yet: one prompt is not evidence.  Next round turns it on and proves equivalence over many prompts and lengths the way the cached-end test did, then re-runs oracle parity and server==cli with it enabled.

history.title: Ran the equivalence test the previous round asked for, and it says the GEMM cannot be the default.  Nine prompt lengths (8-200 words, 48 generated tokens each), scalar server against QW_GEMM_MIN_ROWS=8 server: 8 of 9 are byte-identical, but the 35-token case diverges at character 64 (about generated token 14) and the two continuations are then completely different - scalar continues 'from the 1st century BC to the 5th century AD', the GEMM turns to 'for centuries, and its influence can still be seen today'.  That is the two paths' different f16 accumulation rounding amplified at an argmax boundary, which is expected, but the consequence is real: making the GEMM the default would make the server diverge from the CLI and from the oracle on some prompts and break the token-for-token guarantee (server==cli, spec==plain, oracle parity 6/6) that has held for 60+ rounds.  Decision: keep QW_GEMM_MIN_ROWS opt-in.  Correctness over delivery speed - 2.2x on cold prefill does not buy giving up bit-equivalence.  Recorded the next step: align the GEMM's accumulation with the scalar path.  The suspicion is that q4_gemm_tile accumulates eight f16 MMA steps inside BK=64, each contributing about one f16 epsilon, so about 1e-3 in total; BK=8 would leave one MMA per BK and f32 accumulation across K-steps, which should cut the error to output rounding only, at the cost of 640 K-steps instead of 80 - needs measuring whether it is still faster.

history.title: Investigated the f16-accumulation hypothesis from the previous round and REFUTED it: q4_gemm_tile's accumulator is simdgroup_matrix<float,8,8> (msl.rs:725), so it accumulates in f32, and the scalar k=4 GEMV also uses float acc[NK] (msl.rs:622) with half weights - both are f16 operands with f32 accumulation, so the difference is not f16 accumulation.  More importantly I found and corrected a METHODOLOGICAL ERROR of my own from the round before: I had compared gemm-check's rel = max_abs/max_ref with check's norm_err = max_abs/rms_ref and concluded the GEMM is not less accurate than the shipped GEMV.
