history.title: Analysed the x staging in q4_gemm_tile and explained a 40 percent regression that had been recorded as unexplained.  The staging loop gives the 32 lanes of a warp consecutive TOKENS, so device addresses stride by K*2 = 10240 bytes, fully uncoalesced - which looks like 64x waste but costs only 112 ms per pass because the activation tile is L2 resident.  The earlier attempt to fix it by swapping the two indices made the kernel 40 percent slower, and the reason is now clear: after the swap the lanes read along g (coalesced) but write xsh[kk][t] with kk varying, and since XLD = BK + 8 = 72 the bank index is (kk*72 + t) % 32, so 8*kk % 32 only takes the four values 0, 8, 16 and 24 - a 4-way bank conflict on the writes that costs more than the coalescing buys.  The fix is to make XLD % 32 odd so that kk*XLD cycles through all 32 banks, for instance XLD = BK + 1 = 65, except that simdgroup_load constrains its leading dimension's alignment (half typically needs 8 elements), so 65 may be illegal; the alternatives are a transposed x tile xsh[t][kk] with leading dimension BK+pad, or another odd pad that simdgroup_load accepts.  That has to be settled by experiment rather than by reasoning, and this round did not have the context budget for the change-build-paired-time-recheck-equivalence loop, so it is recorded as the next action.  x staging is 112 ms per pass and the last large un-attacked block on the cold path.

history.title: Re-measured the GEMM's cost breakdown and it reframed the whole cold-prefill problem.  With bench --rows 8 --tokens 32 over all 497 linears: full mode 12.228 ms/token (391 ms per pass), mode 1 with constant weights 12.220 - so dequantisation costs nothing at all - and mode 2 with the MMAs skipped 10.891, i.e. 348 ms.  Staging is therefore 348 of the 391 ms, 89 percent, and the actual matrix multiply is only 43 ms.  Effective bandwidth is 14.412 GB / 0.391 s = 36.8 GB/s, while the GEMV pulls 362-417 GB/s reading the same weights - a 10x deficit.  The conclusion is that cold prefill is not arithmetic-bound at all, it is bound by weight-staging memory efficiency.  The whole pass reads 391 ms here against the 272 ms recorded earlier, which may be machine state, but the composition is stable and mode 1 matching mode 0 proves dequantisation is free.  Two suspected causes, both testable: the GEMV reads weights as uint4 (16 bytes per thread) whereas staging reads one uint (4 bytes) per iteration; and sp[g]/bp[g] are re-read for every word even though eight words share a group, so scale and bias are read eight times redundantly, about 2.7 KB of extra traffic per row.  The next move is to vectorise the staging and read the scale and bias once per group, but the write side has to be redesigned first: a thread handling four consecutive words writes at offset wd*8, whose bank index is (32L) % 32 = 0, a 32-way conflict, so it needs a different mapping or a different wsh layout rather than a direct edit.

history.title: Did the arithmetic before touching the kernel, and it argues against the bank-conflict explanation for the staging's 37 GB/s that the previous round proposed.  The conflict is real: each thread writes eight consecutive halves for one word at wsh[r*WLD + wd*8 + i] with WLD = 72, and with consecutive lanes' wd the value 8*wd % 32 takes only four distinct values, so every i-th store is an 8-way conflict.  But the aggregates do not support it being the bottleneck - the model does about 28.8 G half stores in 391 ms, roughly 0.02 cycles per store, far below the shared-memory ceiling, and 3.6 G four-byte global loads in the same window, about 0.15 loads per SM per cycle across 40 SMs, also far below capability.  So 37 GB/s looks latency- or occupancy-bound, not bandwidth- or conflict-bound; mode 1 matching mode 0 only shows dequantisation is free and cannot tell those apart.  Recorded the discriminating experiment to run first, before any kernel edit: vary Q4_GEMM_BK across 32, 64 and 128 and see whether staging time tracks the number of k0 steps or the amount of data.  If it tracks steps, the per-step fixed cost and the two threadgroup barriers dominate and a larger BK is the answer - and BK=128, refuted long ago, deserves a re-test because that measurement predates the x-staging fix.  If it tracks data, it is memory efficiency, and only then is vectorisation plus removing the redundant scale and bias reads the right move.

history.title: Ran the BK discriminating experiment the previous round called for, found the result confounded, and refused to ship it. history.title: Ruled out the last simple explanation for the weight staging's 37 GB/s.  The staged eight halves are now packed into two half4 stores instead of eight half stores - alignment is guaranteed since the base is a multiple of four halves - which should quarter the shared-store phases.  Accuracy came out bit-identical, but the interleaved A/B gave medians of 12.096 for the baseline against 11.998 for the packed version, 0.8 percent and inside the noise, so it was reverted.  The machine was in a fast state this time (about 12 ms) rather than the previous round's 18 ms, so this tie can be trusted.  With that, every simple explanation for the staging's 37 GB/s is measured and excluded: dequantisation is free because mode 1 matches mode 0, per-step overhead and barriers are not the cause because larger BK is worse, bank conflicts are not the cause at 0.8 percent, and global bandwidth is not the cause since the loads run at 0.15 per SM per cycle against far higher capability.  Latency and occupancy are all that remain: wsh + xsh + osh is roughly 13.6 KB with 128 threads per threadgroup, which is about two threadgroups and eight warps per SM.  Next is to attack occupancy directly - shrink xsh by using BK=32, which takes it from 5.2 to 2.6 KB, or raise Q4_GEMM_NT to 256 so each threadgroup has more warps to hide latency - remembering that NT feeds the sg derivation and so must be validated by an interleaved A/B.

history.title: Worked out the real cost of the occupancy route before touching code, because raising Q4_GEMM_NT is not a one-constant change.  NT is 128 and the mapping r_off = (sg>>1)*16 with t_off = (sg&1)*16 means four simdgroups tile the 32x32 output 2x2; eight simdgroups would need a 64x32 (BM=64, 4x2) or 32x64 (BN=64, 2x4) tile.  Current shared use is wsh 4608 + xsh 5248 + osh 4096 = 13.95 KB per threadgroup and BM=64 would take it to 22.7 KB, so more NT trades shared memory for warps rather than being free.  Ranked the candidates: cheapest is dropping BK to 32, which shrinks xsh from 5248 to 2624 B and the total to 11.3 KB - one line, and although BK=32 and 64 tied on throughput earlier that was with nothing else changed and it deserves a retest now that occupancy is the suspected constraint; next is BN=64 with NT=256, whose shared arithmetic must be redone and may not pay; and the structural option is split-K, since out_f=5120 launches 160 threadgroups against roughly 80 concurrent, two waves, so halving K and reducing doubles parallelism for the price of a second pass.  Chose candidate 1 for next round: one line plus an interleaved A/B, which also tests the occupancy hypothesis itself - if shrinking xsh buys nothing, shared capacity is not the constraint and the other two candidates should be dropped.
history.gates: 19 passed / 0 failed, ACCEPTED (no code change)

evidence.NT256_requires: 8 simdgroups -> BM=64 (22.7 KB shared) or BN=64; trades shared for warps
candidates: BK=32 to shrink xsh (one line, retest)
BN=64 + NT=256 (recompute shared, may not pay)
evidence.next: candidate 1, which doubles as a test of the occupancy hypothesis

history.title: Adopted Q4_GEMM_BK = 32 after six interleaved A/B rounds in which it won every single pair - 11.700, 11.571, 11.702, 11.662, 11.587 and 11.792 against BK=64's 11.872, 11.869, 12.110, 12.092, 11.990 and 11.969, medians 11.681 against 11.980, a 2.6 percent win.  The earlier four-round run that read as a tie had been taken while the machine drifted from 13 to 20 ms, whereas this one held steady at 11.5-12.1 ms with the same direction in all six rounds, which is why it is the one to trust - another confirmation that only interleaved A/B is usable on this machine.  Accuracy stays bit-identical and the gates pass 19/0 ACCEPTED with BK=32 as the default.  More importantly the probe answered the question it was designed for: halving xsh bought only 2.6 percent, so shared capacity is a weak constraint, and that kills the two larger occupancy candidates - BN=64 with NT=256, which would push shared use up to 22.7 KB, and split-K, which needs an extra reduction pass.  Both dropped.  That closes the weight-staging line: five explanations for its 37 GB/s have now been measured and excluded - dequantisation, per-step overhead, bank conflicts, global bandwidth and shared capacity - leaving memory latency itself, set by the per-thread dependency chain, as the structural limit of this kernel.  Cold TTFT is 7.4-10.5 s against Ollama's 2.1-2.9 s while otps and warm TTFT both win comfortably, so the next round should move to a higher-yield direction instead of more two-percent staging attempts.
history.gates: 19 passed / 0 failed, ACCEPTED (BK=32 is now the default)

evidence.probe_conclusion: shared capacity is a weak constraint -> drop BN=64/NT=256 and split-K
evidence.staging_line_closed: five explanations excluded (dequant, step overhead, bank conflict, global bw, shared capacity); latency is structural
evidence.next: move to a higher-yield direction than staging micro-optimisation

history.title: After five memory-side explanations were excluded, counted the instructions per staging iteration and found a hypothesis that explains all of them at once: the staging is instruction-issue bound, not memory bound.  One word (8 weights) costs roughly 33-39 instructions - about 4 for the index division, multiply-subtract and two compares, 3 loads for the word plus sp[g] and bp[g], about 24 for the eight nibble extracts, half conversions and multiply-adds, and 2-8 shared stores.  The model stages 3.6 G words, so 120-140 G instructions in 375 ms, which is 320-370 G instructions per second against 60 G cycles per second of aggregate issue capacity (40 SMs at about 1.5 GHz) - 5.3-6.2 instructions per SM per cycle, above the roughly 4 an Apple GPU can sustain.  This accounts for every earlier exclusion: mode 1 matching mode 0 because the eight conversions and stores remain, BK making no difference, bank conflicts worth 0.8 percent, bandwidth unsaturated, shared capacity irrelevant.  The fix is the GEMV's own trick - one uint4 load per thread covering four words and 32 weights: the index arithmetic amortises 4x, loads fall from twelve to three, and the arithmetic vectorises, cutting about 132 instructions per 32 weights to about 50, a 2.6x reduction.  The 32-way write conflict this introduces is affordable precisely because bank conflicts measured at 0.8 percent.  To implement next round with an interleaved A/B; GROUP_SIZE is 64, eight words, so four words always sit inside one group and one scale and bias read per thread suffices.
history.gates: 19 passed / 0 failed, ACCEPTED (no code change)

evidence.issue_rate: 320-370 G instr/s vs 60 G cycles/s aggregate = 5.3-6.2 per SM per cycle, above the ~4 ceiling
evidence.fix: uint4 per thread (4 words, 32 weights): loads 12 -> 3, ~132 -> ~50 instructions per 32 weights (2.6x)
evidence.next: implement the uint4 staging and validate with an interleaved A/B

history.title: Tested the vectorised staging two ways and adopted neither.  uint4 (four words, 32 weights per thread) with BK=128, chosen so nwords4 is 4 and BM*nwords4 is exactly 128 = NT with every thread busy, came out 40 percent SLOWER across six interleaved rounds - 16.168/16.139/16.136/16.065/16.144/15.950 against 11.578/11.568/11.455/11.606/11.683/11.899, consistent in all six - but the test is confounded because BK=128 alone was already measured at 24.585 against BK=64's 16.580, a 48 percent penalty, so most of the loss is BK rather than the uint4 staging and the instruction-issue hypothesis survives.  The cleaner variant, uint2 (two words, 16 weights per thread) at BK=64, where nwords4 is again 4 so BM*4 = 128 = NT with the weight tile back at BK=64, gave 12.602/14.503/18.077/18.170 against BK=32's 14.510/17.102/18.438/18.119: the first two rounds clearly favour uint2 and the last two are a dead heat, but the machine drifted from 14.5 to 18.4 ms, +27 percent, within the run, so four rounds cannot settle it.  Both variants kept accuracy bit-identical.  Reverted to the committed and verified BK=32 single-word staging, on the principle that a result unresolvable under drift is not evidence.  Next round: cool the GPU, confirm two consecutive baseline readings agree, then re-run uint2/BK64 as an eight-round interleaved A/B - if it holds, it is the second evidence-backed cold-path win after the x staging fix.
history.gates: 19 passed / 0 failed, ACCEPTED (both variants reverted; BK=32 single-word staging is the shipped default)

evidence.uint4_verdict: 40% slower but confounded by BK=128 (+48% on its own), so the issue-bound hypothesis is not refuted
evidence.uint2_verdict: inconclusive - machine drifted 14.5 -> 18.4 ms (+27%) within the run
evidence.next: cool down, verify baseline stability, then eight-round interleaved A/B of uint2/BK64

history.title: Ruled out vectorising the staging with a clean test and, in doing so, found the difference that actually matters.  After cooling the GPU for 150 seconds and confirming the baseline was stable at 11.698/11.589/11.679 (0.9 percent spread), eight interleaved rounds gave medians of 11.668 for BK=32 against 11.714 for uint2/BK64 - 0.4 percent slower and losing 7 of the 8 pairs.  Since uint4/BK128 was confounded by BK, this clean comparison refutes the instruction-issue hypothesis: vectorising the staging buys nothing.  What the run did reveal is that the GEMM runs eight times fewer threads than the GEMV - (out_f/BM)*NT = 160*128 = 20480 for a 5120-row tensor against the GEMV's out_f*32 = 163840 - and that at BK=32, BM*nwords is exactly 128 = NT, so each thread issues a single four-byte load per k0 step inside a serial load-use-store chain, with no memory-level parallelism at all to hide the latency.  Parallelism and latency hiding are now the best remaining explanation, ahead of bandwidth, bank conflicts, shared capacity and instruction count.  That revives split-K, whose rejection no longer stands: the occupancy probe that killed it measured shared CAPACITY, worth only 2.6 percent, which is a different constraint from thread or warp count.  Split-K takes the threadgroup count from 160 to 320 and doubles parallelism for one extra reduction pass; shrinking BM from 32 to 16 doubles it as well at the cost of halving wsh and reducing reuse.  Next: BM=16 as the smaller change, or split-K directly, validated with eight interleaved rounds.
history.gates: 19 passed / 0 failed, ACCEPTED (both staging variants remain reverted; BK=32 single-word staging is the shipped default)

evidence.verdict: uint2 0.4% slower, 7/8 pairs; instruction-issue hypothesis refuted
evidence.root_cause_candidate: parallelism / latency hiding - one 4-byte load per thread per k0 step in a serial chain
evidence.revived: split-K (the probe that rejected it measured shared capacity, not thread count)
evidence.next: BM=16 or split-K, eight interleaved rounds

history.title: Found decisive evidence that parallelism is the cold-path bottleneck, by changing nothing but the token count.  bench --rows 8 --tokens N sets grid.y = N/32 and so the threadgroup count, and ms per token reads 11.548 at 32 tokens (grid.y 1, 370 ms per pass), 7.941 at 64, 7.427 at 128 (grid.y 4, 951 ms per pass) and 8.086 at 256.  That is a 36 percent improvement between 32 and 128 tokens, with 256 slightly worse, so saturation is near 128.  This confirms the parallelism and latency-hiding hypothesis from the previous round: at 32 tokens the GEMM launches only out_f/32 threadgroups - 160 for a 5120-row tensor - roughly two waves across 40 SMs, nowhere near enough to hide the staging latency, while quadrupling the threadgroup count overlaps it.  The consequence is uncomfortable: PREFILL SITS EXACTLY AT THE WORST POINT, because PASS_ROWS_MAX is 32, so grid.y is 1 and every prefill pass pays the 11.548 ms per token case.  Two fixes would capture the same 36 percent - split-K, cutting K into four with a second reduction pass, which leaves the chunk structure untouched and is the lower-risk route, or widening the prefill pass from 32 rows to 128, which requires enlarging BATCH_MAX, PASS_ROWS_MAX and the x, y and conv-ring buffers and changes every existing path.  Chose split-K for next round, confined to the GEMM kernel plus one reduction, validated with eight interleaved rounds.
history.gates: 19 passed / 0 failed, ACCEPTED (measurement only; no code change)

evidence.verdict: parallelism / latency hiding confirmed as the bottleneck
fixes: split-K (K into 4 + one reduction; lower risk)
widen the prefill pass to 128 rows (needs BATCH_MAX/PASS_ROWS_MAX and buffers enlarged)
evidence.next: split-K, eight interleaved rounds

history.title: Designed the parallelism fix, and in the process corrected my own reading of the previous round's numbers.  In bandwidth terms: at 32 tokens the pass moves 14.4 GB in 370 ms, 39 GB/s, and at 128 tokens it moves 57.6 GB - because each y-slice re-reads the whole weight matrix - in 951 ms, 61 GB/s.  Extra threadgroups therefore do lift achieved bandwidth from 39 to 61 GB/s, but not for free: the weights get re-read four times.  The inference that matters is that grid.y = tokens/BN, so dropping BN from 32 to 8 yields grid.y = 4 at the SAME 32 tokens - the identical parallelism and bandwidth of the 128-token case, with the prefill still 32 rows wide.  Expect 11.548 -> 7.427 ms per token and 370 -> 238 ms per pass, a 36 percent faster prefill, and unlike split-K it needs no reduction pass, no extra buffer and no atomics.  The change is concrete: Q4_GEMM_BN 32 -> 8, the simdgroup map becomes r_off = sg*8 with t_off = 0 (4x1 rather than 2x2), the MMA loop collapses from four accumulate calls to one because each simdgroup now owns a single 8x8 tile, XLD becomes 17, xsh drops to 1088 B and osh to 1024 B so shared falls from 9.3 KB to 4.7 KB and occupancy improves for free, the x staging covers 256 elements and the y write uses t < 8.  Weight staging is untouched.  Next round implements it, verifies gemm-check is bit-identical, runs the gates, and does eight interleaved rounds against BN=32.
history.gates: 19 passed / 0 failed, ACCEPTED (design only; no code change)

evidence.insight: grid.y = tokens/BN, so BN 32 -> 8 gives grid.y = 4 at 32 tokens
evidence.better_than_split_k: no reduction pass, no extra buffer, no atomics
evidence.next: implement BN=8, bit-identical gemm-check, gates, eight interleaved rounds

history.title: Implemented the BN=8 design from the previous round and it produced all-zero output, so it was reverted in full.  The change set Q4_GEMM_BN to 8, made the simdgroup map r_off = sg*8 with t_off = 0 (4x1), collapsed the MMA loop from four accumulations to a single a00 chain, did the same for the store, and moved the dispatch bn from 32 to 8 in both bench.rs and linear.rs.  gemm-check then FAILED on all four tensors with rel = 1.000e0 and max_abs of 4.040e1, 2.591e0, 3.306e0 and 3.196e0.  Since rel was exactly 1.0 with max_abs equal to max_ref, the GEMM output was all zeros - it computed nothing rather than computing imprecisely.  The figures were bit-identical before and after the dispatch fix, which briefly suggested a stale build, so I touched all three sources and forced a rebuild; the md5 changed to ff72c395 but the result did not, confirming a real kernel defect rather than a build problem.  All three files are reverted, the binary md5 is back to 35fe8f5f363f352317a379f252f7d83d, and gemm-check passes again at worst rel 3.347e-4.  Next round should locate the fault rather than keep guessing: step through QW_GEMM_MODE, where mode 2 skips the MMAs and so reveals whether the x staging is written correctly, or temporarily dump osh, xsh and wsh into y for a fixed-point observation.  No further edits to this kernel until it is found.  Worth recording that the previous round's finding stands - parallelism is still the bottleneck; only this way of exploiting it failed - and split-K remains an equally valid route that does not require re-tiling the output.
history.gates: 19 passed / 0 failed, ACCEPTED (BN=8 reverted; the shipped binary is restored and gemm-check PASSES at worst rel 3.347e-4)

history.title: Corrected a misjudgement in the BN=8 failure record and laid out the locating experiment.  I had read the bit-identical output before and after the dispatch fix as possible evidence of a stale build; that was wrong, because changing bn from 32 to 8 only moves grid.y from 2 to 5, and with tok0 = tg.y * BN both variants cover all 40 tokens - bn=32 gives tok0 in {0,32} at eight columns each, covering 0..39, and bn=8 gives tok0 in {0,8,...,32}, likewise 0..39 - so identical output was exactly what should be expected, and the forced rebuild changing the md5 while the result held confirms it.  I then verified every index in the kernel and found them all self-consistent: the weight writes fit (max 1271 of 1280), the weight reads use r_off in {0,8,16,24} against kk in {0,8,16,24}, the x writes fit (max 534 of 544), the x read layout matches the write layout, osh is 256 floats with simdgroup 3 writing 192..255, the y write loop yields r in 0..31 and t in 0..7, the dispatch is (160*128, 5, 1) with a (128,1,1) threadgroup, and shared totals 4672 bytes.  With the layout all lining up, the fault is not at a level readable by inspection.  Next is fixed-point observation: add a mode == 9 that copies xsh, wsh or osh verbatim into y and print it from gemm-check, to establish which level is zero.  If xsh is zero the staging is not writing; if xsh is populated but osh is zero then the MMA or simdgroup_load's leading-dimension rule is implicated, because XLD is now 17 instead of 41 and the smaller odd stride may trip an alignment requirement the larger one did not.
history.gates: 19 passed / 0 failed, ACCEPTED (no code change; the shipped binary is the reverted, verified one)

evidence.correction: identical output was expected, not a stale build: both bn values cover all 40 tokens
evidence.verdict: layout self-consistent; fault not readable by inspection
evidence.next: mode == 9 fixed-point dump of xsh/wsh/osh into y to find which level is zero
evidence.suspicion: XLD 41 -> 17 (smaller odd stride) may trip a simdgroup_load alignment rule

history.title: Added the mode == 9 fixed-point probe - copying xsh into y after the first barrier and returning early - and it produced output BIT-IDENTICAL to mode 0, both reading gemm max_abs 4.040e1 with rel 1.000e0.  Switching to a branch that writes and returns changed the kernel's behaviour not at all.  Worth recording as a trap: rel = 1.0 alone cannot distinguish an all-zero output from a successful dump, because max_abs is max|a-b| and a = 0 makes max_abs = max|b| = max_ref, giving rel = 1.0, while dumped activations could reach the same maximum by coincidence - only bit-identical output is meaningful.  Bit-identical output leaves two explanations: xsh is all zeros, so the x staging is not writing, or the kernel never runs at all (invalid dispatch, compile failure, silently dropped) and y simply keeps its initial value, which makes every mode return the same all-zero result.  The second fits better, and the two cannot be separated while y is zero either way.  The way to break the tie is an unconditional constant store - always write 1.0f - since then y stops being zero the moment the kernel executes regardless of any dispatch fault.  Everything is reverted, the md5 is back to 35fe8f5f363f352317a379f252f7d83d and gemm-check passes.  BN=8 has now gone three rounds without converging, so it is paused by discipline and the cold-path effort should move to split-K, which does not require re-tiling the output, or to evaluating a wider prefill pass.
history.gates: 19 passed / 0 failed, ACCEPTED (BN=8 reverted again; the shipped binary is restored and gemm-check PASSES)

evidence.verdict: bit-identical -> the early-returning branch changed nothing

the kernel never executes (y keeps its initial zeros)

history.title: Found the root cause and it was in the harness, not the kernel.  QW_GEMM_MODE has no effect whatsoever in gemm-check: modes 0, 1, 2 and 3 all return bit-identical output (gemm max_abs 1.097e-2, rel 2.715e-4), because gemm-check runs through linear.rs's dispatch, which hardcoded .scalar(8, 0), while the QW_GEMM_MODE read at bench.rs:409 belongs to the bench subcommand only.  The mode == 9 probe therefore never took effect, and the bit-identical output that had puzzled me signified an invalid probe rather than a kernel that failed to execute.  With the mode plumbed into linear.rs, mode 9 was STILL bit-identical to mode 0, which is what finally exposed the culprit: `if let Ok(gk) = batch.kernel(msl::COMMON, msl::K_Q4_GEMM_TILE)` silently swallows a kernel build failure.  When the BN=8 kernel does not compile, batch.kernel returns Err, the whole dispatch is skipped and y keeps its initial zeros - a compile error disguised as an accuracy catastrophe, rel = 1.0, which cost three rounds of chasing the wrong thing.  That branch now reports loudly.  All changes are reverted - msl.rs from the backup, BN back to 32 in bench.rs and linear.rs - the md5 is back to 35fe8f5f363f352317a379f252f7d83d and gemm-check passes.  The lesson worth writing into the discipline is that any branch which silently skips work when a kernel is unavailable must report the error, or a GPU-side problem surfaces as a numerical failure hundreds of lines away.  Next: with the failure now loud, re-apply BN=8 and read the actual Metal compile error, which should name the real constraint - most likely the simdgroup_load leading dimension, since XLD drops from 41 to 17.
history.gates: 19 passed / 0 failed, ACCEPTED (BN=8 reverted; the shipped binary is restored and gemm-check PASSES at worst rel 3.347e-4)

history.title: Found that BN=8 had been CORRECT all along and the fault was a third dispatch site in the test harness.  gemm-check has its own dispatch at bench.rs:527, and I had only been editing bench.rs:395, which belongs to the bench subcommand; bench.rs:528 kept bn = 32 while the kernel expected 8, so grid.y was ceil(40/32) = 2 and tok0 = tg.y*8 covered only tokens 0..15, leaving 16..39 unwritten and rel ~ 1.0.  Correcting all four dispatch sites makes gemm-check PASS with bit-identical accuracy against BN=32.  The measurement refutes it regardless: six interleaved rounds, with the machine drifting 13.7 to 18.5, gave BN=32 13.734/14.585/16.209/17.634/17.992/18.060 against BN=8's 14.653/16.510/18.407/18.083/18.465/18.491 - BN=32 won every pair.  The cause is obvious in hindsight: at 32 tokens grid.y = 4 means the weights are read four times, 57.6 GB against 14.4 GB, and the parallelism does not repay four times the traffic.  This re-reads the earlier 32-vs-128-token result correctly: the lever is not a narrower tile but how many tokens each weight read feeds.  BN=32 at 32 tokens reads the weights once at 370 ms per 32 tokens; BN=32 at 128 tokens reads them four times but takes 238 ms per 32 tokens because the re-read amortises over four times the tokens; BN=8 at 32 tokens reads them four times for the same 32 tokens and loses.  Bandwidth rises from 39 to about 60 GB/s once grid.y >= 2, but it only pays when each y-slice carries 32 tokens.  The right direction is therefore widening the prefill pass from 32 rows to 128, which needs BATCH_MAX, PASS_ROWS_MAX and the x, y and conv-ring buffers enlarged.  BN=8 reverted; the loud kernel-build error in linear.rs kept.

history.title: Added an out_f-aware routing switch for the GEMM, then found the cold-TTFT harness is broken so its A/B is void.  The motivation is well grounded: the GEMM's parallelism is grid.x = (out_f/BM)*128 and the model uses only four out_f values - 48, 5120, 17408 and 248320 - so out_f = 5120 yields a mere 160 threadgroups, roughly two waves across 40 SMs, which is precisely the 39 GB/s regime, whereas the four-row tile kernel launches out_f*32 threads, eight times as many, and could well win on the small tensors.  The switch landed as `if rows >= gemm_min_rows() && self.out_f >= gemm_min_out_f()` with QW_GEMM_MIN_OUT_F defaulting to 0, leaving the shipped behaviour bit-for-bit identical, and gemm-check still PASSES at worst rel 3.347e-4.  The measurement, however, came back impossible: /tmp/pfout.py, which starts a fresh server per run with a fresh random 430-word prompt and alternates the order, reported 0.06 s on all eight runs - 0.066/0.061, 0.076/0.056, 0.061/0.065, 0.061/0.061 - when a 550-token cold prefill at 74 tok/s should take about 7.4 s.  QW_PREFIX_DISK and QW_PREFIX_SNAPSHOT are both unset, and I removed them explicitly in the script anyway.  The harness is therefore reading a cache hit or a stub, and the A/B is void: the exact mirror of the Ollama trap recorded earlier, where reusing a prompt produced bogus timings.  Next round the harness must print and verify prompt_eval_count or usage.prompt_tokens, or enable QW_PREFIX_TIME to read server-side prefill timing, and demonstrate that every run is a genuine cold prefill before any A/B is believed.  Until then no cold-TTFT figure should be trusted.

history.title: Fixed the cold-TTFT harness and used it to refute the out_f routing idea.  The bug was concrete: the server sends a role-only SSE chunk with empty content before generating anything, at 0.063 s, and the old script stopped its clock on the first data: line, so it was timing the role chunk rather than TTFT - the previously recorded trap of not measuring TTFT on the first SSE byte, hit again.  The fix skips empty-content chunks and ':' keep-alives and stops only on the first non-empty content; the server log confirms a real cold prefill, with a prefix cache miss, 0 of 672 tokens skipped, and prefill progress at 192/672 after 3.1 s and 576/672 after 10.0 s.  Four interleaved rounds on a fresh random 672-token prompt then gave the default GEMM-everywhere 18.779/17.177/16.735/17.791 against min_out_f=17408's 20.745/21.154/19.575/20.023: GEMM everywhere won every pair by roughly 15 percent, refuting the hypothesis that the tile kernel's eightfold thread count would win on out_f=5120 even though it avoids the eightfold weight re-read.  QW_GEMM_MIN_OUT_F therefore stays at 0.  Two further notes: stream_options.include_usage does not make this server return usage, so prompt_tokens remains None and the harness currently leans on server logs to prove a cold prefill, which should be fixed next round; and the cold TTFT seen here is 16.7-21.2 s for 672 tokens, about 38 tok/s, which is not comparable with the earlier 7.4-10.5 s for roughly 490 tokens since the prompt is longer and the machine is hotter after many rounds of benchmarking.  The absolute cold-path numbers need one measurement on a cool machine with a fixed prompt before they can be called final.

history.title: Re-measured the cold path after a 300 s cooldown with a paired, alternating harness on a fresh random 672-token prompt.  Cold TTFT was ours 15.102/12.131/14.318 s against Ollama's 2.316/1.646/3.249 s, medians 14.318 against 2.316, roughly 6.2x behind.  Ollama prefills 581 tokens in about 2.3 s, near 250 tok/s, consistent with the 220-260 tok/s recorded earlier, while ours does 672 tokens in 14.3 s, about 47 tok/s, consistent with the earlier 46-74 tok/s - neither side is anomalous and the gap is real.  The otps figures from this round are void: the harness divided non-empty content chunks by elapsed time and a chunk can hold several tokens, so it measured chunks per second, optimistic and not comparable with Ollama's exact eval_count/eval_duration.  The reliable otps result stays the earlier properly counted paired run - plain 15.23 against 11.06 for a 1.377x win and spec 24.52 against 14.88 for 1.647x.  Both sides also declined monotonically over the three rounds, ours from 26.25 to 9.54 and Ollama from 23.57 to 6.75, confirming that this machine throttles hard under sustained load and that comparisons must be interleaved and cooled.  The honest state is: otps won at 1.38x and 1.65x, warm TTFT won by 13-32x, cold TTFT lost by about 6x; because the objective requires winning both metrics, the cold TTFT gap keeps the goal active.

history.title: Shipped the prefill-pass widening and it is the largest cold-path win since the x-staging fix.  Three constants changed - PASS_ROWS_MAX and BATCH_MAX in runner.rs and PREFILL_CHUNK_MAX in engine.rs, all from 32 to 128 - with conv_ring scaling automatically from 64 to 256 and the x and y buffers following BATCH_MAX at a negligible 1.3 MB.  The gates pass 19/0 ACCEPTED including mlx-lm oracle parity.  Paired interleaved cold-TTFT A/B after a 300 s cooldown, on a fresh random 672-token prompt shared within each round, gave pass32 9.846/9.973/11.153/15.404 against pass128's 6.433/6.513/9.716/11.024: 128 rows won all four pairs, with medians falling from 10.563 to 8.115 s, 23 percent, and the two coolest rounds from 9.91 to 6.47 s, 35 percent, matching the 36 percent predicted from the bench curve.  More importantly the cold prefill rate went from about 47 tok/s to about 105 tok/s, a 2.2x improvement against the 1.36x the GEMM change alone predicted, which means the 32-row pass was also paying per-pass fixed overhead - extra dispatches and synchronisation - that the wider pass amortises.  The gap to Ollama is now about 2.4x rather than 5.3x.  Adopted as the default.  Next: the cold path still loses by roughly 2.4x, ours near 105 tok/s against Ollama's 250, so continue - test whether 256 rows helps or hurts, since the bench curve hinted 128 is the sweet spot, and hunt the remaining per-pass overhead now that the GEMM grid is four y-slices deep.

history.title: Built a 256-row prefill pass and declined to adopt it.  Interleaved against 128 rows after a 300 s cooldown, sharing a fresh 672-token prompt per round, pass128 gave 6.423/6.400/6.575/6.815 and pass256 6.189/6.175/6.586/6.583 - medians 6.499 against 6.386, a 1.7 percent edge, winning 3 of 4.  That sits inside the noise while doubling BATCH_MAX takes conv_ring from 256 to 512 and doubles the x and y buffers, so the cost is definite and the gain is not, and by discipline it is not adopted; the tree is restored to 128.  One useful side effect: both sides held steady at 6.4-6.8 s for 672 tokens, roughly 105 tok/s, much better than the 9-15 s of earlier rounds, which demonstrates how strongly cooldown and background load move this machine's readings and pins pass128 at about 6.4 s as the reproducible figure.  The real finding is where the next lever lies.  At a 128-row pass grid.y is 4, so the weights are re-read four times - 57.6 GB and 951 ms per pass - and the achieved bandwidth has already hit a wall near 61 GB/s, since 256 rows bought only 1.7 percent more, meaning parallelism is saturated.  The waste is those four re-reads.  Splitting K four ways so each slice reads a quarter of the weights brings total weight traffic back to 14.4 GB, which at the same 61 GB/s is 240 ms per 128 tokens, 1.9 ms per token against today's 7.4, roughly a 5x gain, for the price of one reduction pass.  Next round: implement split-K.

history.title: Corrected the previous round's split-K reasoning before writing any code, because the traffic algebra shows split-K alone saves nothing.  Each threadgroup (tg.x, tg.y) reads the weights for its BM rows across the whole of K and there are (out_f/BM)*(rows/BN) threadgroups, so total weight traffic is out_f*K*(rows/BN) = W*(rows/BN): it depends only on rows/BN and not on how K is divided.  With grid.y = 4, cutting K four ways makes every (y,z) pair read K/4 of the weights but also quadruples the number of pairs, so the total stays 4W.  The plan from the previous round was wrong.  The correct lever is BN itself: raising it from 32 to 128, the full pass width, takes grid.y from 4 to 1 and traffic from 4W to 1W, paying with parallelism falling from (out_f/BM)*4 to (out_f/BM)*1.  Using the measured bandwidths at out_f = 5120, where out_f/BM is 160 threadgroups: today 4W at 61 GB/s is 944 ms, which matches the measured 951; with BN=128 the traffic is W but bandwidth drops into the 39 GB/s regime, giving 369 ms or 2.9 ms per token against 7.4, a 2.5x win with no reduction pass; adding split-K at grid.z = 4 restores parallelism to 640 threadgroups, so 14.4 GB at about 61 GB/s is 236 ms, 1.8 ms per token, roughly 4x.  Hence two steps: BN=128 first, then split-K.  The kernel work for BN=128 is a 32x128 output tile - 64 tiles of 8x8, sixteen per simdgroup, about 32 accumulator registers per thread, feasible - with r_off = (sg>>1)*16 and t_off = (sg&1)*64, xsh 8768 B, osh 16384 B and wsh 2560 B for 27.7 KB, acceptable given that shared capacity proved to be a weak constraint.  This is the same parameter as the failed BN=8 experiment but in the opposite direction: smaller meant more re-reads, larger means fewer.

history.title: Implemented BN=128 as planned and measured it 73 percent slower, then reverted.  The kernel was correct: gemm-check PASSED with bit-identical max_abs and rel against BN=32 and the gates were 19/0 ACCEPTED.  But four interleaved cold-TTFT rounds after a 300 s cooldown on a shared fresh 672-token prompt gave bn32 5.718/5.771/5.765/5.934 against bn128 9.897/9.954/9.920/10.068, losing every pair by 73 percent.  The previous round's estimate failed in one specific place: I assumed grid.y = 1 would still achieve 39 GB/s, but backing the bandwidth out of the measurement - 14.4 GB of traffic over 9.95 s scaled from 128 to 672 tokens - gives roughly 7.6 GB/s, so dropping to 160 threadgroups collapses bandwidth far below 39 GB/s and swamps the fourfold traffic saving.  So BN=32 with a 128-row pass and grid.y = 4 is already a good local optimum: it trades a fourfold re-read for fourfold parallelism, and parallelism is worth far more than traffic here.  split-K stays the only route that preserves both - one weight read with four-way parallelism - but it needs BN=128, now shown infeasible alone unless split-K brings the threadgroup count back to 640, which is the next thing to test directly.  Note too that bn32 measured 5.7-5.9 s for 672 tokens, about 115 tok/s, better than the previous round's 6.4 s for the same configuration - a 12 percent session-to-session swing, which is precisely why comparisons must be interleaved.

history.title: Finished the BN sweep and found BN=32 to be a genuine local optimum, with all three other directions measured slower.  Since the traffic formula W*(rows/BN) makes BN the only knob that reduces the weight re-read, each value was tested with a 300 s cooldown, a shared fresh 672-token prompt per round and interleaved order: BN=8 lost 6 of 6, BN=32 is the fastest baseline, BN=64 lost 4 of 4 by 27 percent - 5.876/5.929/5.707/5.979 against 7.601/7.603/7.237/7.706 - and BN=128 lost 4 of 4 by 73 percent.  Working the bandwidth back out of each explains it: 640 threadgroups achieve 61 GB/s, 320 only about 20 GB/s and 160 about 7.6 GB/s, so bandwidth is acutely sensitive to threadgroup count and the traffic saving is more than cancelled by the bandwidth collapse.  BN=32 with a 128-row pass, grid.y = 4 and 640 threadgroups is therefore the true optimum of this kernel structure, with every other direction now excluded by measurement.  Further speed needs a different structure - dequantising in registers with no shared staging at all, as the GEMV does, to bring its 400 GB/s across - rather than more tile tuning.  Reverted, md5 restored to 3826791b87de8814392d476370de4612, gemm-check PASSES and the tree is clean.

history.title: Refuted the coalescing hypothesis and ran into a hard limit doing it.  BK=256 refused to build with the message 'Threadgroup memory size (41984) exceeds the maximum threadgroup memory allowed (32768)', which the loud error added in an earlier round surfaced immediately - without it this would have been another all-zero mystery.  Dropping to BK=128 keeps shared at 23296 B, inside the limit, and with a uint4 per lane eight lanes share a row so each warp touches 8 rows x 64 contiguous bytes rather than 8 rows x 16.  Accuracy stayed bit-identical and the gates passed 19/0, but four interleaved rounds after a 300 s cooldown gave bk32 6.011/6.015/5.975/6.081 against bk128+uint4's 8.523/8.511/8.429/8.564 - 0 of 4, 41 percent slower.  Coalescing is therefore refuted, and the reason is worth keeping: at BK=32 the apparently wasted seven eighths of each cache line is not wasted, because the same warp reads the next 16 bytes of that row on the following k0 iteration and L2 catches it.  The 12.5 percent line-utilisation figure was a misleading metric and the true effective bandwidth was never that poor, while BK=128's shared rise from 9.3 KB to 23.3 KB cost more occupancy than the better access pattern bought.  Reverted, md5 restored to 3826791b87de8814392d476370de4612, gemm-check PASSES.  The staging now has eight explanations excluded - dequantisation, per-step overhead, bank conflicts, global bandwidth, shared capacity, instruction count, parallelism past grid.y = 4, traffic via BN, and coalescing - so 61 GB/s is the hard limit of this design and parameter tuning is exhausted.  Any further cold-path gain requires a structurally different kernel.

history.title: Tested BM=64/BN=64/NT=256, deliberately built so that eight simdgroups hold only four accumulators each and register pressure matches the shipped kernel - the flaw that cost the earlier BN=64 attempt 27 percent.  The weight staging then has exactly BM*nwords = 256 = NT work items and shared totals 26176 B, inside the 32768 limit.  Accuracy was bit-identical and the gates passed 19/0.  Interleaved after a 300 s cooldown it won the first three rounds - base 6.447/6.448/6.536 against 6.172/6.178/6.044, medians 6.448 versus 6.172, roughly 4.3 percent - but round 4 returned 935.494 s against the base's 5.510 s, a fifteen-minute outlier no load can explain, pointing to an occasional hang or retry in the 256-thread configuration.  Not adopted: the gain is only 4.3 percent and the stability risk is unexplained, and by discipline it is better to forgo 4.3 percent than to ship a default that may intermittently hang.  Reverted, md5 restored to 3826791b87de8814392d476370de4612, gemm-check PASSES.  The weightier conclusion is that the GEMM is not traffic-bound either: halving the traffic bought only 4.3 percent, which together with staging being 89 percent of the time means the staging's cost is governed by the fixed per-iteration expense - latency, instructions, synchronisation - rather than by bytes.  That fits the instruction hypothesis also having failed: uint2 halved the instructions for nothing and BN=64 halved the bytes for 4.3 percent, so both dimensions are at diminishing returns.

history.title: Worked out why Ollama wins and what beating it requires.  Weight traffic per token settles the question: Ollama prefills 581 tokens in 2.3 s and, if it reads the 14.4 GB of weights once for the whole prompt - they fit comfortably in 128 GB of unified memory - the effective rate is only 6.3 GB/s, far too low to be bandwidth-bound, so its prefill is compute-bound at roughly 14.6 TFLOPS (581 x 28.8 G x 2 FLOP = 33.5 TFLOP over 2.3 s against an M5 Max peak near 36) and it reads the weights exactly once.  We move W/BN = 14.4/32 = 0.45 GB per token, independent of pass width as shown earlier, which is 302 GB for a 672-token prompt, 4.95 s at 61 GB/s and consistent with the measured 6.0 s.  The loss is therefore not bandwidth but repetition: 0.45 GB/token against 0.0248, eighteen times as much, and no tenfold bandwidth advantage survives eighteen times the data.  The plan that wins is BN=128 with split-K(4): BN=128 sets grid.y = 1 so each pass reads the weights once, and grid.z = 4 splits K four ways to bring parallelism back to (out_f/32)*4 = 640 threadgroups, precisely the 61 GB/s sweet spot found in the BN sweep.  Traffic per pass falls from 4W = 57.6 GB to W = 14.4 GB, so six passes total 86 GB instead of 345, an estimated 1.4 s against Ollama's 2.3 s - a win.  Implementation: enable split-K only for out_f <= 5120, because out_f >= 17408 already yields at least 544 threadgroups from grid.x, which keeps the partial-sum buffer at 10.5 MB instead of the 508 MB lm_head would demand; the buffer is f32[S][rows][out_f] with S = 4; a light elementwise kernel reduces the four partials into y; and the BN=128 tile is already written and proved bit-identical, recoverable from /tmp/msl9.bak, leaving split-K and the reduction as the only new work.  This is the last route with numbers behind it, so implement it next.

history.title: Showed that BN=128 is structurally blocked, before spending a round trying to route around it.  A 32x128 tile contains 64 8x8 tiles, so NT=128 forces sixteen accumulators per simdgroup - the register pressure that measured 73 percent slower - while NT=256 needs only eight but leaves the weight staging with BM*nwords = 128 work items for 256 threads, so half the threads idle inside the staging that is 89 percent of the time; raising BM to 64 fills those threads but takes the tile count to 128 and the accumulators back to sixteen.  Both ends are blocked, so BN=128 cannot be reached by tuning NT or BM, and the only remaining trick - splitting each word's eight nibbles between two threads to make 256 work items - would load every word twice and is not worth it.  Split-K is therefore the only route, and the implementation list is now concrete: the kernel change is small (read tg.z and, under mode 4, write the final value as an f32 partial into y reinterpreted as float at offset z*k*out_f, needing no new buffer binding); a reduction kernel of roughly fifteen lines sums the S partials into the real half y; the Rust side allocates a 10.5 MB scratch only when out_f <= 5120 and dispatches with grid.z = 4 before the reduction; and correctness is judged by bit-identity where it holds and by the oracle gates otherwise, because four summed f32 partials need not match a single running accumulator exactly.  Expected: traffic per pass 4W to W, six passes 345 GB to 86 GB, cold prefill 6.0 s to about 1.4 s, beating Ollama's 2.3 s.  Implement next round.

history.title: Implemented split-K to the checklist and it passes every gate, but the performance case is unproven, so it ships default-OFF.  The kernel takes uint3 tg and under mode 4 slices K by Q4_GEMM_S = 4 writing f32 partials into y as scratch; a new q4_gemm_reduce kernel sums the four partials into the half output; CommandBatch gained buffer() for the scratch; and it engages for out_f in [1024, 5120] with rows >= 32, which here means only out_f = 5120.  Gates: 19 of 19 ACCEPTED with split-K ON, mlx-lm oracle included.  The round's most valuable outcome is a bug it exposed.  The first build applied the K slice unconditionally and, since an ordinary dispatch has grid.z = 1, k_hi came out as K/4, so the GEMM quietly computed a quarter of every dot product.  The deception was near-perfect: the server emitted a string of newlines and pipes - plainly wrong - while the interleaved A/B called it 27 percent FASTER, 3.06 s against 3.87 s, a win that was nothing but three quarters of the arithmetic disappearing.  Gating on const bool sk = (mode == 4) fixed it and the server returned sane text at once.  Prove correctness before claiming speed: had only the A/B numbers been read, a bug dropping 75 percent of the work would have been filed as a 27 percent optimisation, and the oracle gate was the only guard.  With the fix, four interleaved rounds after a 300 s cooldown gave sk0 16.894/16.188/15.435/15.624 against sk1 13.357/13.508/15.781/15.872 - 2 of 4 to split-K, median 16.165 to 14.645, roughly 9 percent, inside a 13.4-16.9 s noise band on a machine that measured 3.0 s and 6.0 s earlier the same day.  That is not a verified win, so split-K is default-OFF behind QW_SPLITK=1, kept and proved correct for a retest on a quiet machine.

history.title: Ran an eight-round paired A/B with per-round GPU sampling and learned two things: split-K buys nothing, and this machine cannot currently be measured at all.  The paired differences (B minus A) were -0.201, +0.121, -0.064, -0.574, +0.274, -5.781, +0.041, -0.346, so split-K won 5 of 8 with a median difference of -0.133 s, roughly one percent - a zero effect, consistent with the earlier finding that the GEMM is not traffic-bound.  Cutting traffic from 4W to W gains nothing, so the 5x the theory predicted never materialised and the eighteen-times-traffic analysis, arithmetically sound, is not the reason we are slow; the real cause remains unknown.  The weightier discovery concerns the environment: GPU utilisation sat at 84 to 99 percent for the entire run with no qwen38 process alive, only the first sample reading 0, so an external process - almost certainly the DSH Desktop web GUI - holds the GPU continuously.  Within one run the timings drifted by a factor of 2.4, from a stable 12.4-13.0 s over rounds one to five to 22.8-30.4 s over rounds six to eight, and the machine shows load 3.99, spotlightknowledged at 99.4 percent CPU and 3.7 GB of swap in use.  No absolute cold-TTFT number is trustworthy there and a one-percent effect is unresolvable.  This re-explains the history too: the same configuration measured 3.0 s, 6.0 s, 12.9 s and 30.4 s for 672 tokens within one day, a tenfold spread that is a property of the environment rather than the kernel.  Fixing the measurement environment must precede any further performance judgement, and because the likely consumer is the user's own application I asked instead of killing it.  Next: obtain a quiet measurement window, then re-decide split-K and re-measure the objective.

history.title: Fixed the head-to-head harness and found that our otps figure had been wrong all along.  The old script computed (chunks-1)/(last-first) - chunks per second - while Ollama's side used eval_count/eval_duration, which genuinely is tokens per second, so the two were on different scales and the recorded 1.377x was meaningless.  The new tools/duel.py uses the streaming request only for TTFT, stopping on the first non-empty content chunk because the server emits a role-only chunk about 60 ms in and stopping there gives a bogus 0.06 s, and takes the token count from a second non-streaming request's usage.completion_tokens, since stream_options.include_usage does nothing here but the non-streaming path does return usage; otps is (completion_tokens-1)/(last-first).  Ollama keeps eval_count/eval_duration plus a chunk-rate cross-check.  This also closes a long-standing gap: usage.prompt_tokens works on the non-streaming response - 565 in validation - so a real cold prefill need not be inferred from logs.  A one-round validation at gen=64 gave ours cold TTFT 6.102 s and otps 26.27 against Ollama's 2.338 s and 24.99: otps still wins but by 1.05x rather than the recorded 1.377x, Ollama's chunk-rate 24.60 matching its 24.99 and confirming both sides now share a scale, with cold TTFT 2.6x behind.  The corrected picture is that the otps edge is 5 percent, not 38, and even that was measured with the GPU 84-99 percent busy, so the decisive measurement waits on the quiet window the user agreed to provide.  Next: run tools/duel.py and the paired A/B in that window and re-establish the true standing.

history.title: Tested BN=128 together with split-K - the combination the analysis pointed to, where each pass reads the weights once and grid.z restores 640 threadgroups - and it is 72 per cent slower, ending the BN=128 route for good.  Both halves were correct: the BN=128 tile is bit-identical and the gates pass 19/0 with sane server output, yet six interleaved rounds gave A 5.903/5.870/5.901/5.632/5.865/27.602 against B 10.127/10.113/11.586/28.586/9.978/9.977, so B won 1 of 6 and the median went 5.886 to 10.120, 72 per cent worse.  The BN sweep is complete: 8 lost 6/6, 32 is optimal, 64 lost 4/4 by 27 per cent, 64 with NT=256 won 3/3 by just 4.3 per cent with a 935 s outlier, 128 lost 4/4 by 73 per cent and 128 with split-K lost 5/6 by 72 per cent.  Reducing weight traffic is definitively refuted - sixteen accumulators per simdgroup, and a bandwidth collapse at 160 threadgroups, always cost more than the traffic saved.  Pricing the staging properly produced a new lead.  For out_f=5120, K=6144, rows=128, BM=BN=32, weight staging is (rows/BN)*out_f*K*0.5 = 62.9 MB and activation staging is (out_f/BM)*K*BN*2 = 62.9 MB, exactly equal: the activations are only 1.57 MB but are re-read 160 times, once per out_f block, and although L2 residency keeps the DRAM cost low they still cost shared writes and barrier time, with staging already known to be 89 per cent of the time.  Raising BM from 32 to 64 halves the activation staging, 80 blocks instead of 160, cutting total staging from 126 MB to 94 MB, 25 per cent less, while doubling the MMA work per threadgroup for better latency amortisation; shared comes to wsh 5120 + xsh 2624 + osh 8192 = 15936 B, comfortably inside the limit.  BM=64 sits in the refuted list from an earlier round but with no recorded data and in a different combination, so it warrants a clean retest on this explicit motivation.  Reverted to the shipped build, md5 restored, gemm-check PASSES.  Next: test BM=64 with BN=32.

history.title: Tested BM=64 with BN=32, the configuration the activation-staging arithmetic pointed to, and it is 4.1 per cent slower, refuting that hypothesis as well.  Doubling BM halves the activation staging, from 160 out_f blocks to 80 and total staging from 126 MB to 94, yet five interleaved rounds gave A 5.612/5.830/5.642/5.654/6.643 against B 5.855/6.034/5.896/5.882/7.296 - B winning 1 of 6, median 5.742 to 5.965 - with bit-identical accuracy and gates 19/0.  The staging now has ten explanations excluded: dequantisation, per-step overhead, bank conflicts, global bandwidth, shared capacity, instruction count, parallelism beyond grid.y = 4, traffic via BN, coalescing, and activation staging volume.  Its 61 GB/s is the hard limit of this design and tile parameters have nothing left to give. history.title: Completed the three-way interleaved comparison, which settles the objective's standing.  tools/tri.py keeps all three servers resident and sends the SAME fresh random prompt to each in a rotating order every round, so drift and thermal load are shared rather than attributed to whoever ran first.  Six-round medians: ours cold TTFT 6.821 s with otps 25.35 tok/s, llama.cpp 1.553 s with 22.33, Ollama 1.630 s with 21.89.  otps therefore beats BOTH baselines - 1.135x over llama.cpp and 1.158x over Ollama, winning all six rounds against each - while cold TTFT loses to both, by 4.4x and 4.2x.  Half the objective is achieved and half is not.  The efficiency comparison says why: llama.cpp prefills 592 tokens in 1.55 s, roughly 381 tok/s or about 26 TFLOPS and 72 percent of the 36 TFLOPS peak, while we reach 87 tok/s, about 7.8 TFLOPS or 22 percent of peak.  The gap is kernel efficiency rather than traffic, precisely what the ten excluded explanations indicated.  Our staging achieves only about 76 GB/s against the GEMV's 400, leaving two routes: a structural rewrite that dequantises into registers and feeds the MMA directly with no shared staging, or producer/consumer double buffering so the memory system is not idle during the MMA phase and vice versa.  Warm TTFT has also been added to the harness, since all three engines cache prefixes and that is the common case for a served model. history.title: Measured the cold prefill's internal breakdown and it changes the plan.  With QW_PREFIX_TIME a 602-token cold prefill logs 256/602 after 2.6 s, 512/602 after 5.2 s and prompt in after 6.3 s, so every 256 tokens costs exactly 2.6 s, 10.2 ms per token, linear and unremarkable.  Compared with the GEMM microbenchmark, where a 128-token pass takes 0.95 s and 256 tokens therefore 1.90 s, the GEMM is 73 per cent of the cold prefill and everything else - conv1d, norms, gating, attention - is 27 per cent, roughly 1.7 s for 602 tokens, more than twice the 12 per cent estimated earlier.  The ceiling arithmetic matters more than the split: with an instantaneous GEMM the cold prefill would still be 1.70 s against llama.cpp's 1.60, only drawing level; a fourfold faster GEMM gives 2.85 s and still loses by 1.8x; and a fourfold faster GEMM with the non-GEMM work halved gives 2.0 s, still 1.25x behind.  So the GEMM alone cannot reach the objective - it has to be paired with batching the per-token non-GEMM operators.  That is the round's most important judgement and it redirects the work away from one more tile experiment: next come a structural GEMM speedup, since we run at about 7.1 TFLOPS against llama.cpp's 27, and batching conv1d, the norms and the gating so they stop costing a per-token dispatch.

history.title: Pulled the per-kernel dispatch histogram for prefill and found the structural difference between us and llama.cpp: one 128-token prefill pass issues 41,874 dispatches, whereas a decode step issues 1,234.  The prefill histogram is dominated by per-token operators - copy_off 6144, conv1d_silu_ring 6144, gdn_step 6144 and rmsnorm_gated 6144, each exactly 128 tokens times 48 GDN layers, plus rmsnorm_s 4096 and rope_partial 4096 at 128 times 32 - giving 327 dispatches per token, none batched along the token dimension.  That accounts precisely for the 27 per cent non-GEMM share: 0.35 s per pass divided by 41,874 is 8.4 microseconds per dispatch, pure launch overhead with the GPU idling in between.  Of those, 26,624 or 64 per cent are trivially batchable - copy_off, conv1d_silu_ring, rmsnorm_gated, rmsnorm_s and rope_partial are elementwise, convolutional or per-token independent - while gdn_step's 6144 form a linear recurrence across tokens needing a chunked parallel scan, an algorithmic change.  This is the most valuable lead in many rounds and attacks the non-GEMM 27 per cent head on, so next is converting those five operators to one dispatch over the whole 128-token pass.

history.title: Acted on the dispatch-count lead by hoisting rmsnorm_gated out of the per-token recurrence loop and batching it over all n rows.  The kernel gained a stride scalar at buffer 6 where stride == 0 reproduces the old one-row-per-dispatch mapping exactly, so the decode path needed only a .scalar(6, 0), while prefill dispatches a one-dimensional grid of hv * n * NT and decomposes tg into (token, tile) inside; MSL refuses to mix scalar and vector input declarations, so a uint2 tg beside uint lane would not compile and the final form is a plain 1-D grid.  Dispatches per pass fell from 41,874 to 35,778, a 14.6 per cent cut, gates passed 19/0, and the output is word-for-word identical - yet six interleaved A/B rounds gave 6.312/6.277, 6.367/6.313, 6.104/6.087, 6.372/6.214, 6.684/6.663 and 6.783/6.742, B winning 6/6 with the median moving only 6.369 to 6.295, a 0.6 per cent gain.  The dispatch-count hypothesis is therefore refuted: removing 6,096 dispatches should have saved about 4 per cent at 8.4 microseconds each and saved 0.6, so the GPU overlaps dispatches far better than I estimated and the 27 per cent is real if fragmented GPU work rather than launch overhead.  The change is kept as verified, risk-free and directionally right, but it is not a lever that changes the conclusion.  Next: the GEMM remains the only substantial lever, and since the ceiling arithmetic says even an instantaneous GEMM only draws level, the real question is why our per-token work is fragmented where llama.cpp's is not.

history.title: Found and fixed the real fragmentation: not the dispatch count but a barrier per token.  A prefill pass issued 128 gdn_step dispatches and 128 barriers per GDN layer - 6,144 barriers per pass over 48 layers - repeatedly draining the GPU.  The gdn_step kernel has no threadgroup_barrier at all, each thread (hv, dv) owns its own state slice at state + (hv*Dv+dv)*Dk, and threads never communicate, so the token loop fuses into the kernel with no barrier between consecutive tokens.  The new gdn_step_seq wraps the body in a loop over t and advances each buffer by a per-token stride (s_q, s_k, s_v, s_ab and s_y in half elements, s_snap through a char* so its unit cannot be misread), and the caller guards with one_seq, rows.iter().all(|r| r.0 == rows[0].0): a prefill pass's n rows are consecutive positions of ONE sequence sharing a single state slice and must be applied in order, which the fused kernel does internally, while a batch pass of unrelated sequences keeps the per-row loop.  Dispatches per pass fell from 35,778 to 29,682, a 29 per cent cut from the original 41,874, GDN barriers went from 6,144 to zero, gates passed 19/0, and the output is word-for-word identical.  Six interleaved A/B rounds put A at a 6.201 median against B at 6.071, B winning 6/6 at -3.1 per cent with every difference negative and tightly clustered.  The real lever is not issuing fewer dispatches but draining the GPU less often.  The largest remaining target is copy_off 6,144 plus conv1d_silu_ring 6,144, 41 per cent of what is left, both entirely independent per token and fusible the same way.

history.title: Pulled the complete prefill dispatch histogram, having previously looked only at its top seven entries, and it names the largest remaining target: the full-attention layers are still processed one token at a time during prefill.  Of 29,682 dispatches per pass, copy_off 6144 and conv1d_silu_ring 6144 form the GDN phase-2 pair at 41 per cent - per-token but with no barriers - while the attention path is 16,384 or 55 per cent: rmsnorm_s 4096 and rope_partial 4096 at 128 tokens times 32, then kv_append, attn_scores_softmax, attn_out and gate_mul at 2048 each, 128 tokens times 16 layers.  In other words prefill drives the single-token attention path, with its chain of per-token barriers.  round_bf16 does not appear, so bf16_residual is off by default and no hidden 8192 lurks there.  Since the gdn fusion showed that removing barriers pays far more than removing dispatches, the priority is clear: rmsnorm_s, rope_partial, kv_append and gate_mul total 12,288 dispatches or 41 per cent and are entirely independent per token, so they can be batched immediately, while attn_scores_softmax and attn_out total 4,096 or 14 per cent and need a causal mask over the query block, which is harder.

Four token-batched kernels were added - rmsnorm_s_rows, gate_mul_rows, kv_append_rows and rope_partial_rows - with one_seq guarding rope and kv_append since they need pos = pos0 + t, while the norms and the gate batch unconditionally. The trap: after reverting, the binary's md5 was identical to the verified /tmp/q.gdseq and the gates still failed, because pkill -f qwen38 does not match the /tmp/q.* copies - their command lines contain no qwen38 - so a stale server from the broken build kept holding port 8199 and accept.sh kept talking to it, with lsof showing q.attn1 pid 90583 listening. history.title: Found and fixed the bug that forced last round's revert, so the attention batching now ships.  The diagnosis used a runtime mask, QW_ATTN_BATCH with bit 1 the q/k norms, bit 2 the output gate, bit 4 rope and bit 8 the kv append, where mask 0 reproduces the pre-batching code exactly and so acts as a usable control, plus a fast checker that starts the server, sends a fixed long prompt and compares the output md5 in about forty seconds rather than ten minutes.  Against a baseline md5 of 5b5f6e93 at 182 characters, masks 0, 1, 2 and 4 matched, mask 8 did not, and mask 15 did not - the bug was in kv_append_rows alone and the other three were correct all along.  The root cause is that the k and v scratch rows are not the same length: scratch.k is shared with the delta-net path and is laid out with key_dim = linear_num_key_heads times linear_key_head_dim = 16 x 128 = 2048 elements per token, while the attention k this kernel copies is only num_key_value_heads times head_dim = 4 x 256 = 1024 of them, and scratch.v is exactly 1024.  The original used two different expressions, key_dim for k and nkv*hd for v, whereas my batched kernel used a single Hkv*D for both, so k[i] walked into the next token.  The fix adds krow and vrow scalars addressing k[token*krow + j] and v[token*vrow + j] separately, after which every mask including 15 matches the baseline word for word.  Dispatches per pass fell from 29,682 to 17,490, gates pass 19/0, and six interleaved A/B rounds gave a median of 6.066 to 5.952, B winning 6/6 at -2.0 per cent with all differences negative and tightly clustered.  With the gdn fusion, cold prefill is down from 6.69 s to about 5.95 s.

history.title: Found the fused convolution kernel already in the tree as dead code and wired it into prefill, removing 70 per cent of the remaining dispatches.  conv1d_silu_ring_tile had a constant and a full implementation but no call site: its comment says it convolves a whole tile of rows at once, reading the current pass's rows straight from the staging buffer, and folds the ring update in, so it replaces both the per-row copy and the per-row convolution.  Wiring it behind the one_seq guard took copy_off and conv1d_silu_ring from 6,144 each to zero and added 48 conv1d_silu_ring_tile, so dispatches per pass fell from 17,490 to 5,250.  Correctness is argued in the kernel's own comment: every window read in that dispatch is for a position before pos0, at least three slots behind the ones it writes, so no thread reads a slot another is writing.  Gates pass 19/0 and masks 0 and 15 both match the baseline word for word.  Six interleaved A/B rounds gave a median of 6.102 to 6.031, B winning 6/6 at -1.2 per cent.  Across three rounds dispatches fell from 41,874 to 5,250, 87 per cent, for a cumulative speedup of only about 6 per cent - reconfirming that dispatch count is not the bottleneck unless it carries barriers, since the gdn fusion was most effective precisely because it removed 6,144 barriers at once.  Of the 5,250 left, attn_scores_softmax and attn_out are 4,096 or 78 per cent and need a causal mask, while about 73 per cent of the cold prefill's time is still the GEMM.

history.title: Re-measured the cold prefill: the GEMM's share has risen to 79 per cent, 0.95 s of each 1.2 s pass, because the dispatch work cut the non-GEMM side to 0.25 s, and even zeroing it would leave 4.75 s, so the GEMM is the whole game.  Used the kernel's existing QW_GEMM_MODE diagnostic, which is plumbed through the real linear.rs path, to decompose a 602-token cold prefill: mode 0 full 5.9 s, mode 1 constant weights with no dequantisation 6.4 s and therefore not faster, killing dequantisation as a target, mode 2 MACs skipped 4.7 s, mode 3 x staging skipped 4.8 s.  With the non-GEMM at about 1.24 s and the GEMM at about 4.66 s that gives roughly 2.4 s weight staging, 1.1 s x staging and only 1.2 s MMA - the GEMM is staging-bound at 26 per cent MMA, so its 7.76 TFLOPS is a data-movement ceiling rather than a tensor-pipe one.  Two fixes were then tested and both refuted, gates 19/0 with word-for-word identical output, and both reverted: double buffering halved the barrier count but doubled shared memory from 9,280 to 14,464 bytes and came out 0/6 at 9.5 per cent SLOWER, while aliasing the accumulator staging onto the dead tiles to cut shared memory 44 per cent to 5,184 bytes came out 1/6 at plus 1.1 per cent, a tie.  So it is neither intra-threadgroup stalls nor shared-memory residency, which points at memory-level parallelism: the weight staging loop issues exactly one uint load per thread per step, exposing its full latency.

history.title: Tested register prefetching in the GEMM weight staging, carrying the next K step's word, scale and bias in three registers across the dequantisation, the activation staging, a barrier and the MMAs with no extra shared memory, and it came out a tie: gates 19/0 with word-for-word identical output, but 2/6 and plus 0.2 per cent in the A/B, so it was reverted.  That is the third refutation of the staging bottleneck in two rounds, after double buffering (halved the barrier count but doubled shared memory and lost 9.5 per cent, 0/6) and aliasing the accumulator staging to cut shared memory 44 per cent (a tie at 1/6), so it is not intra-threadgroup stalls, not shared-memory residency and not memory-level parallelism.  I also killed the obvious alternative design: the GEMV path sweeps weights at 481 GB/s while the GEMM's staging moves them at about 24 GB/s, so a K-token GEMV would read each weight once per K tokens.  bench --tokens measures that path and it floors at about 20.5 ms per token from k=4 onward, so 128 tokens would take 16 sweeps of 166.8 ms at k=8, which is 2.67 s against the GEMM's 0.95 s - the GEMM is 2.8 times faster and the K-sweep idea is dead.  The staging puzzle is narrowed to something that is neither bandwidth, latency, buffering nor residency, with fourteen explanations excluded; within the BM=32/BN=32/BK=32/NT=128/simdgroup_matrix design, 7.76 TFLOPS looks like a hard ceiling, and beating llama.cpp on cold TTFT would need the GEMM roughly four times faster.

history.title: Halved the GEMM's weight traffic and it got SLOWER, overturning the staging-bound model.  Weight traffic is W * (rows / BN), so BN 32 to 64 should cut 57.6 GB to 28.8 GB; BN=64 had failed before at NT 128, but that left sixteen accumulators per simdgroup, so this time I used eight simdgroups at NT 256 in a 2x4 arrangement, keeping four accumulators per simdgroup, and generalised r_off/t_off to sg/(BN/16) and sg%(BN/16).  Gates passed 19/0 with word-for-word identical output and the A/B came out 1/6 and 2.6 per cent SLOWER, so it was reverted.  The result matters more than the change: last round the kernel's diagnostic modes decomposed the GEMM into about 2.36 s weight staging, 1.1 s x staging and 1.2 s MMA, which I read as staging-bound - but halving the weight data moved nothing, so that 2.36 s is not weight data movement.  Modes 2 and 3 both keep the two barriers per K step and the whole loop skeleton, so the bulk must be barrier and loop overhead rather than memory traffic.  Sixteen GEMM directions are now refuted: double buffering, shared-memory aliasing, register prefetching, BN of 8, 64 and 128, BM of 64, BK of 64, 128 and 256, split-K, K-major layout, x coalescing, uint4 staging and the K-sweep GEMV.  Within BM=32/BN=32/BK=32/NT=128/simdgroup_matrix, 7.76 TFLOPS is a hard ceiling.  The comparison is not unkind to us - llama.cpp loads a 16.8 GB GGUF against our 14.4 GB and is still 3.7 times faster.

history.title: Found the way out of the sixteen refuted staging ideas: MetalPerformancePrimitives exists on this machine (macOS 26.6.2, SDK 27.0) and its matmul2d type table includes half x uint4b_format -> half/float, which is exactly our quantised linear.  The 4-bit weights go to the tensor units as they sit in memory, with no dequantisation, no threadgroup staging and no hand-built simdgroup_matrix fragments, because the kernel parameters are device tensors and op.run reads them directly.  I added an msl::MPP probe kernel (half x uint4b_format -> float, NT layout, 64x32 tile, four simdgroups) and a compile check in linear.rs that stays silent when it works and shouts when it breaks.  Three namespace traps cost a few iterations: matmul2d_descriptor and matmul2d live in mpp::tensor_ops rather than mpp, while execution_simdgroups is in the global namespace and in neither.  With those fixed the probe reports built OK, so the path compiles for our exact shapes.  What remains is the affine part: w = q*s + b with s and b per 64-weight group, while matmul2d computes only sum A*q, so the plan is to pre-scale the activation by s, run one matmul2d, get the per-group activation sums S[m,g] with a cheap O(rows*K) reduction, and add sum_g b_g * S[m,g] with a second matmul2d whose K is only 96 - about 1.6 per cent extra tensor work, while cutting weight traffic from 57.6 GB to 14.4 GB and removing the staging entirely.

history.title: Dispatched the MetalPerformancePrimitives probe for real under QW_GEMM_MODE=7 and measured a 602-token cold prefill at 1.9 s against q4_gemm_tile's 6.0 s - a 3.2x jump, the largest single win in the project. The probe is not shippable because it computes only A x q and ignores the affine, and the affine is genuinely hard to fold in: our scales and biases have shape [out_f, K/64], so s depends on the output column n and cannot be pre-multiplied into the activation ([m,k], n-independent) nor folded into the 4-bit weights without losing precision. history.title: Found the key to the affine: matmul2d exposes get_destination_cooperative_tensor<left_t, right_t, element_t>() returning an in-register accumulator, and cT[i] with cT.get_mask(i) is the element access. The Metal stdlib builtin headers are readable at /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/GPUCompiler.framework/Versions/32023/Libraries/lib/clang/32023.886/include/metal, which is how metal_cooperative_tensor was read; the path came out of a compiler error after find / timed out.  The trap: cooperative_tensor takes three template arguments and the third is an implementation-defined Layout with no public alias, so it must come from the op - cooperative_tensor<float, dextents<int32_t,2>> gives too few template arguments and neither void nor a repeated extents works. history.title: Implemented the complete affine-aware MPP GEMM; it compiles, runs and produces coherent text, but the output does not yet match the baseline (md5 c934afba len 161 vs baseline len 182). history.title: Narrowed the affine kernel's failure to three measured but contradictory facts.  (1) The affine path really executes: making q4_store_half write the constant 999 garbles the output to md5 f89d2716, so the narrowing kernel runs and its result reaches y.  (2) The affine kernel's output equals the plain matmul sum_k A*q exactly and is independent of sc and bi - mode 7 with no affine, mode 8 with sc=1/bi=0, mode 8 with the real bf16 scales and biases, and mode 8 with sc hardcoded to 2.0f all give the identical md5 c934afba len 161, against the baseline's 5b5f6e93 len 182.  Hardcoding sc=2.0 having no effect rules out a wrong lookup value, a misbound buffer and a bad bf16 conversion, and says the accumulation line is not taking effect.  (3) Swapping the two components of get_multidimensional_index also leaves the md5 unchanged, so the m/n mapping is not the cause.  Ruled out by measurement: a silently swallowed kernel build failure (eprintln added, zero failures), a failed cargo build leaving a stale binary (full build output shows Finished release, exit 0), and Metal caching by kernel name (renaming to q4_mpp_affine_v2 changed nothing).  Strongest remaining hypothesis: cT and part are cooperative tensors built from the same op with identical template arguments and layouts, so they may share thread storage - then part.set(i,0) also zeroes cT and cT.set(i, cT.get(i) + part.get(i)*sc) collapses to X = X + X*sc and is wiped each iteration, so the stored value is not the weighted sum of 96 groups. history.title: Cracked the affine puzzle to one mechanism and found a confound poisoning every earlier comparison.  The confound: QW_GEMM_MODE is not private to the new code - linear.rs line 345 hands it to q4_gemm_tile as a scalar, so setting it to 7 or 8 made the old kernel take a debug branch and emit c934afba instead of the baseline 5b5f6e93, meaning the earlier 'mode 8 equals mode 7' results were untrustworthy.  The MPP paths now use a dedicated QW_MPP variable (1 probe, 2 affine).  With that fixed, isolation gives three clean results: a raw 777 write inside the affine kernel garbles the output to ef46dd23 (the kernel executes); q4_store_half writing 999 garbles it to f89d2716 (the narrowing kernel works); and setting every cT element to 555 before store leaves the output unchanged at c934afba, so cT.store(mC) is a no-op and the accumulator never reaches cacc.  That is the root cause.  Ruled out: slice without explicit extents (slice<64,64>, slice<32,64>, C.slice<64,32>), implicit buffer indices colliding with explicit ones (gave A, B, C explicit indices), cT and part sharing thread storage (switched to a plain thread float acc array), and the QW_GEMM_MODE confound.  store's enable_if needs is_same_v<element_type, value_type> and get_rank() >= E::rank(); both are float rank 2, so the next suspect is that element_type and value_type differ under the tensor_handle tag, or that store wants a tensor_offset rather than a tensor_handle.  More robust next step: bypass store and write cw[m*outf + n] = cT.get(i) via get_multidimensional_index, since cw's direct writes were proven to reach the output.

history.title: Shipped a verified single-pass prefill: 602 tokens now run in one pass instead of five, 5.94 s to 5.42 s, 6/6 paired with byte-identical output.  The real per-pass limit was never 128 - engine.rs PREFILL_CHUNK_MAX was a separate conservative cap while the runner enforces max_per_seq = (conv_k + PASS_ROWS_MAX).next_power_of_two() - conv_k = 252, and conv_ring only needs to be a power of two, so PASS_ROWS_MAX 1020 costs a few hundred MB of scratch.  runner.rs:1537 also enforces rows must be 1..=BATCH_MAX, so BATCH_MAX rose with it; it only sizes small scratch buffers (about 100 MB) and the invariant is BATCH_MAX >= PASS_ROWS_MAX.  The decisive strategic result: reading weights once instead of five times bought only 9 percent, so prefill is NOT weight-bandwidth-bound but compute-bound - 32.5 TFLOP over 5.42 s is about 6.0 TFLOPS effective, matching the measured 7.76 TFLOPS GEMM.  That explains why sixteen earlier GEMM tuning directions all failed and means MPP matmul2d is the only route that can close the gap.  The affine scale lookup is still unresolved: sc depending only on g (row 0) hangs the server with no output and no error, so that variant produces NaN and stalls generation, while sc=1 with bi=0 still reproduces mode 7 exactly, pinning the fault on the scales[n*ngroups + g] lookup rather than the group machinery.

history.title: Built a 10-second numeric measurement bench for the MPP path and proved the cooperative-tensor read path is dead on this toolchain.  The MPP affine path is now wired into gemm-check and measured against the same CPU reference as the GEMM and GEMV, so a 40-second yes/no md5 became a relative-error number in ten seconds. Hence part.get(i) is always zero.  Hoisting part out of the loop, swapping coordinate order, dynamic_extent K, and deleting the loop so op.run runs once all leave it intact - one op.run still reads back zero.  Ruled out: slice without explicit extents, buffer index collisions, cT/part sharing storage, array overflow, static vs dynamic K, where part is created, and the documented coordinate order.
