history.title: Eliminated the two remaining alternative routes to the affine with documented evidence, leaving exactly one viable structure.  Route one: the MPP matmul does support hardware block scales (the __impl run symbols carry left/rightScaleDataType and ScaleBlockSize0/1, exposed publicly via metal::tensor_plane_scales) but it hard-asserts scale type metal_fp8_ue8m0_format with blockSize0 == 32 and blockSize1 == 1 and a non-transposed left tensor.  fp8_ue8m0 has only an 8-bit exponent, so scales would round to powers of two - up to 2x per-group error, far outside the 2e-3 tolerance the current 3.3e-4 gemm meets.  Route two: q4_mpp_affine_v3 accumulating each group in threadgroup memory failed to compile because tensor<threadgroup T, ...> is rejected - metal_tensor asserts a tensor_handle element type must be device or constant qualified - so threadgroup accumulation is closed at the type level.  I also checked store's constraints exactly (is_same_v of element_type and value_type, get_rank() <= E::rank()): cT is float, mC a device float tensor, both rank 2, and slice() does put its tensor_offset in Tags, so every constraint holds and store is still a no-op, closing that path too.  The one structure left uses the proven primitive: op.run into a device tensor.  Each threadgroup owns a 64x32 tile, loops the 96 groups calling op.run into a device scratch slice per group, and a second cheap narrowing kernel computes y[m,n] = sum_g s[n,g]*scratch[g,m,n] + b[n,g]*gsum[m,g].  The scratch is 96 * rows * out_f * 4 bytes - tens of GB for lm_head at out_f 248320 - so it must be tiled over out_f, about 100 MB at 4096 columns.  That tiling is next.  Enum values: float32 0x10000000|32, float16 0x10000000|16, bfloat16 0x80000000|0x10000000|16, uint4 4, invalid 0.

history.title: Corrected last round's reasoning and found the real bottleneck.  Cold TTFT on 602 tokens, interleaved: default 6.705/6.468 s, MPP probe 1.725/1.730 s (3.8x, very stable), skip-MACs 4.663/4.105 s.  The 32.5 TFLOP of MACs is only about 2.1 s (15.5 TFLOPS) while 4.4 s is staging and dispatch - MPP wins by bypassing threadgroup staging entirely, which explains why all sixteen earlier GEMM tuning directions failed.  MPP ceiling 1.73 s vs llama.cpp's 1.60 s.  Then the overturning find: cooperative_tensor::get() is 'return is_valid_element(idx) ? (*this)[idx] : value_type()', so it returns zero for an invalid index, meaning every earlier 'part.get(i) is always zero' observation was equally consistent with the mask being false - those experiments never separated 'not written' from 'invalid index', so last round's conclusion needed correcting.  Direct measurement of the mask (capacity and valid-count dumped from the kernel) gives capacity=16 valid=16: 16 per thread times 128 threads is exactly the 2048 elements of the 64x32 tile and the mask is true for all of them, so the mask is fine.  Removing the guard and using operator[] as Apple's example does still gives rel 1.000e0, bit for bit identical to the guarded version.  Source confirms the cooperative implementation is selected: MPPTensorOpsMatMul2dImpl.h:9129 matches half/uint4b_format/float with both operands in device and calls __tensorops_impl_matmul2d_op_run_cooperative_dv_f16_dv_ui4_f32_v2, and 128 threads is the four SIMD groups execution_simdgroups<4> requires.  So op.run into a device tensor works while op.run into a cooperative tensor yields no data on this machine - a driver-level issue, no longer worth probing from MSL.  Next: the device-scratch route - per-threadgroup 64x32 tile, 96 group calls into per-group device scratch slices, then y[m,n] = sum_g s[n,g]*scratch[g,m,n] + b[n,g]*G[m,g], tiled over out_f at 4096 columns.

history.title: Corrected a vacuous measurement and produced a precise decomposition of the cold prefill.  The 602-token cold prefill returns '<think>' for both mode 0 and mode 2 (which skips every MAC), so a max_tokens=1 cold-prefill md5 carries almost no information - this model's first token on that prompt is always '<think>'.  Earlier correctness claims resting on that comparison, including the single-pass prefill change, were therefore vacuous; that change is still validated by accept.sh's mlx-lm oracle so the conclusion stands, but correctness must now go through gemm-check or the oracle.  The diagnostic modes do work - mode 2 changes output on a 26-token generation (a97e4ebb to fc75a676).  Decomposition of the 5.39 s cold prefill: mode 1 (skip dequant) 5.246/5.384, mode 2 (skip MACs) 3.827/3.830, mode 3 (skip activation staging) 3.978/4.126.  Cross-check: weight+output = 3.83-1.35-0.1 = 2.38 and 2.38+0.1+1.56 = 4.04 vs mode 3's 3.98-4.13.  So weight staging plus output plus dispatch is about 2.4 s (44%), MACs 1.56 s (29%), activation staging 1.35 s (25%), dequant 0.1 s (2%).  Dequant is free and MACs already run at 20.8 TFLOPS; staging as a class is 3.75 s or 70%.  The BK sweep refuted coalescing in the opposite direction: BK=32 gives 9.28 KB and 5.387/5.397, BK=64 gives 12.9 KB and 5.558/5.536, BK=128 gives 23.3 KB and 8.077/8.077.  Performance degrades monotonically with threadgroup memory, so the kernel is occupancy/latency bound rather than bandwidth bound - which also explains why all sixteen earlier staging optimisations failed, since they all reduced bytes and bytes are not the bottleneck.  Next: cut threadgroup memory.  Of the 9.28 KB, wsh is 2560, xsh 2624 and osh 4096; osh alone is 44% and exists only to bounds-check partial row blocks.  Store simdgroup accumulators straight into device y: rows are safe because y is sized for BATCH_MAX (1020) and the overflow rows land inside the allocation unread, but columns need out_f % 32 == 0.  Target 5.18 KB, about 1.8x occupancy.
history.gates: kernel restored to the committed BK=32 state; default path and gemm-check re-verified

evidence.vacuous_check: 602-token cold prefill returns '<think>' for both mode 0 and mode 2, so max_tokens=1 md5 proves nothing; mode 2 does change a 26-token generation (a97e4ebb -> fc75a676)
evidence.conclusion: occupancy/latency bound, not bandwidth bound - performance degrades monotonically with threadgroup memory
evidence.explains_sixteen_failures: all earlier staging optimisations reduced bytes; bytes are not the bottleneck
evidence.next: drop osh (4096 B, 44% of the 9.28 KB) by storing accumulators straight into device y; rows are safe via BATCH_MAX padding, columns need out_f % 32 == 0

history.what: MPP tensor path is real and is now the default GEMM: cold prefill 5.59 -> 2.51 s (2.23x), output byte-identical, 497-tensor sweep worst rel 4.668e-4, accept.sh 19/0
GDN state resident in registers: 2.11 -> 1.54 s cold prefill (27%), byte-identical, accept 19/0; cumulative 5.59 -> 1.54 s, now below llama.cpp's 1.60 s

CORRECTION: paired duel (8 rounds, same prompts, order swapped) shows llama.cpp wins cold TTFT 8/8, median ratio 1.129. otps and warm TTFT still won 8/8. Round 199's 'cold prefill now ahead' was a non-paired comparison and is withdrawn.

Paired duel reproduced: cold TTFT ratio 1.130 vs 1.129 in the prior run, so the ~13% deficit is real. otps won 8/8 again. NRB 160/192/224 all slower, closing the tensor-tile line. Writeback isolated at up to 0.36 s via new QW_GEMM_MODE=6.
fp32 bulk-store writeback implemented, verified numerically exact, measured 1.8% SLOWER in 4/4, reverted. Mode-6 style subtraction is invalid when it changes what later kernels read.

New default MPP tile NRB=256/NRA=32 (same 64-register accumulator, weight sweeps 5->3): 7/8 rounds faster, ~2%. Round 203's NRB conclusion was a single-axis generalisation error - the accumulator is NRB*NRA so tiles must be swept along constant-product lines.

Landed NRB=256/NRA=32 tile (+2%, all gates green). Closed as negative: encoder splits (QW_NO_ENC_SPLIT is not faster), KT=32/relaxed, lm_head last-row restriction (batchcheck contract). 4th paired duel 1.181 under much heavier load - we are more contention-sensitive than llama.cpp.

Added gemm-bench and prefill-bench. Honest split: GEMM 0.83 s (37 TFLOPS), in-model non-GEMM only 0.22 s. But HTTP cold TTFT 1.60 s vs server-side forward 1.16 s => ~0.4 s outside the model, the new top lead. Found the 598+4 last-chunk split costs cold prefill one extra weight sweep.

Found 265 ms of cold TTFT outside every kernel: argmax(logits_row(i)) ran per prefill row, 597 of 598 samples discarded. Made it lazy at the point of use. Cold TTFT 1.60 -> 1.32 s (17%), variance tightened 10x. accept.sh 19/0.

Corrected round 143: reset_seq is 3.4 ms warm, not 145 ms - the 200-300 ms is GPU clock ramp after the harness's 2 s idle (removing the sleep took the request from 1.783 to 1.467 s). Landed a vectorised zero_half kernel and a startup prefill warmup; accept.sh 19/0.
Keep-warm tick implemented and on by default with a 30 s post-request window: cold TTFT 1.45 -> 1.37 s, accept.sh 19/0. Cumulative since round 143: 1.60 -> 1.37 s.
Tile-sized prefill tail: no gain, and accept.sh caught it breaking prefix-cache determinism (18/1). Reverted to 19/0. Arithmetic reasoning about the snapshot boundary was wrong.

Inco Splash's 74 tok/s single-stream is only possible via speculative decoding. We already have an MTP head loaded and a QW_SPEC path that was off: measured 5/5, ~1.37x, byte-identical. But enabling it by default fails 4 accept.sh gates - the server's spec path diverges at char 5 on any request after the first. Reverted to opt-in. Fixing the cross-request state is the top item.

Fixed a real MTP-cache leak in reset_seq (single cache addressed by absolute pos, never reset per request), but it did not fix the 4 gates. Minimal repro shows the PLAIN path is nondeterministic on a 602-token prompt (3 different md5s) while spec is stable - so the reference itself is unreliable on long prompts.

Corrected round 148: the 'plain is nondeterministic' reading was inverted (that binary had spec on by default). Spec's real bug is prompt-dependent - byte-identical on a 300-token CLI case, diverges at char 5 on a 64-token raw-completion PIN case. Also found the oracle-parity gate is flaky (18/1 then 19/0 on the same tree). Spec stays opt-in, 19/0.

accept.sh's spec==plain gate compared two servers differing in two env vars (QW_PREFIX_SNAPSHOT), so its verdict was unattributable. Fixed to one variable; 19/0 with spec opt-in. Spec is NOT reproducible as broken on the PIN case standalone (218 everywhere). New lead: keepwarm_tick writes into scratch.logits, the sampler's buffer.

Found the real otps gap: aggregate throughput is flat with concurrency (13.55/12.43/16.81 at 1/2/4) while Splash gets 3.9x. Scheduler batches fine (127 passes x 4 rows) but a 4-row pass costs 3.44x a 1-row pass (132.2 vs 38.4 ms) instead of ~1x. Single-stream is already 78% of the bandwidth floor. Fixing row amortisation would give ~104 tok/s at 4 concurrent.

Corrected round 151: GEMM row amortisation is fine (gemm-bench flat 1->16 tokens; 4 rows from 1 sequence costs ~40 ms like 1 row). The excess is per-sequence work not batched across slots: 4 rows from 4 slots = 132.2 ms vs 66.9 ms from 1 sequence. That is why aggregate throughput is flat where Splash gets 3.9x.

QW_DISPATCH_HIST shows identical dispatch counts at 1 and 4 slots (1186 both, every kernel ratio 1.00) - the scheduler already fuses slots. So the problem is inside the non-GEMM kernels: each extra row costs 31 ms, about 4x more than linear, most likely because four slots' state/window/KV bases are scattered and coalescing is destroyed.

The 4-row cliff was thermal throttling (132.2 ms in a 30 s run vs 60.9 ms in a 12.9 s run), so rows do amortise. Wall time is mostly non-decode. With a short prompt (Splash's methodology) our 4-concurrent aggregate is 51.77 tok/s vs Splash's 170. Decisive: Splash's 74 tok/s single-stream exceeds the 33 tok/s bandwidth floor, so speculative decoding is a necessary condition for the otps objective, not an option.

FOUND AND FIXED the three-round spec mystery: QW_SPEC was tested for presence in three places (runner.rs spec_snap, engine.rs, gen.rs) and defaulting only engine.rs left the verify pass without its per-row snapshots, so a rejected draft corrupted the state. Unified into spec_enabled(). accept.sh 19/0 WITH SPEC ON BY DEFAULT. Single-stream otps 22.33 -> 36.20 (above the 33 tok/s bandwidth floor).

Confirmed spec's single-slot limit is architectural (documented at engine.rs:986-992): the MTP head keeps one k/v cache, forward2 hardcodes sequence 0 and commit_row copies into sequence 0's state. So concurrency never gets speculation, which is why aggregate is 51.8 vs Splash's 170. Roadmap: slot offset for the MTP cache (buffer already batch-sized), then a slot-aware verify, then a seq parameter on commit_row.

TILE=6 tested and reverted as inconclusive: it looked like a 1.8x regression at 512 tokens (median 23.74 vs 43.04) but re-running the SAME TILE=4 binary immediately gave 26.72/16.16 where it had just given 45.19/43.04/39.18, so machine load drifted mid-experiment and the A/B is void both ways. Tree clean, nothing unverified shipped. Machine noise is now a hard blocker on verifying any performance change; a performance A/B must be interleaved.

TILE=6 verified as a regression via interleaved A/B: TILE=4 won all 3 pairs by 1.16-1.45x while both columns drifted down together, proving pairing cancels drift. TILE stays 4, tree clean. Methodology now binding: all performance claims use interleaved paired A/B. Next target remains spec-for-concurrency (aggregate 51.8 vs Splash 170), whose first step is purely additive.

Landed step 1 of spec-for-concurrency with no kernel change, using the existing Dispatch::buf_offset to bind the MTP k/v caches per sequence; seq threaded through every call site but all pass 0, so accept.sh is 19/0 and behaviour is byte-identical. This earns nothing alone: forward2 and commit_row still hardcode sequence 0, so spec_ok stays limited to slot 0 until steps 2 and 3.

Steps 2 and 3 landed (forward2 and commit_row take a sequence; snapshot layout pinned sh as elements via snap_stride == TILE*2*sh) and spec_ok relaxed from slot 0 only to the unique decoding slot, with spec_warm fixed to use the request's own slot. accept.sh 19/0. Limitation stated plainly: this does not help the concurrent aggregate, since spec_ok still requires decoding == 1; multi-slot speculation needs a multi-sequence verify design.

Strategic correction: at n=1 spec there are no 1-row passes (every pass is a 4-row verify yielding 4.32 tokens) and at n=4 the pass is also 4 rows yielding exactly 4, so aggregate ~= single-stream (27.22 vs 34.84). The only lever is making a 4-row pass cost what a 1-row pass costs: 38.4 ms would give 104 tok/s aggregate. So the multi-sequence-verify redesign is unnecessary and row amortisation in the 4-row pass is the real target.

Batched pass row-scaling: 1 row 48.6-66.8 ms, 2 rows ~92, 4 rows 96-111, so entering the multi-row path costs a fixed step. Made the GEMM gate reachable for rows <= TILE and measured the GEMM at 642-686 ms vs the tile kernel's 61-131 ms for 4 rows - 5-10x worse, hypothesis refuted, reverted. The tile kernel is correct; the 4-row excess is its 4x MACs, and the 1-row pass is already 1.6x above the bandwidth floor, so it is not bandwidth-bound.

Zero-code measurement ruled out CPU/dispatch overhead: consecutive QW_STEP_TIME passes have a 0.00 ms median gap and the GPU is busy 99.1% of the span, so the 1-row pass's 48.6 ms is pure kernel time. That is 296 GB/s = 62% of the 481 GB/s achievable (67% including GDN traffic), so ~1.5x remains but it is inside the kernel's access pattern, not in scheduling, dispatch count or row amortisation.

bench --rows shows the isolated 497-linear sweep runs at 464 GB/s = 97% of peak and is insensitive to rows, so the GEMV is not the bottleneck. The real 1-row pass is 48.6 ms against a 31.0 ms sweep, leaving 17.6 ms (36%) spread over 689 non-GEMM dispatches at ~25 us each - latency, not bytes, since GDN traffic is only ~2.4 ms. Fusing those small kernels is the corrected target, and it explains why 4 rows are expensive: the GEMM is row-immune while this pile scales with rows.

Two corrections: encoder splitting is free (31.8 vs 31.7 ms), and a 1-row pass is 31.7 ms not 48.6, i.e. 455 GB/s = 94.5% of peak, so the 689 small dispatches are free and the round-164 fusion plan is withdrawn. Also QW_STEP_TIME does not log the spec path (only 2 samples), so the 4-row reading was unreliable; inferring from 40.5 tok/s, a spec pass is ~105 ms = 3.3x a 1-row pass, and it is one verify plus three MTP draft steps, so the draft head is the next thing to measure.

Instrumented the spec step's draft/verify split (previously discarded): median draft 7.2 ms (15%), verify 41.6 ms (85%), so the draft head is not the bottleneck and the verify's 4-row pass is only 1.31x a 1-row pass. A spec step costs 48.8 ms and yields ~2 tokens at 40.5 tok/s, so reaching Splash's 74 needs either acceptance 2->4 (2x) or verify 41.6->31.7 (1.31x). The ntok field is a position, not an acceptance count, so acceptance must be measured separately.

Acceptance is 1.93 of 3 drafts (48% of steps accept all three), 2.93 tokens per step. Using means rather than medians, a spec step is 51.2 ms so steady-state single-stream is 57.3 tok/s, not the harness-reported 40.5 - the gap is 0.91 s of wall outside the spec steps (prefill plus first-request overhead). So single-stream is 77% of Splash's 74, not 55%. The verify at 43.4 ms vs the 31.0 ms floor is the only remaining headroom. Methodology: rate metrics need means.

Aggregate steady state is 79.4 tok/s (47% of Splash's 170), not the 27.2 previously reported - that was a noisy reading. n=4 has spec off so passes are logged: 127 four-row passes at a 50.8 ms mean sum to 6.45 s of 8.71 s wall, leaving 2.26 s for prefills and overhead. The four-row pass is 1.60x the one-row pass and driving it to the 31.0 ms floor would give 130 tok/s. Both headline figures (single 77%, aggregate 47%) are much better than earlier reports.

Row-amortisation curve (spec off, means): 1 row 31.7 ms, 2 rows 44.2, 3 rows 48.1, 4 rows 50.8, so the second row costs 12.5 ms while the third and fourth cost only 3.9 and 2.7. The 1-row pass is already at the isolated sweep's 31.0 ms (94.5% bandwidth), so that 12.5 ms is the price of switching from q4_gemv_hx to K4_U4HX, whose bandwidth efficiency is lower. Lifting it would give ~121 tok/s aggregate.

bench --tokens shows the multi-row GEMM is NOT row-immune: the same 497 linears cost 27.0/46.4/61.5/75.5 ms per sweep at 1/2/3/4 tokens, i.e. 534/310/234/191 GB/s, with nearly linear marginal cost. So the row-amortisation failure is in the multi-row tile kernel K4_U4HX itself, whose bandwidth efficiency at four rows is 36% of the single-row kernel's. Both of the previous two rounds' intermediate claims are withdrawn. Next: read K4_U4HX and test whether small-out_f linears are starved because the grid falls from out_f to out_f/4 threadgroups.

Found K_Q4_GEMV_K3_U4 via bench --rows: at tokens=3 it runs at 30.5 ms = 472 GB/s, the bandwidth floor and twice the round-3 kernel's 235 GB/s, and is no worse at 1 token. The real multi-row pass uses K4_U4HX at 50.8 ms = 284 GB/s. Switching the multi-row path to that efficiency would take the aggregate from 78.8 to ~129 tok/s. Trap: K3_* are k=3 kernels unrolled over NK, so the tokens=4 result probably computed only 3 rows and must be verified before use.

Closed last round's lead: NK=3 is compile-time so the bench's 472 GB/s at tokens=4 was only 3 rows, and U4H vs U4HX A/B in the real path showed no gain (49.6/49.9 vs 47.9/49.2 ms). encode_tile's doc comment shows row blocking was already measured ~5% slower end-to-end over 8 interleaved pairs, because the bench's cache-hot x understates the traffic it removes and small-out_f linears leave the grid empty. Lesson: bench wins must be confirmed by an interleaved model A/B.

Corrected the n=4 wall accounting: decode 6.45 s (74%, 79.4 tok/s), prefill 1.16 s (13%, already fused into one 164-row pass), outside passes 1.10 s (13%); including prefill 67.3 and end-to-end 58.8 tok/s. So prefill concurrency is not a missing feature, and with 74% of time in decode and no usable kernel lever left, the remaining distance to Splash has no untested lever.

Killed the multi-slot shared verify plan by measuring the far end of the row curve: 4 rows 50.8 ms (78.8 tok/s), 8 rows 361.2 ms (22.1), 16 rows 384.9 ms (41.6). There is a cliff above TILE=4 because rows>4 takes the grid-mapped path. So a 16-row verify would give 41.6 tok/s, worse than today's 78.8. Four tokens per pass is the architectural ceiling; going higher needs the rows>4 path rewritten.

Settled TILE with arithmetic reproducing the measurement: with the measured acceptance survival function, TILE=2 gives 45.3 tok/s, TILE=3 53.1, TILE=4 57.2 - and 57.2 matches the measured value exactly, explaining TILE=6's loss too. So single-stream 57 tok/s is the mathematical consequence of TILE=4 plus 1.93 acceptance, not a defect; the only ways up are a 43.4->31.8 ms verify (which would give exactly Splash's 74) or higher acceptance.

Added the NK=4 member of the U4 family (one output row per threadgroup, full out_f parallelism) and pointed TILE=4 at it. It passed correctness exactly but the interleaved A/B showed 63.8 ms vs U4HX's 52.0 ms on the real 4-row pass - 23% slower - so it is reverted. Second confirmation that the bench's cache-hot x makes it unable to predict model behaviour; U4HX is already the fastest four-row kernel.

Consolidated verification on clean HEAD: cold TTFT 1749 ms (first request after ready, excludes model load), warm 34/19 ms, single-stream 57.3 tok/s, aggregate 79.4 (decode only). Labelled the llama.cpp/Ollama comparison as historical rather than fresh. No code changes; objective still not met on the otps half.

Re-measured TTFT fresh against both competitors and corrected my own claim: ours 1749 ms cold / 34-19 ms warm, llama.cpp 863 / 93-88, Ollama 2131 / 71-73. Warm comfortably beats both (2.6-4.6x vs llama.cpp), but cold is 2.03x SLOWER than llama.cpp - my earlier '10 per cent behind' was wrong. So the TTFT half is only half met (warm), not fully met as I had been recording.

Decomposed cold TTFT: prefill 761.5 ms (63%), a 375 ms CPU-side gap between prefill and decode with no pass running (31%), decode 49.6 ms (4%). Eliminating the gap would give 826 ms, beating llama.cpp's 863 ms. Lowest-risk target found so far - no kernel, no rows>4 path, cannot affect warm TTFT.

Narrowed the 357-375 ms cold-TTFT gap but did not locate it. Ruled out logits_row+argmax (0.5 ms), the already-fixed per-row sampling, and the prefix snapshot (disabled). A pipeline-compile hypothesis persists across requests but the test was confounded by shared prefixes. Location is certain (between the prefill pass and the tail pass); cause is not. Instrumentation reverted to keep the verified tree intact.

Refuted the tail-pipeline-compile hypothesis for the 357 ms cold gap: adding a 4-row warmup gave median 1397 ms vs 1401 without - no improvement, reverted. Also found cold TTFT readings range 1201-1749 ms (±19%), so my round-180 '2.03x slower than llama.cpp' sat at the noisy high end; ~1400 vs 863 is about 1.6x. Cold gap cause still unlocated.

next: Refuted the pipeline-compile hypothesis for the 357 ms cold-TTFT gap. The reasoning was that the server's startup warmup runs 64-row passes, which take the grid-mapped path and never the four-row tile path (K4_U4HX), so that pipeline would be compiled during the client's first request. I added a four-row tail-shaped pass to the existing warmup and A/B'd it interleaved over three pairs on cold TTFT: without it 1401, 1393, 1401 ms (median 1401); with it 1539, 1393, 1397 ms (median 1397). No improvement, so the hypothesis is refuted and the change is reverted; tree clean. IMPORTANT OBSERVATION ABOUT THE METRIC ITSELF: across this session the cold TTFT readings are 1201, 1236, 1749, 1393, 1401, 1397 and 1539 ms - a range of 1201 to 1749, about plus or minus 19 per cent. Two consequences. First, cold TTFT is a very noisy metric here and no change smaller than roughly 20 per cent can be judged from a single measurement, so any future work on it needs interleaved paired runs like the ones above. Second, my round-180 headline of 1749 ms against llama.cpp's 863 ms, quoted as 2.03x, sits at the noisy high end; the more defensible statement is about 1400 ms against 863 ms, roughly 1.6x. So the cold gap is real but smaller than I first reported, and the correction flows in the user's favour. The 357 ms gap's cause is still not located. Now excluded: logits_row plus argmax at 0.5 ms, the per-row sampling that was already fixed, the prefix snapshot which is disabled, and this round the tail pipeline compile. OBJECTIVE STATUS: warm TTFT met (2.6-4.6x faster than llama.cpp), cold TTFT not met (roughly 1.6x slower than llama.cpp, though still faster than Ollama), otps 57.3 single (77 per cent of Splash) and 79.4 aggregate (46 per cent). The delivered tree remains exactly the state verified at round 180 with accept.sh 19 passed / 0 failed. Note the working tree has untracked stock/ files belonging to the user that must not be touched.
goal: raise single-decoder throughput target from 40 to 50 tok/s

open_issues.summary: accept.sh's `spec==plain: byte-identical over 300 tokens` gate FAILED once (230 of 300 tokens differ, first at 68) during this round's acceptance run, having passed 12/12 earlier in the same session. Not reproducible deterministically: 7 further plain/spec pairs on the same prompt were byte-identical (3 plain runs identical to each other, 4 spec runs identical to each other and to plain), including one pair run in exactly accept.sh's order (verify + check first).

evidence.observed_failure: accept.sh: 1 failure in 6 gate executions this session
evidence.not_reproduced: plain1==plain2==plain3, spec1==spec2==spec3==spec4, plain==spec in 3 independent pairs, and again after verify+check

hypotheses: near-tie argmax: the batched verify computes 4 rows in one GEMV (q4_gemv_k4_u4hx) whose accumulation order differs from the single-row kernel (q4_gemv_hx), so when the top-2 logits are within rounding, spec and plain may legitimately choose different tokens

a race in the speculative path under load (the failure occurred on a hot, heavily loaded machine immediately after the verify and GEMV-reference gates); the prefill warms the MTP head's state with one mtp_step per prompt token, the most likely place for a timing-sensitive read
open_issues.next: run the pair N>=10 times on a hot machine and count; if the tie hypothesis holds, compare the top-2 logit margins near the divergence point; if it is a race, instrument command-buffer completion in the mtp_step prefill loop
